How should a Houston owner approach a fast sale?

Three paths exist: a broker listing, a private sale, or a cash purchase. Houston is a market of its own, with 2,397,315 residents in the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate, so prices swing from street to street.

Owners occupy only 42.1% of Houston homes, so landlords, investors and first-time buyers all bid for houses. A cash proposal suits a house with deferred upkeep, storm damage, a tenant or a cloudy title. A listing fits a house that shows well.

  • Pull the deed and any survey, and find out whether your street has deed restrictions.
  • Check which appraisal district and taxing units cover the address.
  • Gather two written offers, each stating a closing date.

What do Houston's history and land rules mean for a seller?

Houston began on August 30, 1836, when two brothers advertised the Town of Houston. The Handbook of Texas says it became the state's largest city by 1930, that the Ship Channel opened in 1914, and that annexations in the late 1940s and later decades took it to 627 square miles by 2015. The Census Bureau lists 640.44 square miles of land for 2020.

The detail that matters most is the lack of zoning. The Handbook says voters rejected it and that subdivision deed restrictions steer most construction. Those private restrictions can limit what you build and how a lot is used, so read yours and disclose them to the buyer.

The city's planning department adds that a plat, a surveyed map of the lot, is required before building permits. It notes that single-family classification can include a duplex or a garage apartment under 900 square feet unless the deed restrictions forbid it. Houston also reviews plats in an area about five miles beyond its limits, where its permit and inspection rules do not apply.

What does the Census say about Houston owners and renters?

QuickFacts shows a $277,800 midpoint home value for 2020 to 2024, with $2,240 in monthly costs for owners who carry a mortgage. The city has 930,404 households.

A median rent of $1,361 alongside that ownership rate marks a deep rental market. That depth helps a landlord selling a rental, yet anyone with a tenant should read the lease and the notice rules before accepting an offer.

How does the Harris Central Appraisal District affect a sale?

The Harris Central Appraisal District values most Houston property for tax, and its site lets owners file protests, renditions and homestead exemptions online. It also offers an Exemption Wizard and a deed protection feature that lets you register your home with the Harris County Clerk to help guard against deed fraud.

The Comptroller's calendar gives the yearly beat. Appraisals are pegged to January 1. Homestead notices start about April 1, and the protest deadline is May 15 or 30 days past the notice, whichever is later. If the board's ruling disappoints, an owner can take the case to district court or binding arbitration, or to the State Office of Administrative Hearings once the board value passes $1,000,000. Appealing owners generally still pay the undisputed part of the tax on time.

  • Once the exemption is active, a homestead's appraised value can rise no more than 10% in a year.
  • Heirs missing from the recorded deed must supply an ownership affidavit, the death certificate and a recent utility bill to get the exemption.
  • A new owner who closes after January 1 can apply for the exemption for what remains of that year when the seller never did.

Check your tax bill to confirm which district and taxing units cover your parcel.

Which Houston neighborhoods and job centers shape what buyers want?

The Handbook of Texas traces Houston's spread through developer-built suburbs: Houston Heights and Pasadena in 1892, Bellaire in 1911, West University Place in 1919, and River Oaks in the mid-1920s. Those names still anchor listing descriptions, and buyers often search by them, though you should check whether a given address sits inside the city or in a separate municipality.

Jobs pull buyers toward particular corridors. The Handbook calls the Texas Medical Center the world's largest medical complex, with about 106,000 employees in 2016, and describes the Ship Channel refineries and petrochemical plants that made Houston an energy capital. Add a 27.2-minute average commute from QuickFacts and a drive-time pitch becomes part of your selling story: tell buyers how long it takes to reach the medical center, downtown or the channel from your front door.

Schools matter too. The Handbook says a free school system began in 1877 and became the Houston Independent School District in 1924. Confirm which district serves your address before you list, and say so in the listing.

Does flood history matter when selling in Houston?

Yes. Buyers and lenders ask about it. The Handbook of Texas describes paving and rapid runoff as sources of flooding, and says severe floods in 1929 and 1935 led to the Harris County Flood Control District and later to the Addicks and Barker reservoirs.

The city's planning department says flood mitigation, drainage, water and sewer are outside the Planning Commission's plat review, so a plat does not settle a house's flood risk. Ask the city and the county for flood records on your address, and collect repair records and insurance claims to share with buyers.

The Handbook also cites about 48 inches of yearly rainfall, high humidity and summer averages near 94 degrees, conditions that wear on roofs, siding and air conditioning. A cash buyer will take storm damage as is, and a clear paper trail helps both sides agree on a price.

What do tenants, heirs and tax debt change in a Houston sale?

Renters first: the usual written notice to vacate is three days unless the lease sets another period, and an eviction suit starts in justice court. The State Law Library puts the hearing 10 to 21 days after filing. Appeals to county court must come within five days of the judgment, and the writ of possession waits six days after final judgment.

Inherited house? The state repealed its inheritance tax effective September 1, 2015, according to a Comptroller notice. A probate case should open within four years of a death. The small estate affidavit route is reserved for estates of up to $75,000 apart from the homestead.

If taxes are behind, the lien that attached on January 1 stays on the house, and penalty and interest start February 1. A taxing unit can sue and sell the property at auction. County clerks record deeds, and a recorded plat can be requested from the Harris County Clerk's records office using the contact details on the city's plat page.

More questions about Houston, TX

How big is Houston?

Census figures: 640.44 square miles of land in 2020, 2,397,315 residents in 2025. Confirm the county and appraisal district for your own address before relying on a tax figure.

Does Houston zone land?

No citywide zoning exists. The Handbook of Texas says voters rejected it. Private deed restrictions and the city's plat and permit rules still apply, so read your restrictions.

Can I protest my Houston property value?

Yes. Go to the appraisal review board by May 15, or up to 30 days after your notice arrives if that is later. The Harris Central Appraisal District site offers online filing.

Where do I find the plat for my lot?

Plats are filed with the Harris County Clerk's records office after approval. The city's planning site also has a map viewer and a Plat Tracker for searching by address.

Does $277,800 predict my sale price?

It is a midpoint for the whole city in the 2020 to 2024 survey. Rely on written offers or an appraisal for your own house.

What makes San Antonio different from a small town sale?

San Antonio sits at the head of the San Antonio River in Bexar County, and its reach across the region is shaped by three interstates and two loops.

The Texas State Historical Association points to Interstate 10 running east and west, Interstates 35 and 37 running north and south, plus Loop 410, State Loop 1604, the international airport and daily Amtrak service. The Handbook describes about three centuries of history, starting with a presidio, a town and five Franciscan missions strung along the river, and notes that San Antonio was the biggest city in Texas through the later 1800s. Nicknames such as Alamo City, River City and Military City, U.S.A. reflect that story. The Handbook also lists the international airport and Stinson Airport among the facilities serving the city. Size is the practical lesson for a seller, because blocks inside and outside the loops can differ enormously in age, price and commute.

  • Compare recent sales within a mile or two of your house, not citywide numbers.
  • Note whether your house lies inside Loop 410, between the loops or beyond 1604.
  • Look at flood maps if the lot is close to the river or a creek.

Which way of selling fits a San Antonio house?

A broker listing rewards a sound house and patience, and an investor sale rewards a house needing work or a firm deadline.

A city this big produces a wide range of buyers and bids. Retail sales often yield the top figure and bring inspections, showings and lender conditions along. An owner sale skips the commission and loads marketing and paperwork on you. Investors buy as-is on a date you set, with the number trimmed for repair and resale expense. Compare each written bid by what you net after costs.

  • Listing: updated house, flexible date.
  • Investor sale: lien, empty inherited house or tenant trouble.
  • Before signing, read who pays title, recording and repair credits.

Who appraises and bills property tax in San Antonio?

Two offices touch your bill: BCAD decides the value, and the Bexar County Tax Assessor-Collector collects.

BCAD's front page states that it takes no tax payments and refers payment questions to the assessor-collector. A banner there says 2026 notices went to new owners and to owners whose value rose $1,000 or more, and adds that a protest needs no notice. The valuation date is January 1 statewide, bills arrive in October and the payment deadline is January 31. Every taxing unit on your lot sets a rate of its own.

Which dates should a San Antonio owner keep in mind?

Five milestones frame the year for a Bexar County owner.

Texas property tax schedule as it applies to Bexar County owners (Texas Comptroller)
DateWhat it means
January 1Valuation date and lien date
April 30Common exemption filing cutoff
May 15Usual protest deadline
July 20Review board approves appraisal records
September 29Deadline for most units to adopt rates
February 1Delinquency begins on unpaid taxes

The full list is on the Comptroller calendar.

How do I handle back taxes before selling in San Antonio?

Get the amount due from the Bexar County Tax Assessor-Collector and plan to settle it by closing, since the lien does not leave with you.

Delinquency opens at 6 percent penalty plus 1 percent interest in February and reaches a 12 percent penalty in July while interest continues. Collection lawyers can add up to a fifth more. Homestead owners may request an installment plan, which some offices extend to 36 months. A lawsuit can lead to a tax sale, and surplus proceeds can be claimed by the former owner for two years.

  • While appealing a value, pay at least the part nobody disputes.
  • Save each receipt.
  • Let the closer know about any plan.

What homestead relief could a San Antonio owner claim?

Owners can claim the residence homestead exemption, with added relief for age, disability or veteran status.

Schools take $140,000 off a homestead and a further $60,000 off for seniors and the disabled. A taxing unit may add its own exemption of up to 20 percent of value, floor $5,000. A yearly cap of 10 percent limits growth in a homestead's appraised value. Veterans receive $5,000 to $12,000 by rating, and a full 100 percent rating gives a total homestead exemption. Heirs missing from the recorded deed show an affidavit, a death certificate and a recent utility bill.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy San Antonio houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What do squatters and holdover occupants mean for a San Antonio sale?

Someone who stays after being told to go can be removed by a justice court case or, narrowly, by a request to the sheriff or constable under Property Code chapter 24B.

That shortcut requires a refusal to leave, a property that was closed to the public at entry, no pending suit between the two of you, and an occupant who is no relative and no past or present tenant. Wrongful removal exposes the owner to suit. Tenants usually get three days' notice, and a writ of possession waits for judgment plus six days.

How is a San Antonio deed recorded?

Deeds for Bexar County land are filed with the clerk, and a notary or similar officer must attest the signature first.

The clerk manual puts the first page at $5.00 and later pages at $4.00, plus other records fees. The title company usually files.

What can a Bexar County heir do with an inherited house?

Heirs have several routes to clear title, and the right one depends on what the owner left behind and what the house owes.

With a will, the executor or an heir files it for probate, which Texas permits for four years after death. If no administration is needed, a muniment of title order and the will go on record with the county clerk. Without a will, a small estate affidavit may work for modest estates. A deed that names a beneficiary and was recorded before the owner's death moves the house outside probate, and a Lady Bird deed lets the owner keep selling rights while alive. Expect the closer to ask for whichever paper applies.

  • Get certified copies of the death certificate.
  • Find the last recorded deed for the parcel.
  • Ask the appraisal district about the homestead exemption before the next tax year.
You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

How does a Texas foreclosure reach a San Antonio house?

Most Texas mortgages allow a sale without a court case, which makes the timeline short.

Federal rules generally hold a servicer back until a home loan is more than 120 days behind. A default notice then opens a 20 day period to bring the loan current, and the sale notice must be sent, posted at the courthouse and filed with the clerk at least 21 days before the auction. The auction itself takes place on a first Tuesday, with the first Wednesday used if that Tuesday is January 1 or July 4. Selling before that date can preserve equity and spare you a foreclosure on your record.

More questions about San Antonio, TX

Which office collects San Antonio property tax?

The Bexar County Tax Assessor-Collector. The Bexar Central Appraisal District says it does not accept payments.

Do I need a notice to protest my value in San Antonio?

No. The Bexar Central Appraisal District says you do not need a notice to submit a protest. Check your notice for the cutoff, which most years falls in mid May.

What homestead exemption do school districts give?

A $140,000 deduction from value, with $60,000 more for owners who are seniors or disabled.

What happens to the lien when a San Antonio house sells?

It remains on the house, so any old tax is deducted at closing.

When do foreclosure auctions occur near San Antonio?

On a first Tuesday, during daytime hours, after a sale notice at least three weeks earlier.

How can a Dallas owner get a house sold in a hurry?

An owner in Dallas can put the home on the market with an agent, run the sale yourself, or sell directly to a cash buyer. The first reaches the most buyers, the second saves commission, and the third trims the timeline.

Whichever you pick, collect the vesting deed, each lender's latest statement, tax bills for every taxing unit and any city notices. With those, you can judge offers by what lands in your account.

  • Confirm whose name is on the deed.
  • Request payoff letters for every lien.

How did railroads, annexation and growth shape Dallas housing?

The pattern traces to a trading post and two railroads. The Handbook of Texas says John Neely Bryan settled near a Trinity River ford in November 1841, the town charter came in 1856, and the Houston and Texas Central and the Texas and Pacific arrived in 1872 and 1873, making Dallas an early rail crossroads.

East Dallas was annexed on January 1, 1890, when Dallas ranked as the largest Texas city with 38,067 residents, and Oak Cliff joined in 1904. The first residential subdivision, the Cedars, appeared south of downtown in the 1880s, and later building ran mostly north and east. Highland Park, a premier suburb, incorporated in 1913 and University Park in 1924, and both fought Dallas over annexation into the 1940s.

Postwar growth added aviation and electronics employers, the Dallas Market Center after 1957, and Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport in 1974. By the entry's 2019 estimate the city held 2.63 million people. A house built in the 1920s near Swiss Avenue and a 1990s suburb home answer very different inspection questions, so describe your own house by era.

Which historic districts and landmarks affect Dallas sellers?

Some streets carry landmark rules. The same entry says the city's Landmark Commission has designated buildings and neighborhoods including Swiss Avenue, Munger Place, South Boulevard-Park Row and State-Thomas, and calls Fair Park the largest Art Deco district in the world.

If the house sits in a designated area, ask the city what review applies to exterior work before a buyer plans changes. Preservation Dallas, which began in the 1970s as the Historic Preservation League, is another place owners go for guidance. Deep Ellum storefronts from the 1920s and the West End brick warehouses show how older commercial blocks were adapted, which can lift interest in nearby homes.

Which county offices handle a Dallas property sale?

Most of Dallas sits in Dallas County, where the County Clerk's Recording Division handles deeds and liens. Its page lists the Records Building at 500 Elm Street, Suite 2100, and says the office records roughly 400,000 documents a year.

Part of the city extends into Collin, Denton, Kaufman and Rockwall counties, so confirm which clerk holds your parcel.

How do Dallas property taxes work at a sale?

Dallas bills come from the county, the city, the school system and other local units. The Comptroller's deadline calendar says each year's value is fixed on January 1, the day a lien attaches, and protests are generally due by mid-May.

Bills go out near October 1 and turn delinquent after January 31. Since whoever owns the house on January 1 stays liable, have the title company explain how each unit's bill is handled at closing. For relief, school districts give a $140,000 homestead exemption, and seniors and disabled owners receive an extra $60,000 plus a school tax ceiling. Ask the county appraisal district which units add a local exemption.

What should a buyer in Dallas know about schools, roads and parks?

Commute and district are the first questions. The Handbook says Interstate highways 20, 30, 35 and 45 cross the city, the Dallas Independent School District enrolls more than 155,000 students, and 406 parks cover about 50,000 acres, anchored by White Rock Lake, Bachman Lake and Lake Cliff.

Southern Methodist University dates to 1911, UT Southwestern Medical School to 1943, and a University of North Texas campus opened in South Dallas in 2007. The Arts District covers 68 acres, and Klyde Warren Park sits over Woodall Rodgers Freeway. Confirm school boundaries for a specific address with the district, not by neighborhood name.

What if a Dallas house is behind on its mortgage?

A lender normally cannot start foreclosure on a home loan until it is 120 days late. You then get 20 days after the default notice, and the sale notice goes out three weeks or more ahead of a first-Tuesday auction at the area the commissioners court designates.

Any money above the debt goes to junior lienholders and then to you, and a deficiency claim must be filed within two years. A sale before the auction date lets you set the price and the closing date. Ask your servicer for the payoff and the scheduled sale date.

How does the City of Dallas handle code concerns and city services?

The city runs a 311 service, and its Planning and Development site lists code concerns, missed garbage, street repair, loose animals and water line locates among frequently requested items. The city's Code Compliance department and permitting pages sit on the same site.

Per the Handbook, Dallas operates under a council-manager form adopted in 1930, with fourteen single-member districts and a mayor elected at large since a 1992 amendment. The useful step is to check for open code complaints or unpermitted work at the address, then fix or disclose them before listing. Public library branches, numbering twenty-nine in the entry, and the Dallas Zoo and Arboretum are also quality-of-life points buyers like to see in a description.

Can I rent a Dallas house instead of selling?

You can, though short-term rentals carry city registration and hotel occupancy tax rules. The City of Dallas lists Short-Term Rentals (HOT) registration among its licenses, so check the current requirements before you advertise.

A long-term tenant can be removed only through a justice court eviction suit, and the court cannot issue a writ of possession for six days after judgment. If you sell while the lease is active, buyers will want the lease and rent history.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

More questions about Dallas, TX

How long does a Dallas closing usually take?

Plan on a few weeks for a cash sale and longer when a buyer needs financing and an appraisal. Payoff letters and a title search set the minimum, and a lien or probate issue can stretch it.

Which clerk records a deed for a Dallas house?

The clerk for the county where the parcel lies, which is Dallas County for most addresses. A few Dallas parcels lie in Collin, Denton, Kaufman or Rockwall counties, and those clerks keep their own records. Bring photo ID if you file a conveyance in person.

Are taxes split at a Dallas closing?

Closings normally divide the year's bill between seller and buyer. The January 1 lien travels with the house, so the title company checks every taxing unit and holds back money for anything unpaid.

Can I protest my Dallas appraisal before selling?

Yes, the cutoff is mid-May or 30 days after your notice arrives, whichever is later. A lower value cuts the bill the buyer inherits, though a protest does not by itself change the sale price.

What if a Dallas house has a lien or back taxes?

The payoff is paid from sale funds or cleared before closing. Delinquent taxes cannot be skipped because the lien follows the property. Request a payoff list from the title company so you know the true net.

Which fast-sale routes work for a Fort Worth house?

A Fort Worth owner can take a cash offer, list with an agent, or sell to an investor who plans to renovate. A cash sale trades some price for speed and certainty, and a listing trades time for a wider pool of buyers.

The city is large and varied. The city fact sheet counts 334,230 households, 56.7 percent of them owner occupied, and says single-family homes cover 24.1 percent of the land. That mix means a bungalow near downtown, a ranch house on the far north side and a newer subdivision near Alliance are three different sales with three different buyer pools.   • Agent listing: staging, photos, showings, and repair negotiation after the inspection.
  • Investor purchase: common for dated homes, rentals with tenants, or houses with code or foundation concerns.

Whatever route you pick, request an itemized estimate of what you will walk away with.

What does Fort Worth's size mean for a seller?

Fort Worth is a large city that, per the city population page, passed one million residents. Its fact sheet calls it the 11th largest city in the nation and the fastest-growing large city, with a gain of 170,237 people between 2010 and 2020.

The city history page traces the town to a frontier outpost on the Trinity River. It lists a first street car line in 1876, a first telephone exchange in 1881 and the first Fat Stock Show in 1886. The stock show and rodeo continues today and the fact sheet says it draws over 1.2 million visitors a year. The Stockyards National Historic District, the Kimbell and Modern art museums and the zoo sit on the same list of attractions, which helps explain why close-in neighborhoods hold their appeal.

Planners expect more growth: the fact sheet projects a population of 1,306,400 by 2050. A seller benefits when demand is steady, but new construction on vacant land, which makes up 37.6 percent of the city's land use, also gives buyers alternatives to your house.

How do jobs, schools and weather shape the market?

Large employers anchor demand. The city lists American Airlines, Lockheed Martin, the Fort Worth Joint Reserve Base, Alcon, Bell Flight, BNSF Railway, JPS Health Network, Tarrant County College and the Fort Worth school district among the biggest. A house close to one of those workplaces or campuses should say so in its listing.

The city says it is served by 13 independent school districts, so the district name on a house matters as much as the city name. Check the district for your exact address with the district boundary tools before you advertise. Universities in the city include Texas Christian University, Texas Wesleyan, Texas A&M and a UT Arlington campus.

The fact sheet reports about 42 inches of annual rain, an average high of 77 degrees, an average low of 54 and roughly 2 inches of snow. Weather wear on a roof and gutters is worth checking before you list. Fort Worth also lies over the Barnett Shale, though that is a gas field and seldom affects a home sale.

What does a Fort Worth seller owe in property tax at closing?

Whatever is unpaid for the year stays attached to the house, whoever owns it when the bill arrives. Ask the county tax office for a statement showing each unit's share, because school, county, city and special district bills differ by address. The Comptroller's payment page explains that late charges start in February and climb through the summer.

Do Fort Worth exemptions go with me when I move?

Mostly no. Your homestead exemption ends with your ownership. The exception is the school tax ceiling for older or disabled owners, which the Comptroller's limits page says can carry over in proportion to a new Texas homestead.

  • Homestead appraisals are capped at a 10 percent yearly increase once the exemption is first claimed.
  • A local taxing unit may adopt its own exemption of up to 20 percent of value.
  • Disabled veterans may receive partial or full relief on the home.

Tell the appraisal district about the sale so your account is closed correctly.

What if the Fort Worth house is inherited, in default, or rented?

Each situation has a clear route. For an heir, the State Law Library describes a muniment of title that can pass a house when no administration is needed. For a borrower behind on payments, its foreclosure guide says a servicer generally waits until the loan is more than 120 days late, and a notice of default carries time to cure. That window leaves room to sell rather than lose the house; see the guide.

For a rented house, many buyers will take the property with the lease intact, which can spare you an eviction. If you need it empty, the eviction guide outlines the written notice and justice court steps.

The county clerk where the land sits. Your closing agent usually does the filing and the fee comes from closing funds, so check the settlement statement. A notary or similar officer must acknowledge the deed, per the county clerk manual.

  • Order a payoff letter from your lender.
  • Locate the last recorded deed and any releases of old liens.
  • Have a lien search done for judgments or tax liens.
  • Leave keys, openers and warranty papers for the buyer.

What local features add to a Fort Worth sale?

Parks and open space are a strong draw. The city says its parks department maintains 300 parks covering 13,000 acres, and the Fort Worth Nature Center and Refuge spans 3,621 acres with more than 20 miles of trails. The same fact sheet lists three public swimming pools or spray grounds, three golf courses and five skate parks.

Travel is another point. Dallas/Fort Worth International sits among the city's airports along with Alliance, Meacham and Spinks. The city also lists a $700 million convention center expansion and a Texas A&M campus at the site of the Texas A&M law school as major projects. Large projects like these can shift traffic and nearby demand over several years, so ask a local agent or the city planning office what is under way near your street before you set a price. Mention the nearest park, trail or transit route in your listing, and keep any recent upgrades on hand for the buyer.

More questions about Fort Worth, TX

Is a sale possible in Fort Worth while a mortgage is open?

Yes. Your lender is paid first at the closing table and the remainder is yours. Request a payoff letter that stays valid through your closing date.

Which clerk records my Fort Worth deed?

The clerk for the county that holds the lot. Your tax bill names the county, so check it before you file.

Must I fix things before a cash sale in Fort Worth?

No, as-is buyers take the house in its current state. Roof, foundation and plumbing issues lower the offer, so set it beside a listing net after repairs.

Who pays unpaid Fort Worth property tax at a sale?

The closing agent clears the balance from your proceeds. Ask the county tax office for a statement before you sign.

Can a Fort Worth rental be sold with the tenant inside?

Yes. Many buyers accept the lease. If you want the house empty, written notice and a justice court case come first.

Which sale routes suit an Austin owner who needs to move quickly?

Austin owners generally choose between a standard listing, a self-managed sale and a straight cash purchase. A cash buyer closes on a date you pick and buys the property in whatever state it is in, whereas a listing depends on showings, appraisals and the next buyer's financing.

Prices run high. The Census Bureau's 2020-2024 figures put a typical owned home at $555,300, and only 43.4 percent of households own the home they occupy. With so many renters, plenty of Austin houses have been rentals or could become one, which affects what an investor will pay and how fast the deal can move.

  • Standard listing: fits an updated house priced near its closest comparable sales, with weeks to spare for showings and a buyer's lender.
  • Self-managed sale: you handle pricing, contracts and negotiation, and a title company still runs the closing.
  • Cash purchase: fits deferred maintenance, an inherited house, a tenant who is staying, or a hard deadline.

What shaped Austin's neighborhoods, and why would a buyer care?

The city was platted in 1839 as the capital of the young Republic of Texas, and the housing here reflects layers of growth from that first grid to the chip-making boom. Commissioners bought 7,735 acres along the Colorado River that included the hamlet of Waterloo, then platted a 640-acre grid between Waller Creek on the east and Shoal Creek on the west, split by Congress Avenue.

The city won the statewide vote to stay the capital in 1872, and the University of Texas was chosen as its site in 1881. Dams on the Colorado River in 1940 and 1941 ended the flooding that had ravaged the town and created Lake Austin and Lake Travis. High technology took off after IBM located here in 1967, followed by Texas Instruments in 1969 and Motorola in 1974.

Fast growth set off resistance by the 1970s. Neighborhood groups, more than 150 by 1983, fought apartment complexes and clogged roads, and environmental ordinances protected creeks, lakes and wooded hills. A seller with an addition built without a permit, or a lot beside a creek, should expect questions from a buyer's inspector.

Where does Austin sit on the map, and what do its creeks and lakes mean for a house?

Austin sits where the Hill Country and the Edwards Plateau meet the Colorado River, on Interstate 35 in central Travis County. The original 640-acre town ran from the river up to Capitol Square between Waller Creek and Shoal Creek, and the incorporated area has grown far past that: from about 31 square miles in 1940 to 225.40 square miles by 1990, and a land area of 319.94 square miles in 2020.

Water shaped the place. Tom Miller Dam, finished in 1940, formed Lake Austin, and Mansfield Dam followed in 1941 to hold back Lake Travis. The Handbook of Texas credits the dams with ending the floods that had hit the town as recently as 1935. The city acquired the spring-fed Barton Springs pool in 1918, and a downtown lake was impounded in 1960. Buyers know the waterways, so a house near a creek or on one of the lakes may draw questions about flood exposure that a house on higher ground will not.

Bergstrom Air Force Base, which began as an Army air base in 1942, stayed open until 1993, and a new convention center opened in 1992. State government, the university and technology employers have anchored the local economy since the mid-twentieth century.

How large and how costly is the Austin housing market?

Austin's July 2025 population estimate is 1,002,632, about 4.6 percent higher than the 958,151 baseline for April 2020. The 2010 Census counted 790,390.

About 78.8 percent of residents stayed at the same address over the prior year, and 59.6 percent of adults 25 or older have finished a bachelor's degree or more. The average commute is 23.7 minutes.

How do Austin's short-term rental licenses work for a seller?

A license belongs to its holder and cannot be passed on, so a buyer who wants nightly guests must apply for a fresh one. The city confirms that short-term rental operating licenses are non-transferable.

In February 2025 Council made short-term rental a secondary use on residential property in every zoning district for anyone holding a license. Changes in October 2025 stretched each license to two years and dropped the occupancy certificate and insurance proof for new applicants and renewals. Tenants may now run one with the landlord's permission.

  • One person may run two units on a single-family site, and any more must be 1,000 feet apart.
  • On multifamily sites the cap is the larger of one unit or a tenth of the units.
  • A local contact must be in Travis, Williamson, Hays, Bastrop or Caldwell County and reachable within two hours.
  • Properties within 100 feet receive written notice of that contact at issuance and renewal.
  • Since July 1, 2026, booking platforms must show license numbers and pull unlicensed listings when the city asks.

Land in the extraterritorial jurisdiction needs no city license or local hotel tax, so check the jurisdiction map on the city's short-term rental page before telling a buyer what is allowed.

How do homestead exemptions and the appraisal cap affect an Austin sale?

If you live in the house, your taxable value is probably below the market value a buyer sees on the listing. Texas school districts exempt $140,000 of a homestead, and the appraised value of a homestead cannot rise more than 10 percent a year beyond new improvements.

That cap follows the owner who claimed the exemption, so an investor starts without it. Have the title company work out the buyer's first full-year tax bill so nothing in the contract is a surprise. Owners past 65 or with a disability also receive $60,000 more in school exemption and a school tax ceiling that can transfer to a new Texas homestead.

Travis County's tax office explains that the Travis Central Appraisal District grants exemptions while the tax office collects bills; its tax breaks page links to each one. The Comptroller's limitations page covers the cap and the ceiling.

What steps and paperwork close an Austin sale?

The deed is the closing document. It must be acknowledged before a notary, or sworn before two witnesses, before the county clerk will record it.

  1. Collect your deed, payoff letters and the latest tax statement.
  2. Request a payoff for any lien, since each year's tax lien attaches January 1.
  3. Check which county records the deed for your parcel, because the city is large.
  4. Sign the settlement papers and deed, and let the title company file the deed.

An inherited house adds a title question: an executor's deed, a muniment of title order or an affidavit of heirship. The last is a sworn statement that no law makes a third party accept, so ask early which one the title insurer will honor.

How should I compare offers on an Austin house?

Compare what lands in your account and when, not the headline figure. A higher price loaded with repair credits, a long financing window and a commission can net less than a lower cash bid with a firm date.

Ask each buyer how they treat tenants, unpermitted work and open code complaints, and whether the bid survives an inspection. Note each deadline in writing and choose the offer that clears your payoff and fits your move.

More questions about Austin, TX

Can an Austin short-term rental license be handed to the new owner?

No. The city says operating licenses cannot be transferred, so a buyer must apply for a new one. Give the buyer your license history so the application goes smoothly.

Is Austin in Travis County?

Austin is the Travis County seat, and the city sits in the central part of the county. Check your tax bill for the county of record on your parcel, since it decides which clerk files the deed.

Does my homestead tax cap pass to the person who buys my Austin house?

No. The cap starts the January after an owner first qualifies for the exemption, so a buyer who moves in and applies starts a new one. A buyer who rents the house out cannot claim it.

What if my Austin house has unpaid property taxes?

The balance is paid out of your sale proceeds, because the lien sticks to the property. Unpaid bills turn delinquent on February 1, with a six percent penalty and one percent interest.

What is Austin's population and size?

The Census Bureau estimates 1,002,632 residents for 2025, a 4.6 percent rise over the 2020 base. The land area is 319.94 square miles.

Who buys a house in Arlington, TX, and how quickly can a sale close?

Arlington sellers deal with three kinds of buyers: households using a mortgage, other individuals paying out of pocket, and investors who purchase houses in whatever shape they are in. Closing speed turns on the buyer: cash moves when the title work is done, while a loan needs an appraisal and underwriting first.

The Census Bureau counts 402,134 people in the city for mid-2025. Just over half of the homes, 54.3 percent, are lived in by the people who own them, so a seller here competes with many rentals and other resale houses.

  • Financed buyer: tends to pay most for an updated house, but an appraisal or inspection can sink the deal.
  • Individual cash buyer: still negotiates repairs and usually wants a typical inspection period.
  • Investor: prices the repairs in, skips showings and agrees to a date that fits your move, a probate schedule or a lender's deadline.

How did a railroad stop between Dallas and Fort Worth turn into this city?

Arlington started as a market town on the Texas and Pacific Railway in 1876 and was incorporated in 1884, according to the Handbook of Texas. A Presbyterian minister who surveyed land beside the new tracks is credited with the first town plat, and the post office was renamed Arlington in 1877.

Farm trade carried the town for decades. Then came the postwar surge: 7,692 residents in 1950, 44,775 in 1960, 160,123 in 1980 and 261,717 in 1990. A General Motors assembly plant began production in January 1954, Lake Arlington was built in the mid-1950s as a water supply, and the turnpike that became Interstate 30 opened in 1957. Six Flags Over Texas arrived in 1961, and the Rangers moved to town in 1971.

The University of Texas at Arlington grew out of a vocational college founded in 1917 and enrolled 41,515 students in September 2021. The school district ran 78 schools that year. AT&T Stadium has been the Cowboys' home since 2009, and the 5,000-acre Great Southwest Industrial District, shared with Grand Prairie, dates from the turnpike era. Houses built in the boom decades sit beside newer subdivisions, so an older home's roof, foundation and wiring are worth a look before a buyer's inspector does it for you.

What do the 2020-2024 Census estimates say about Arlington housing costs?

A typical Arlington owner-occupied home was worth $304,700 in the latest five-year estimates, and a typical renter paid $1,470 a month. Treat both as middle-of-the-road numbers: a house in a tired condition or in a less sought-after pocket will sit below them.

Does an Arlington short-term rental permit move to the buyer?

No. The city ties each short-term rental permit to one owner and one address, and it cannot be transferred or assigned, so whoever buys your house must apply on their own.

Arlington defines a short-term rental as a home or part of one used for lodging for fewer than 30 consecutive days. Council approved the rules in April 2019, and rentals running before the August 1, 2019 start date were not grandfathered. Houses qualify in a zone anchored on the Entertainment District, in medium-density and multifamily residential districts, and in some commercial and mixed-use districts.

  • Occupancy tops out at two guests per bedroom plus two, up to 12 people.
  • Amplified sound and outdoor gatherings are off limits from 10 p.m. to 9 a.m.
  • Converting space into extra bedrooms is prohibited and can lower the allowed headcount.
  • Three citations in a year, or ignoring a written notice for ten days, can lead to revocation.

If your house has hosted guests, collect the permit, and the inspection checklist results before you show it. The city's short-term rental page lists what inspectors check, including smoke alarms, escape windows, a posted floor plan and a fire extinguisher.

What property tax dates should an Arlington seller watch?

Texas appraises on January 1, so the owner on that date carries the year's liability, and Arlington bills arrive about October 1. Notices of value for homesteads land near April 1. A homeowner who disagrees with the figure has until May 15, or 30 days after the notice, whichever falls later, to file a protest with the appraisal review board.

Payment is due by January 31 for most accounts. Paying in two halves is allowed, with November 30 and June 30 as the marks. Miss the January cutoff and February 1 brings a six percent penalty with one percent interest; by July the penalty grows to 12 percent. Because the lien for the year attaches in January, a house that closes in March still has to settle that year's bill.

  • School districts exempt $140,000 of a homestead's value.
  • Homeowners aged 65 or older, or disabled, gain another $60,000 school exemption and a ceiling on school tax.
  • If you sell after January 1 to someone who will live in the house, that buyer may be able to claim the exemption at once when you had not.

The Comptroller posts the calendar on its deadlines page. For a payoff on your own account, contact the Tarrant County offices that cover your address.

What documents does an Arlington closing require?

Ownership passes when a signed, acknowledged deed goes into the property records of the county where the lot sits. Texas will file a conveyance only after a notary or similar officer has taken the signer's acknowledgment, or two witnesses have sworn to it.

Pull these together before accepting an offer:

  • your current deed and photo ID
  • mortgage and home-equity payoff statements
  • this year's tax statement and any back-tax notices
  • HOA payoff and transfer paperwork, if one applies
  • leases, deposits and tenant contacts, if someone lives there
  • any rental permit and inspection records

A house that came through an estate needs the right title paper. Executors use an executor's deed; a muniment of title order works when a will is probated without administration; and an affidavit of heirship is only a sworn, court-unverified statement that a title company may decline.

How should I weigh a cash offer against listing the house?

Count what each path leaves you after payoffs, repairs and time. A listing can bring a higher price for a well-kept house, but a cash sale removes the repair list, the open houses and the chance that a buyer's loan falls through.

Collect each offer in writing: the price, the closing date, who pays settlement charges and any exit clauses. Ask whether the buyer will take the house with a tenant or with open city notices. Subtract your payoffs and carrying costs, then choose the figure and date that fit your plans.

More questions about Arlington, TX

Will a buyer pay for a house in Arlington that needs a new roof?

Yes, investors and cash buyers regularly take on roof work, and the offer reflects it. Nothing has to be repaired before closing, so compare the offer with a repaired house's likely price after your own repair bills.

Can I sell a house in Arlington that has been used as an Airbnb?

Yes. The permit stays behind, because it belongs to the owner and address, so the buyer files a new application and passes the city's inspection. Say plainly whether the address sits inside an eligible zone.

What happens to unpaid tax when my Arlington sale closes?

Whatever is owed comes out of your proceeds when you sign, since the lien stays on the house. Ask the tax office for a payoff figure early so the closing statement has no surprise.

Where is the deed filed after an Arlington sale?

At the county clerk's office for the county where the house stands, Tarrant County for most Arlington addresses. A lot near a county line is worth confirming against your tax bill.

How large is Arlington by population and area?

The Census Bureau estimates 402,134 residents for 2025 and counted 142,455 households in 2020-2024. The land area is 95.87 square miles.

Selling in Corpus Christi?

What should a Corpus Christi owner consider before choosing a sale route?

Condition and timing carry the most weight. A well kept house can do well in a listing, while a storm-damaged, inherited or rented one often moves faster to a buyer who takes it as it stands.

The Texas State Historical Association calls Corpus Christi a seaport at the mouth of the Nueces River on the west end of Corpus Christi Bay, the county seat of Nueces County and the largest city on the South Texas coast. It sits where Interstate 37 meets U.S. highways 77 and 181, 210 miles southwest of Houston. Salt air, wind and storm history make roofs, windows and foundations the first things coastal buyers check.

  • Open listing: widest reach for a house that shows well.
  • Owner sale: no commission, more paperwork for you.
  • Cash purchase: quicker and as-is, useful after storm damage or for an estate.

How did hurricanes and the port shape Corpus Christi?

A hurricane on September 14, 1919 destroyed much of the North Beach area and the central business district and killed some 350 to 400 people, according to the Handbook of Texas. The city then pushed for a deepwater port, which opened on September 14, 1926.

The port brought rapid growth: the population more than doubled from 10,522 in 1920 to 27,741 in 1930. Oil was found in the county in 1930, and the Naval Air Station and refineries became pillars of the economy. The Handbook also lists Padre Island National Seashore and the bay among recreation draws, along with Del Mar College and Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi.

Corpus Christi milestones from the Handbook of Texas

Source: Handbook of Texas, Corpus Christi. Keep storm repair receipts and insurance claim records, since buyers and lenders will ask about that past.

What are Corpus Christi's short-term rental rules?

The city defines a short-term rental as renting all or part of a residential unit for less than 30 days and not less than 12 hours, and it requires registration for any property rented that way. Permits are valid for the calendar year and renewed each January.

The ordinance approved on June 28, 2022 allows rentals with restrictions in single-family districts citywide, but not in single-family districts within the Padre and Mustang Island area plan. Type 1 means the owner or operator lives there; Type 2 means no one does, and Type 2 rentals were limited to 15 percent of a block face, first come first served. Hotel occupancy tax filing applies to short-term rentals, hotels and bed and breakfasts.

A later city news release described a moratorium on new Type 1 permits through November 17, 2026, with staff to bring changes to council on or before that date, and said permits valid through December 31, 2026 would stay active. It also directed staff to apply the density limit to renewals, with at least one Type 2 rental per block face. Rules may have changed since, so ask Development Services for the current version.

  • Applications ask for owner and agent contacts, a floor plan with sleeping areas, a guest maximum and exits, and a 24-hour contact person.
  • The printed permit fee was $250 for 2023; ask the city for the current fee.
  • Development Services is at (361) 826-3240.

Sources: city short-term rental page and council action release. Do not tell a buyer a permit transfers with the house unless the city confirms it.

Where do Corpus Christi deeds and tax records live?

City parcels in Nueces County are filed at the Nueces County clerk, and the appraisal district for that county sets values. Addresses near the city edge can lie in a neighboring county, so your latest tax bill is the quickest check.

The courts' clerk manual says a deed needs an acknowledgment or two witnesses to be accepted for filing. It prices a first page at $5.00 and later pages at $4.00, with extra charges for names beyond five and for records funds. Ask the clerk for today's schedule; your title company usually handles the filing.

Reference: county clerk manual.

What happens if property taxes on a Corpus Christi home go unpaid?

A bill unpaid after January 31 is delinquent as of February 1. Interest of one percent a month starts then, a six percent penalty applies at the outset, and by July 1 the penalty reaches 12 percent. A taxing unit's attorney may add up to 20 percent on top.

The lien that secures each year's tax attaches on January 1 and follows the house through a sale, so a buyer cannot obtain clear title until back taxes are cleared. At closing the title company pays what you owe out of your proceeds. Seniors, disabled owners and disabled veterans may use installments, and some collectors offer payment plans up to 36 months on a homestead.

Pages: paying property taxes and deadlines.

What if the Corpus Christi house is tied up in a land contract or has an occupant?

A contract for deed, also called an installment land contract, keeps title with the seller until the buyer pays in full, and Texas Property Code chapter 5, subchapter D governs those for residences. The purchaser has a statutory right to cancel under that law, so get legal advice before selling a house under such a contract.

If someone stays after being told to leave, an owner may ask the sheriff or constable for removal under Property Code chapter 24B, but only when conditions are met, including that the occupant is not a family member or a current or former tenant. Wrongful removal can lead to a lawsuit. Otherwise, the usual route is an eviction suit in justice court.

Sources: the Attorney General's opinion on executory contracts and the State Law Library eviction guide.

What should a Corpus Christi seller gather before an offer?

Pull together the deed, loan payoff, tax bill, insurance claim history and permits for any storm work. Coastal buyers raise flood and wind coverage early, so know what your policy covers and which company writes it.

Line up offers by net proceeds and by weeks to closing. A cash buyer may close sooner and will price in repairs; a listing may net more after a longer wait. Have each buyer state in writing who pays title, recording and the tax split.

  • Ask whether the buyer will take the house with storm damage unrepaired.
  • Ask whether an insurance claim still open on the house can be assigned or must be settled first.
  • Ask how soon funds are available after the title company clears the file.

Corpus Christi sellers who are relocating or settling an estate often value a firm closing date more than a few extra dollars, so weigh certainty alongside price.

More questions about Corpus Christi, TX

Is Corpus Christi the county seat of Nueces County?

Yes, according to the Handbook of Texas. City parcels are recorded at the Nueces County clerk's office.

Can I run a short-term rental in Corpus Christi?

Only with a registration permit. The city requires one for any rental under 30 days, and the rules have been under review, so ask Development Services which permit type applies and whether new ones are issued.

What happens to a rental permit when I sell?

Do not assume it carries over. Permits are issued annually and renewals face density rules, so get the city's answer before you describe the permit to a buyer.

Which date do Texas property taxes become delinquent?

February 1, for most bills. Penalty and interest start then, and the penalty rises monthly until July 1.

Do I need to keep hurricane repair records?

Keep them. Buyers, insurers and lenders often ask about past damage, and receipts back up your answers.

Is a quick sale realistic for a Plano house?

Plano is pricey: Census data for 2020 to 2024 puts the midpoint home value at $465,900, a price most buyers finance. Financing brings an appraisal and an inspection, two places a deal can slip, so hurried sellers often like cash.

  • Listing: more buyers see it and the price may be higher, at the cost of prep time.
  • Repairs first: sensible only when the fix is cheap and visible, like paint, flooring or a roof leak.

What kind of city is Plano?

Plano lies in southwestern Collin County on U.S. Highway 75, roughly fifteen miles north of Dallas. Per the Texas State Historical Association, it was laid out and incorporated in 1873, and postal officials approved the Spanish word for flat as its name.

For nearly a century it stayed a farm town. The town had 3,695 residents in 1960, then reached 17,872 in 1970 and passed 72,000 by 1980 as Dallas pushed north. By the mid-1980s Plano had overtaken McKinney as the commercial and financial center of Collin County, and it hosted Frito-Lay and several computer makers.

The Census Bureau now counts 293,028 residents on 71.69 square miles of land, about 3,982.5 per square mile. With so little open land, your house competes with similar homes nearby. Look up its build year in your appraisal record, because age drives how buyers weigh the roof, foundation and plumbing.

Every September the city hosts balloon races and carries the nickname Balloon Capital of Texas, a detail that shows how much the city has changed from its cattle-trail and cotton-gin days.

Rail shaped the early town. The Houston and Texas Central reached it in 1872, a second line crossed in 1888, and an 1881 fire destroyed fifty-two buildings and briefly left a tent city. The Farrel-Wilson Farmstead Museum on a former sheep ranch is described as the one remaining sign of that farming past, and the handbook ties most of the city's growth to the 1970s boom.

What does Plano's economy mean for buyers?

Many Plano buyers are corporate or professional workers. The state handbook says Frito-Lay and computer makers made their homes here, and Census figures show 69.0% of residents 16 and older in the labor force. Health care and social assistance took in $6,679,789,000 in 2022, and retail sales were $10,946,748,000.

Census figures also show 29.3% of residents born abroad, 38.0% speaking another language at home, 9,938 veterans and 14.7% aged 65 or older. A listing that is plain, accurate and easy to forward to relatives reaches more households, and older or veteran owners may qualify for the tax relief covered below.

The mean commute is 25.4 minutes and 96.6% of households have broadband, so a quiet home office is a fair selling point.

Three dates matter. Value is fixed as of January 1. October bills go delinquent after January 31, and penalty and interest begin February 1. A protest of value is generally due by May 15.

Where does the Plano deed get filed?

At the county clerk's office for the parcel's county, usually Collin County. The title company drafts the deed and you sign it before a notary. The state clerk manual builds the recording fee from a first-page charge, a charge per added page and several records fees, so let the title company give you the total.

If the owner has died, the paperwork differs: an affidavit of death, an executor's deed, or a court order paired with the will, depending on the estate.

A direct sale can beat a listing's pace. Foreclosure auctions in Texas fall on first Tuesdays, so get the sale date and reinstatement amount from the servicer in writing. A will is generally probated within four years of death, and a small estate affidavit suits estates up to $75,000 not counting the homestead.

How should I compare a cash offer with listing in Plano?

Compare what you keep and when. Start with each price, deduct commissions, repairs, carrying costs, concessions and title charges, then set the totals next to each other.

At Plano prices a small percentage is a big sum, so a sound house in a popular school zone often earns more listed. Deferred repairs, a tenant, a lien or probate is where a direct sale competes. Get every offer in writing, check dates and contingencies, and keep two to compare.

Why were Plano's farms replaced by houses?

Dallas grew northward in the 1970s. The Handbook of Texas says the city's population more than doubled by 1975 and again by 1980, and that a 1970 land reappraisal raised taxes and helped end farming.

$112,253 for 2020 to 2024, in 2024 dollars. The median owner-occupied home value is $465,900 and median gross rent is $1,841, so buyers here are mostly dual-income households.

The county clerk for the county where the parcel sits, usually Collin County. The title company confirms this and files the deed at closing.

Which selling route suits a Lubbock owner short on time?

A short timeline usually points to a cash buyer, while a full listing suits an owner who can wait. Lubbock sellers weigh three things: how the roof, plumbing and floors look, whether any liens sit on the title, and how soon the proceeds are needed.

Texas Tech University, a large medical center and the farm trade give the city steady demand. A house near campus or a hospital tends to draw investors and renters as well as families, so even a dated property has a market.

  • Agent listing: widest exposure, though showings, repair requests and lender timelines stretch the calendar.
  • Owner sale: skips the commission and puts pricing and paperwork on you.
  • Cash offer: quick close, no repairs, typically priced under a polished retail sale.

How did the South Plains city of Lubbock take shape?

Lubbock sits at 3,256 feet on the flat South Plains, along Interstate 27, 327 miles northwest of Dallas. The Handbook of Texas, published by the state historical society, says two rival settlements, Old Lubbock and Monterey, merged in December 1890, and the city incorporated on March 16, 1909.

The Santa Fe railroad arrived that same year, and in 1923 the legislature chose Lubbock for Texas Technological College, renamed Texas Tech University in 1969. A medical school followed in 1970. The Handbook counts seven hospitals with over 2,000 beds, which anchors health care as a major employer.

Farming still shapes the economy. Irrigation pushed the region toward cotton and sorghum in the 1930s, and Lubbock became a wholesale hub for dozens of West Texas and eastern New Mexico counties. Reese Air Force Base closed in 1997, and its land became the Reese Technology Center.

Weather is part of local memory. A tornado struck the city center on May 11, 1970 and killed twenty-six people. Expect inspectors and buyers to look hard at roofs, hail damage and storm protection.

Who bills Lubbock property tax, and what changed in 2026?

Valuation and tax collection run through the Lubbock Central Appraisal District. Texas levies no state property tax, so your bill is the sum of local rates.

The district reported mailing 2026 statements on October 23, 2026, and said bills for Lubbock Cooper ISD would wait for the result of a November 3, 2026 voter-approval tax rate election. Owners there should ask the district office which rate their bill uses, since the amount listed online assumed the rate on the ballot.

At the state level, the lien for a year's tax attaches January 1 and unpaid bills turn delinquent on February 1. In a sale, the closing statement shows how the year's bill was divided.

One warning on the district's own home page deserves repeating: firms sometimes charge a one-time processing fee to file a homestead exemption, and the district says filing never costs anything.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Lubbock house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Which homestead breaks can Lubbock owners claim?

Owners can file for a residence homestead exemption online through the district's property search. The district lists the general exemption and separate ones for disabled owners, seniors, 100 percent disabled veterans and certain surviving spouses.

  • Every Texas school district takes $140,000 off a homestead's value, and seniors or disabled owners get a further $60,000 off the school levy base.
  • Appraised value on a homestead may grow no more than 10 percent a year, counting from the year after the exemption begins.
  • Seniors and disabled owners may defer taxes while they stay in the house as their residence, with the debt, penalty and interest falling due 181 days after the property stops qualifying.

Questions go to 806-762-5000. Because an exemption does not travel with the seller, the next occupant files a fresh application.

How do I pay or look up taxes on a Lubbock house?

Search the account on the district site, mail a check to P.O. Box 10568, Lubbock, TX 79408, drop it at 2109 Avenue Q, or pay online or by phone. Processing charges on card and online payments go to Certified Payments rather than the district.

The district also publishes GIS maps, accepts documents and address changes by email, and says the office accepts visitors. A tax foreclosure sale was held on September 1, 2026, and the deadline for the written-statement request for that sale was August 28, 2026, so any future sale will carry its own posted dates. The board of the district was also taking requests to serve on the Lubbock County appraisal review board for terms starting in 2027, the body that hears value disputes.

If the title company needs a tax certificate, ask the district for one. Accounts that reach tax foreclosure involve a notarized written-statement request, form 50-307, with a $10.00 fee in certified funds.

What if a Lubbock owner is late on the mortgage or taxes?

Options shrink with each missed month, so move early. A lender must give a default notice with twenty days to catch up, and an auction notice must come three weeks ahead. Auctions run monthly, during daytime hours, in an area the county designates.

Back taxes work differently. A collector may offer a payment plan of up to 36 months on a homestead, and penalty relief is possible if you pay quickly and ask in writing.

  • A sale ahead of the auction protects equity and keeps a foreclosure off your record.
  • Get the lender's payoff number in writing, and raise a short sale if the balance exceeds value.
  • Search county records for liens so nothing surprises the title company.

Can Lubbock estates and rented houses sell fast?

Yes, once the paperwork is sorted. For an inherited house, a will may be probated up to four years after death, and a muniment of title can let the will and court order stand in for a full administration. Without a will, a small estate affidavit covers modest estates, and an heirship affidavit is just a sworn statement a buyer may turn down.

A rented house raises timing questions. Written notice to leave is normally three days, a justice court hears the case, with possession by writ available six days after judgment. Cash buyers often accept a tenant in place, which skips that sequence.

Where is a Lubbock deed filed?

The Lubbock County Clerk keeps the official records. The signature needs a notary's acknowledgment first. Ask the clerk for the fee schedule, since state caps and county charges vary, and expect the closing agent to file and pay from your proceeds.

More questions about Lubbock, TX

Does a Lubbock house with big repair needs still sell?

Yes. A cash buyer accepts the house as it sits, so an aging roof or old plumbing can stay unrepaired. Expect the offer to reflect repair cost, and set it beside an agent's listing price before you choose.

When do Lubbock property taxes go delinquent?

Texas treats most unpaid taxes as delinquent on February 1, when penalty and interest begin. The Lubbock district publishes statement dates on its site, and its office can confirm your account at 806-762-5000.

Does filing a homestead exemption in Lubbock cost anything?

No. The appraisal district says there is never a charge to file any exemption, and it warns owners to ignore firms asking for a one-time processing fee.

Does a tax lien stop a Lubbock sale?

It complicates the sale but does not stop it. The lien attaches each January 1, and a buyer cannot get clear title until delinquent taxes are paid, which a title company can do from your proceeds.

Who files the deed when a Lubbock house sells?

The title company normally submits it to the Lubbock County Clerk. The signature must be acknowledged before a notary, and the clerk can quote the recording charges.

What should a Laredo homeowner know before selling fast?

Laredo sellers usually choose between a cash sale as-is and a traditional listing, and the right pick depends on how much work the house needs and how soon the money matters. Laredo is a border city with a long record of trade, and its housing stock ranges from older homes near downtown to newer subdivisions farther out.

Cash buyers usually accept the property as it stands, which spares you permit fees and contractor bids. A listing can reach more buyers, but it brings repairs, showings and the wait for a buyer's lender. Compare both on your own timeline before signing anything.

Where is Laredo and how did it grow?

Laredo stands on the Rio Grande in southwestern Webb County, about 150 miles southwest of San Antonio and 135 miles west of Corpus Christi, according to the Texas State Historical Association. Interstate 35, U.S. 59 and U.S. 83 all serve the city.

The Handbook of Texas dates the settlement to 1755 and says Laredo became the Webb County seat in 1848. Railroad links in the 1880s tied it to Mexico City and San Antonio, and the same source credits trade with Mexico, including maquiladora growth and NAFTA, for much of its later expansion. Its population passed 176,000 by 2000. For a seller, that trade economy means many buyers have jobs linked to freight, customs and logistics.

What did railroads and trade do for Laredo housing?

The Handbook of Texas ties Laredo's modern growth to 1881, when the Texas Mexican Railroad arrived from Corpus Christi and the International and Great Northern reached the border from San Antonio. By 1887 a Mexican line linked Nuevo Laredo with Mexico City. Onion farming began in 1898 and opened irrigated land north of town, and oil and gas finds in the early 1900s added jobs.

Fort McIntosh, founded a mile west of the city in 1849, served until 1947, when its grounds passed to the new Laredo Junior College. Laredo Air Force Base ran from 1952 until 1973. Population rose from 3,521 in 1880 to 13,429 in 1900 and 122,899 in 1990. Older close-in neighborhoods grew around the downtown plaza and rail lines, while later subdivisions spread outward, so a house's age tells you which era of codes it was built under.

What can you sell, and what will a buyer ask about?

Buyers in Laredo tend to ask about a short list of items before they make an offer. Having these answers ready speeds up any sale.

  • Whether the house sits in the floodplain, which the city handles through a separate floodplain development permit.
  • Whether past additions, porches, carports or block fences were built with permits.
  • How old the roof is, and whether electrical, plumbing and cooling work came from licensed trades.
  • Whether the property tax bill is current and which exemptions are on file.

Unpermitted work does not stop a cash sale, but it lowers what an informed buyer will pay.

Do Laredo permits matter when selling a home?

Yes, because the city requires a building permit for remodels, additions, porches, carports, block fences and demolitions. Its Building Development Services page says the city follows the International Residential Code and allows up to 21 days for residential review.

Electrical, mechanical, plumbing, irrigation and mobile home installation permits must be pulled by a licensed contractor in that trade. A homeowner can pull a general permit but is treated as the contractor on the job. Laredo also offers an Amnesty Certificate of Occupancy for owners whose records are missing, with proof that the structure has been occupied continuously since August 2, 1983.

The same page lists a separate $20.00 technology fee. Ask the city for the current schedule before budgeting, since the ordinance list shows newer fee updates.

How does Webb County bill property tax on a Laredo home?

Webb County's tax office sends statements every October, and the lump-sum deadline is January 31, with penalty and interest starting February 1. Owners can also split the bill into two halves due November 30 and June 30.

Homeowners with a homestead exemption plus an over-65, disabled person or disabled veteran exemption can use a four-payment plan due January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31. Webb County also runs a monthly prepayment plan through September 15 for owners without a mortgage escrow. A delinquent plan requires the applicant's name on the account and a homestead exemption, and interest on it builds month by month up to 12 percent.

Texas law puts the tax lien on the property each January 1, so any unpaid bill follows the house to a buyer. The Comptroller explains that the owner on January 1 stays liable. Request the exact balance from the Webb County tax office early, so the closing date works.

Which state rules affect a Laredo closing?

  • School districts owe homestead owners a $140,000 exemption, with $60,000 more for seniors and disabled owners.
  • Valuation date for appraisals is the first of January.
  • County clerks record deeds, and the signature must be notarized.

Webb County's appraisal district posts its own exemption forms. If a loan is in default, a sale that closes before the auction date can stop it.

What are the steps to sell a Laredo house fast?

  1. Gather the deed, the last tax statement, any permits and a list of repairs you know about.
  2. Ask the Webb County tax office what is owed so there are no surprises.
  3. Request offers from cash buyers and, if you like, a listing agent, and compare net amounts.
  4. Choose a title company and sign the deed.

If an heir is selling an inherited Laredo home, the appraisal district asks for an affidavit of ownership interest and a death certificate to move the homestead exemption.

What other Laredo city permits come up around a sale?

Sellers often forget the small permits that buyers inspect for. The city's permit page lists several that touch a residential lot.

  • A residential right-of-way permit for driveway work costs $50 and must be obtained by a registered contractor.
  • A garage sale permit costs $15 and is limited to five per year, per the permit page.
  • A solar panel permit has a non-refundable $200 fee and must be obtained before work starts.
  • Permits expire six months after issuance if work has not started, and all work must finish within twelve months.

General contractors must register with the city, and the page lists a $60 registration fee. If you hired someone to work on the house, ask for their registration and the final inspection record, because a buyer's inspector may want proof the work was approved.

The city's ordinance list shows it adopted the 2021 International codes in 2024 and keeps a separate floodplain ordinance, a fence ordinance and residential setback rules. Call Building Development Services if a porch or fence was added without a permit. A cash buyer may accept it, while a lender-financed buyer often will not.

Can I sell a Laredo house that needs repairs?

Yes. Many cash buyers take homes needing work, and the offer reflects the repairs. Two or three offers show how much condition moves the number.

Is a permit required before putting a Laredo home on the market?

No permit is needed just to sell. A permit matters if you plan to remodel, add a porch or carport, or build a block fence first. Laredo's Building Development Services can tell you which projects need one.

What is the Webb County tax deadline?

The lump-sum payment is due by January 31 each year. Statements go out in October, and a split plan splits payment between November 30 and June 30.

Who pays property tax when a Laredo house sells?

Texas ties the tax lien to January 1, so the unpaid year's tax stays with the property. Closing usually settles the balance, and the buyer and seller divide it as the contract says.

What happens if my Laredo home is in foreclosure?

The lender must give at least 21 days' notice of sale, and auctions are held on a set Tuesday each month. Selling first can pay off the loan and stop the auction.

Competing listings are plentiful, so price and condition decide how long a house sits.

  • A listing suits a house that is ready for the market.
  • A private sale avoids the listing fee and adds paperwork.
  • A cash sale skips repairs and showings.

What shaped Irving's neighborhoods?

Irving started as a rail town. Two surveyors for the Chicago, Rock Island and Gulf Railway bought 80 acres and held a lot auction on December 19, 1903, and voters incorporated the city in 1914, per the Handbook of Texas.

The population was 2,615 in 1950, 45,895 in 1960 and 100,996 by 1970, as farmland became subdivisions. Texas Stadium hosted the Dallas Cowboys from 1971 to 2008, Dallas-Fort Worth Airport grew along the western edge, and Las Colinas began on the north side. The same entry says Irving now has 8,500 businesses and ten Fortune 500 headquarters. The city says eight, so confirm current numbers on its site.

For a seller, the result is a mix of mid-century neighborhoods, newer Las Colinas areas and a lot of rental property, each with a different buyer pool.

What does Irving's economy mean for buyers of my house?

Irving's employment base is corporate. The city calls Las Colinas the Headquarters of Headquarters and reports eight Fortune 500 headquarters, while the Handbook of Texas says ten, and counts 8,500 businesses. The Handbook adds that Dallas-Fort Worth Airport runs along the city's western edge and that the University of Dallas, founded in 1956, and a Dallas College campus opened in 1977 are here.

That mix produces steady demand from relocating employees and renters, and it also means a lot of buyers work to a deadline. Sellers who can offer a firm closing date, clear title and move-in-ready condition tend to hold an advantage with that group.

The city's own site reports a population of 264,546, which differs from the Handbook's 2024 estimate of about 256,000, so quote the source you cite and check the date.

The city also reports that more than 60 percent of its general fund goes to public safety, and it lists four museums, three symphonies and the Irving Arts Center among its cultural draws. The Handbook also notes that Irving has a council-manager form of government, so permit questions go to city staff. Check the city's pages for permits if you completed work such as a remodel or a deck, because an open permit can hold up a closing.

Who collects property tax on an Irving house?

Dallas County Tax Office handles collection for Irving. The downtown office is in the Records Building at 500 Elm Street, Suite 3300, the customer care line is 214-653-7811, and payments can be made online.

Its home page carries a notice that Dallas County adopted a rate that will raise more maintenance and operations taxes than last year, listed as an effective increase of 22.02 percent. What if tenants occupy my Irving house?

Irving has many more renters than owners, so sellers often deal with tenants. Texas calls for written notice to vacate, a short period of days unless the lease sets a different one, handed over in person, mailed, or e-mailed if the lease permits.

  • The landlord sues in justice court and the tenant is served before trial.
  • The hearing comes within a few weeks of filing.
  • An appeal to county court has a very short deadline after judgment.
  • A writ of possession follows a final judgment, with notice before removal.

Some covered properties fall under a longer federal notice. See counsel before you promise a buyer a vacant house.

Can a cash sale help with tax or lien problems in Irving?

It can, if the sale proceeds cover them at closing. A tax lien attaches in January and follows the house, so the closing agent will insist that unpaid taxes be resolved. The Comptroller adds that the January owner stays liable for that year's levy even after a sale.

Penalty and interest start on February 1 and a collection attorney's surcharge may follow, while some collectors offer installment plans on a homestead. Request a payoff figure from the Dallas County Tax Office, and have the closing agent confirm every lien before you accept an offer.

What happens if an Irving owner dies without a will?

An heir who wants to sell must first show authority. A will is generally offered for probate within four years of death. With no will, a small estate affidavit can work for a modest estate when every heir agrees, and the court must approve it.

A transfer on death deed moves the house outside probate if it was recorded before the owner's death. An affidavit of heirship is another route, though buyers need not accept it. Heirs of an Irving house can ask a Dallas County probate lawyer which fits and then line up the paperwork before marketing.
