Can adverse possession or squatters affect an Irving house?

In Texas, adverse possession means open and visible use of land under a claim hostile to the owner. A ten-year statute, section 16.026 of the Civil Practice and Remedies Code, applies, and a claim proceeds as a trespass to try title suit.

For an empty Irving house that has sat unattended, the practical risk is a squatter, not a title claim. Property Code chapter 24B offers an owner a removal request to the sheriff or constable, subject to conditions. Keeping vacant property secured, visited and insured is the better protection, and a quick sale can end the exposure.

In writing, usually for a few days unless the lease says otherwise, and some covered properties fall under a longer federal notice.

Garland has its own Code Compliance Department, which runs a permit program for single-family and short-term rentals. For a rental house, that program affects a sale more than any market swing. An investor can buy as-is and handle the permit change, while a retail buyer expects an inspected, move-in ready home.

What does Garland require of rental houses I want to sell?

Garland requires every single-family rental, duplexes included, to hold a permit from Code Compliance. The city's program page says the permit cannot be assigned or transferred, so a buyer who keeps renting must apply in their own name.

Can code violations stop a Garland sale?

Yes. Code violations do not stop a sale, but they can cut buyer interest and need to be disclosed to anyone who asks. A cash buyer is often the easier choice because the house is bought as-is.

If you have received a notice of violation and need more time, the city tells owners to contact their Code Compliance Officer. How do unpaid taxes complicate a Garland sale?

Delinquent tax follows the house. The year's lien takes hold on January 1, and clear title waits until the balance is paid.

Bills mail in October and go delinquent after January 31. Charges then build monthly, the penalty hitting 12 percent by July 1, and a collection attorney's fee can add up to 20 percent on top.

Relief may exist. Certain collectors allow payment plans stretching to 36 months for a homestead, and a written request can seek penalty relief if you meet the printed deadlines. Ask the office that bills your Garland parcel for its payoff and plan terms.

What happens if my Garland taxes go to a tax sale?

A constable or an agent of the taxing unit auctions the property, and no statewide list exists. County clerk and tax office websites are where notices appear.

Former owners of homestead, farm or mineral property may buy it back for two years after the purchaser's deed is filed, paying a 25 percent premium in year one or 50 percent in year two, along with the bid and costs. A sale you close first spares you that process. Request a current payoff, and ask whether suit has been filed.

Can I sell a Garland house I inherited?

If the owner recorded a transfer on death deed, the property skips probate. A Lady Bird deed instead let the owner sell freely while alive. Lacking either, the county clerk can explain probate filings and small estate affidavits.

How does Garland's inspection schedule affect closing dates?

For a single-family rental, the city page says a full inspection happens at each change of tenancy unless the property is certified, and the owner must tell Code Compliance about the vacancy and book the appointment. For a short-term rental, an inspection is required every year to renew the permit.

Timing matters when a tenant is moving out of a rental you are selling. A buyer planning to re-rent will want to know whether an inspection is pending, what it might flag, and who pays to fix it. A copy of each inspection report goes to the landlord or manager, so ask for the latest one and pass it to the buyer or the title company.

  • Ask Code Compliance, at 972-485-6400, what your permit status is.
  • Request the most recent inspection report.

What should a Garland rental buyer agree to?

Ask who will apply for the new permit, who pays for any inspection, and how existing tenants will be treated. Those three answers decide whether the closing runs smoothly.

  • Whether the offer is as-is, including any items the city inspection might flag.
  • Whether the buyer takes over the lease and the security deposit, or needs the house vacant.
  • Who covers the permit fee and the inspection at the change of tenancy.
  • What the closing date is and which title company will handle the funds.

Put every answer in the written contract. If the house is a short-term rental, also confirm that the buyer understands the annual inspection and insurance steps the city lists for renewal.

What if someone is living in my Garland house without a lease?

Sometimes an owner can ask the sheriff or constable to remove an occupant with no lawsuit, if specific conditions hold. Property Code chapter 24B sets them, and the State Law Library eviction guide summarizes it.

  • The person refused to go after a request to leave.
  • The house was closed to the public when the person walked in.
  • You and the occupant are not in a pending suit over the property.
  • The occupant has never rented from you and is not kin.

Removing the wrong person can expose the owner to a lawsuit, so check every item. A former tenant goes through the regular justice court eviction instead. In both cases, disclose the occupant to prospective buyers in writing; an investor may accept an occupied house where a retail buyer will not.

The seller signs before a notary, and the deed is then filed with the clerk serving the parcel's county. Recording charges vary, so get the total from the clerk or title company.

No. Per the city's program page, permits cannot be assigned or transferred, so a buyer who rents the house needs a new one.

Frisco is a well-known destination for movers, which gives sellers of updated homes a ready pool of financed buyers. A cash offer fits a different seller: someone relocating, settling an estate, facing a tight deadline or dealing with repairs that would cost time and money before listing.

  • Cash route: fewer contingencies and a closing date you can often set, with a price below a fully prepared listing.
  • Listing route: broader exposure, plus commission, showings and possible repair requests.
  • Hybrid route: list first, then take a cash offer if showings stall.

Whichever you pick, request a written net sheet showing payoff, taxes, fees and the amount you receive.

Where does Frisco sit and how did it grow?

Frisco lies in west central Collin County and east central Denton County, about 25 miles north of downtown Dallas near the Dallas North Tollway and the Sam Rayburn Tollway, per the city financial report. That report names U.S. Highway 380 as the northern border, FM 423 as the western edge, Custer Road as the east edge and State Highway 289 as a major north-south route.

The state's historical association says the town began as Emerson and took the name Frisco City when a post office opened in 1902, after the railway of that name. It served farmers with gins and grain elevators. The population was 1,184 in 1960, 6,141 in 1990 and 33,714 in 2000. The state history also notes that the Frisco RoughRiders baseball team and FC Dallas soccer club are based in the city.

The city runs under a home-rule charter that voters approved in 1987, with a council-manager structure. The city report puts 2020 housing units at 73,633 and says 34 percent of residents rent, so a Frisco seller may also be selling to an investor or to a landlord.

What do schools, jobs and neighborhoods mean for a Frisco sale?

Schools are a large part of the pitch. The city report lists Frisco ISD enrollment at 63,533 in 2020, and Frisco ISD is the city's largest employer by headcount in that report. Parts of the city also fall in Lewisville ISD, Little Elm ISD and Prosper ISD, so check the district for your exact address before advertising.

Major employers named in the report include T-Mobile, Baylor Scott and White, Oracle, IKEA and Conifer, along with a regional shopping mall and corporate campuses. About 59 percent of the city's assessed value is residential, and 85 percent is single-family homes and commercial property combined.

Fire and street services are staffed by the city. The same report lists nine fire stations, 2,401 street miles and 2,373 residential building permits in fiscal 2021, which shows how much construction was under way. New homes compete with resale houses, so price a resale house against new builds nearby, not just against old sales. Check the current permit and development activity with the city planning staff before you list a house that backs onto a development site.

The same report shows how Frisco pays for its growth. Voters approved a $345 million bond authorization in May 2019 covering public safety, streets, public works, the library and parks, and the report lists streets as the largest share of the city's bond-funded work. Street and park projects can change traffic near a house, so a buyer may ask what is planned near your lot. Ask the city engineering staff for the capital project list, and mention finished improvements like new roads or trails in your marketing.

What Frisco amenities can a seller point to?

The city's financial report gives concrete numbers you can use in a listing. It counts 1,545 acres of developed parks and 990 acres of undeveloped parkland, 24 baseball fields, 35 soccer fields, six tennis courts, three museums or art galleries and a recreation center. Library visits topped 405,000 in the fiscal year it covers.

Sports are part of the identity too: the state history notes the Frisco RoughRiders and FC Dallas play here. The city sits close to major roads, with DFW Airport and Love Field within about a half hour's drive according to the same report, and a commute of about 29 minutes on average in 2020.

  • Name the nearest park or trail and the school zone in your listing.
  • Note proximity to the tollway or Highway 121 if it applies.
  • Keep records of recent updates, since buyers compare homes against newer builds.

What should a Frisco seller know about the tax bill?

A Frisco bill can carry several line items. The city report says a house in Collin County and Frisco ISD pays the city, the county, the school district and Collin College, while Denton County parcels pay that county instead.

Under the state calendar, bills are mailed around October 1 and unpaid tax turns delinquent after January 31, per the Comptroller's calendar. The closing agent settles the current year from your proceeds.

Source: City of Frisco Citizen's Financial Report, fiscal 2021. Those are past figures, so ask the Collin or Denton County tax office about the exemptions on your current bill.

Which exemptions and caps follow a Frisco owner?

Exemptions stay with the property. The buyer applies for new ones, while the school tax ceiling for an older owner can follow them to another Texas homestead, per the Comptroller's exemptions page.

  • A homestead appraisal cap limits yearly increases after the first exemption year.
  • Disabled veteran relief runs from $5,000 to $12,000 by rating, and a 100 percent rating can exempt the entire homestead, according to the veteran exemption FAQ.

The Collin Central Appraisal District or its Denton counterpart can show the exemptions on your account.

What if the Frisco house is inherited, behind on payments, or leased?

Each case changes the paperwork more than the price. The State Law Library's informal methods page compares the small estate affidavit, the affidavit of heirship and the muniment of title for heirs.

For a loan in default, a lender may sue for a deficiency within two years after a foreclosure sale, per the library's after-the-sale page. Selling first can avoid that exposure.

For a leased house, the eviction guide outlines notice and court steps, though many buyers simply take the lease.

How is the deed recorded after a Frisco sale?

The Collin County or Denton County clerk files the deed, depending on the parcel. The county clerk manual notes the instrument must carry an acknowledgment from an authorized officer.

Your closing agent handles the filing and the fee, so read the settlement statement the day before you sign.

  • Have your payoff letter and tax statements ready.

Is Frisco in Collin County or Denton County?

Both. The city report places it in west central Collin County and east central Denton County, so your tax bill and deed show which applies.

A clear title closes fastest, and the buyer should give you a date in writing.

No. The buyer files fresh applications.

Can a Frisco house with a loan still be sold?

Yes. Yes. The lender is paid at the closing table and the balance is yours. Ask your servicer for a payoff letter.

With the Collin or Denton County clerk, whichever county holds the lot.

What drives a quick house sale in McKinney?

Clear title, a believable price and a house a buyer can move into without a long repair list. McKinney has strong demand, but also plenty of competing listings, so those three points separate quick sales from slow ones.

McKinney had an estimated 236,001 residents on July 1, 2025, far more than neighboring Melissa. The Census Bureau shows 20.8 percent growth over the 2020 base of 195,331, and 26.2 percent of residents are under 18, which keeps family-sized houses in demand.

  • With an agent you reach the largest audience, at the cost of commission and weeks on the market.
  • Skipping the agent keeps the fee in your pocket and makes you the negotiator.
  • A cash buyer works on a shorter calendar and accepts the house in its present state.

How much is a McKinney home worth, and who lives in them?

Another 19.5 percent of residents were born abroad, and 7,835 are veterans, which affects the exemptions some owners can claim.

How did McKinney become the Collin County seat?

The first county seat was Buckner, but it fell outside the distance the Legislature required, so a special election chose McKinney by ten votes to one. Town and county both take their name from Collin McKinney, who signed the Texas Declaration of Independence.

William Davis gave 120 acres for the townsite on March 24, 1849. The Houston and Texas Central Railway reached McKinney in 1872 and the Missouri, Kansas and Texas Railroad in 1881, feeding cotton gins, mills and an opera house. The Army opened a 1,500-bed hospital in 1943, and a tornado on May 3, 1948 killed three people.

By the 1980s the town was a commuter base for people working in Plano and Dallas, and the count reached 54,369 in 2000. Expect older homes around the historic center and large newer subdivisions farther out.

Which offices handle McKinney homes in Collin County?

Request the total owed from the county tax office. An unpaid earlier year stays attached to the house.

What are McKinney's rules for short-term rentals?

McKinney now requires every short-term rental inside city limits to register each year. The city's page says registration opened on April 6 and that the program is free.

The city describes a short-term rental as a house, apartment, room or other dwelling rented through Airbnb, VRBO or similar platforms for thirty days or less. Long-term leases, apartment complexes renting standard units, hotels, motels and licensed bed and breakfasts are not covered.

  • Each rental unit is registered separately, and every owner gives contact information.
  • A responsible person must be reachable 24 hours a day about concerns.
  • Registration does not override HOA or deed restrictions, and it does not ban short-term rentals.
  • All short-term rentals must pay Hotel Occupancy Tax.

Owners register through the city's Customer Self-Service portal or in person at Development Services on the second floor of City Hall. If you plan to sell a house that has been rented to guests, confirm its registration is current so the buyer inherits a clean file.

Which Texas tax exemptions can a McKinney owner use?

Texas has no state property tax, so these exemptions come off local bills. Any taxing unit may adopt an optional homestead exemption of up to 20 percent of appraised value with a $5,000 minimum, and the Collin appraisal district's taxing entity page shows which units offer one.

Veterans rated 100 percent disabled may qualify for a total homestead exemption under Section 11.131, and lesser ratings earn smaller exemptions printed on the Comptroller's table. A buyer of a veteran's former home should ask the appraisal district what carries over.

What should heirs of a McKinney house do first?

An heir has several routes, and the choice sets the schedule. Texas allows four years from the death to offer a will for probate.

  • Muniment of title, for an estate with no debts beyond real-estate liens.
  • Small estate affidavit, used when no will exists and assets come to $75,000 or less, homestead excluded.
  • Affidavit of heirship, which buyers need not accept.
  • Transfer on death deed, recorded during the owner's life.

Ask the Collin County clerk what is filed on the property and have a title company confirm it before you accept an offer.

What hotel occupancy tax applies to McKinney short-term rentals?

McKinney charges a 7 percent city Hotel Occupancy Tax on lodging, including vacation rentals, in addition to the 6 percent state rate remitted separately. Since September 2, 2025, booking platforms that take payment for a short-term rental must collect and remit the city tax for the operator.

  • Reports and payments are due on the 20th of the month after each reporting month.
  • A report is required even in a month with no tax collected.
  • Late payment adds a 5 percent penalty at 1 to 30 days, 10 percent after 30 days, and 10 percent plus 10 percent annual interest at 60 days or more.

A seller who has run a rental should have these filings in order, because a buyer or title company may ask whether any tax is unpaid.

What can McKinney sellers pull from the Collin appraisal district before listing?

The Collin Central Appraisal District's homepage points owners to several tools worth a look before you set a price. A property search shows your value and exemptions, an interactive map shows parcel lines, and a forms page carries applications.

  • A Notice of Estimated Taxes link sends owners to the state's property tax database so they can see what local units are expected to levy.
  • A taxpayer liaison officer handles public access questions that the Tax Code requires the district to answer.
  • The district also posted a news item on a homestead exemption audit tied to Senate Bill 1801, so owners should confirm that the exemption on their account is correct.

A buyer's agent will usually pull the same record, so fixing errors in square footage or exemption status early prevents surprises during the option period.

How did McKinney grow so much so quickly?

Census counts went from 131,117 in 2010 to 195,308 in 2020, and the estimate for 2025 is 236,001. Land area grew from 62.21 to 66.96 square miles between 2010 and 2020, and population density climbed from 2,107.7 to 2,916.7 people per square mile.

Newcomers tend to be educated and well paid: 54.1 percent of adults have a bachelor's degree, per capita income is $55,643, and only 5.7 percent of residents live in poverty. About 85.5 percent of people lived in the same house a year earlier, so most owners stay put and listings come from a smaller pool than the population suggests.

Which county handles McKinney property records?

Collin County. McKinney is the county seat, about thirty-two miles north of Dallas, and the Collin Central Appraisal District and county clerk handle values and deeds.

What is a typical McKinney home worth?

The Census Bureau puts the 2020-2024 median at $471,800 for owner-occupied homes. Individual houses vary a great deal by age, size and neighborhood.

How quickly can a McKinney sale close?

It depends on the buyer and on title. A clean title closes sooner than one with liens, probate or missing heirs, so order a title search early.

Must a McKinney house go through probate before I sell it?

Usually some court or recorded step comes first. A transfer on death deed recorded before the death is the main exception, and a Texas attorney can say which route fits.

Does the Collin appraisal district publish homestead forms?

Yes. Its site lists residential homestead exemption information and forms. Ask the district for the filing deadline that applies to you.

Pick between a cash buyer, a listing and a private sale based on your deadline and the house's condition. Grand Prairie owners have an extra step before any of them: the city covers pieces of three counties and, by its own count, six school districts, so identify which combination your parcel belongs to.

That answer tells you which appraisal district holds your file and which office mails your tax bill. Pull it up early, since a buyer's title company will ask for the same information within days of a signed contract, and keep the legal description from your deed beside it so the two match.

  • Cash buyer: no financing contingency, so the closing date is negotiable.
  • Agent listing: wider exposure, slower timeline, repair requests likely.
  • Private sale: keeps the commission, adds paperwork you manage alone.

What is Grand Prairie's geography and history?

The city lies about thirteen miles west of downtown Dallas in western Dallas County and eastern Tarrant County, with a smaller piece in Ellis County. The state historical association describes a townsite of roughly eighty-one square miles hemmed in by Dallas, Arlington, Irving and Cedar Hill, crossed by Interstates 20 and 30 and State Highways 161, 180 and 303.

Mountain Creek Lake sits on the east, part of Joe Pool Lake lies to the south, and Kirby, Cottonwood and Fish creeks plus the West Fork of the Trinity River run through town. Parcels along those waterways are the ones where lenders and inspectors raise drainage questions, so keep any flood or elevation paperwork handy.

A railroad stop named Grand Prairie existed by 1877 and the community incorporated in 1902. Then came a boom: a defense aircraft plant just east of town employed as many as 38,500 workers at its peak, and the population swelled from 1,595 to about 18,000 between 1940 and the end of the war. When the plant closed on August 14, 1945, 15,000 employees lost their jobs, yet the city recovered through furniture, boat and chemical manufacturing.

Dallas annexed the industrial district east of town in 1947, so Grand Prairie began annexing neighbors itself in 1948 and adopted a home-rule charter with a city manager. It reached 30,000 people by 1960, 99,616 by 1990 and 175,396 by 2010. Tourism followed, with Six Flags Over Texas nearby, Traders Village on weekends, Lone Star Park opening in 1997, a 6,300-seat theater in 2002 and a minor league ballpark in 2008.

One more local wrinkle: the city absorbed nearby communities over the decades, including Dalworth Park in 1943 and, by the 1980s, Burbank Gardens, Florence Hill, Freetown, Idlewild-Mountain Creek and Shady Grove. Ask your title company about any older plats or easements that predate the merger.

Which taxing units bill a Grand Prairie house?

The city's own tax rates page lists the two dominant pairings: Dallas County with Grand Prairie ISD, and Tarrant County with Arlington ISD. Because the boundaries overlap six school districts, two neighbors a few blocks apart can pay different combined rates. The page sends owners to the Dallas Central Appraisal District and the Tarrant Appraisal District to work out a bill, and the rates it prints are for an earlier fiscal year, so ask for the current ones.

Texas has no state property tax; each local unit sets its own. Whoever owns the property on January 1 carries the lien for that year, so the settlement sheet apportions that year's bill.

The same page prints an average annual city property tax of $1,089 on a $248,000 home with a homestead exemption, labeled for fiscal year 2024-25, and a combined sales tax of 8.25 percent (6.25 percent state, 2 percent city). Treat both as reference points and read your own notice for current figures.

What does Grand Prairie require of nightly-rental hosts?

Yes. Grand Prairie's council adopted a short-term rental ordinance on May 17, 2022, requiring an annual permit and hotel occupancy tax paid straight to the city every month. It applies to any residence advertised for stays of one to thirty consecutive days, whether the listing is on a booking site or social media.

Operators who do not own the property need written permission from the owner. If an HOA governs the neighborhood, check its rules first, because the city warns that the application fee cannot be refunded. A seller who inherits or buys a house with a rental history should ask for the permit paperwork and the tax filings, since the buyer takes on whatever the property has been doing.

  • Permits renew every year.
  • Hotel tax is paid monthly to the city.
  • Non-owner operators need an owner's statement.

What if I owe more than I can pay on a Grand Prairie mortgage?

Texas lenders normally skip the courthouse and sell under the deed of trust's power of sale. The sale is a public auction held on a month's first Tuesday, preceded by a notice of default with a 20-day window to catch up and a notice of sale at least 21 days before the auction. Posting at the courthouse and filing with the county clerk are required.

That gives you a short runway. Closing a sale before the auction pays the lender from the proceeds and protects any equity you have. If a foreclosure happens anyway, the lender may sue for the shortfall within two years, and you can ask the court to credit fair market value. Extra sale money goes to junior lien holders first and then to you.

Federal rules usually prevent a servicer from starting the process until the loan is more than 120 days late, so contact the servicer and a housing counselor as soon as you see trouble coming.

How are inherited Grand Prairie houses handled?

Heirs need legal authority before they can sell. Which paperwork supplies it depends on the estate: a probated will, a muniment of title, an executor's deed, a recorded transfer on death deed or an affidavit of heirship. The Texas State Law Library guide walks through each, and a will usually has to be probated within four years of death.

A Grand Prairie estate can touch the Dallas, Tarrant or Ellis County clerk, depending on which county the parcel is in.

Often within a few weeks, if title is clear. Liens, unpaid taxes and unfinished probate are the usual causes of delay.

Which appraisal district applies to my address?

Check your tax bill or the city's tax rates page. Dallas County addresses use the Dallas Central Appraisal District and Tarrant County addresses use the Tarrant Appraisal District.

Who pays the current year's taxes when I sell?

The settlement sheet usually apportions them. Unpaid prior balances come out of your proceeds because Texas tax liens follow the property.

Is hotel occupancy tax due on a Grand Prairie rental?

Yes, if guests stay one to thirty days. The city collects it monthly from permitted short-term rental operators.

Can heirs sell a Grand Prairie house before the estate is settled?

Only with proper authority, such as a court-approved route or a recorded transfer on death deed. Ask the title company which document it will accept.

Data source: the Census Bureau's QuickFacts table for Amarillo.

A mean commute of 19.6 minutes is short for a city of 102 square miles. The Census Bureau also counts 10,973 veterans in the 2020-2024 estimates, so disabled veteran exemptions are worth asking about when you sell or buy.

How did Amarillo develop, and what does it mean for homes today?

Amarillo was platted in April 1887 along the Fort Worth and Denver City Railway in Potter County and named for a nearby lake and creek, probably after the yellow soil or spring wildflowers. The Texas State Historical Association says the first site was on low ground that would flood, so a rancher and his partner bought land to the east in 1888 and drew merchants to higher ground. By 1890 the town's center had moved a mile east, and the county seat followed in 1893.

The economy grew from cattle shipping into wheat, gas, oil and helium. Gas was discovered in 1918 and oil in 1921, and the Cliffside field's helium led to a federal helium plant in 1928. In World War II Amarillo hosted an Army Air Field and the nearby Pantex plant, and the city's population hit 51,686 by 1940. Interstate 40 and Interstate 27 later pulled new housing and shopping toward the south and west, according to the Handbook of Texas.

The same source describes a city that by 1980 had 149,230 residents and more than sixty square miles within Potter and Randall counties. Gas, petroleum, agriculture and cattle remain the entry's named income sources, and the Census data shows a large health care sector, with healthcare receipts of $2,777,390 thousand in 2022.

How do taxes work for a house in the Randall County part of Amarillo?

Randall County's tax office mails statements each October 1, and they are due on receipt. Paying by January 31 avoids penalty and interest, and February 1 starts delinquency. A payment sent by first-class mail counts as paid on the date of the post office cancellation mark.

The Randall County tax office also explains how a sale affects the bill:

  • The taxing unit does not prorate the year. Most sales contracts split the year's taxes between buyer and seller, so check the contract and closing statement.
  • Whoever owned the house on the first of January of the prior year remains liable for that year's tax, and the unit can also pursue the buyer through the lien.
  • Over-65, disabled and veteran homesteads can pay in four installments, with the first fourth and a signed agreement due by January 31. A first payment received by February 28 carries 7% penalty and interest, and a missed installment adds 6% penalty plus 1% interest each month.

A tax certificate shows delinquent taxes, penalties and interest for each taxing unit. The fee is $10, paid in certified funds at pickup, and you can request it by email and pick it up at either the Canyon or the Amarillo office. If taxes are due and you want a zero-balance certificate, pay with cash or certified funds or wait 10 working days for a check to clear.

The Potter Randall Appraisal District is at 5701 Hollywood Road, Amarillo, with a phone number of 806-358-1601 and a mailing address of P.O. Box 7190, Amarillo, TX 79114. For a parcel in Potter County, ask the Potter County tax assessor-collector for the same certificate.

Which Amarillo permit and platting rules affect a sale?

Amarillo's Building Safety office is in the Simms Municipal Building at 808 S Buchanan Street, Suite 104, open weekdays from eight to five, and permits go through the MGO Connect online portal. The city's ordinance Sec. 4-10-21 says land cannot be used unless a Certificate of Occupancy and Compliance has been issued.

A Certificate of Occupancy is issued automatically for new buildings when the permit is completed. A separate certificate is needed when the use changes or when none was ever issued, and alterations require a remodel or repair permit with a registered contractor. For a house with a converted garage, a rented room or a business use, ask Building Safety whether the certificate matches what the house is today.

Platting matters if you want to sell part of a lot. The county's FAQ explains that a plat is required when land is divided for sale, and that in Amarillo it applies to any tract inside the city limits and to tracts of five acres or less in the extraterritorial jurisdiction extending five miles beyond the limits.

Does flood risk affect an Amarillo sale?

It can. The original town site was moved to higher ground after flooding concerns in 1888 and 1889, and drainage on the High Plains is still a buyer question. Randall County's floodplain page explains that a 100-year flood is a flood level with a 1% or greater chance of being equaled or exceeded in any year, not one that happens once a century.

  • You can request flood information from the county floodplain administrator by giving the Randall appraisal ID, the address and the legal description.
  • The Flood Insurance Rate Map shows special flood hazard areas, and a Letter of Map Amendment can remove a property that was mapped in by mistake.
  • Under the county's floodplain rules, improvements or repairs costing 50% or more of a building's market value count as substantial improvement or substantial damage.
  • Building without required county floodplain permits can bring fines up to $500 per day.

Lenders can require flood insurance independently of a map change, so a buyer's lender has the final say.

What if the Amarillo house is inherited, behind on payments or rented?

Texas gives owners a few timelines to work with, and Panhandle counties follow the same rules as the rest of the state.

  • Inherited: an heir not on the recorded deed must give the appraisal district an affidavit of ownership interest, the death certificate and a recent utility bill to claim the homestead exemption.
  • Behind on payments: lenders generally wait until a loan is more than 120 days late. A notice of sale must go out at least 21 days ahead of the first-Tuesday auction.
  • Tenants: written notice to vacate is at least three days unless the lease says otherwise. Eviction cases are filed in justice court, and a writ of possession is available six days after judgment.

Each of these paths can end in a sale, and the earlier you pick one, the more room you have.

More questions about Amarillo, TX

Is Amarillo in Potter County or Randall County?

Both. The Handbook of Texas says the city is in southern Potter County and extends into Randall County, so a house's county depends on its parcel.

What is the due date for Randall County property tax?

On receipt. Pay by January 31 to avoid penalty and interest. Statements are mailed each October 1, and unpaid taxes are delinquent on February 1.

How much is a tax certificate in Randall County?

The fee is $10, paid with certified funds when you pick it up at the Canyon or Amarillo office. The certificate lists delinquent taxes for each taxing unit.

Does Amarillo require a Certificate of Occupancy?

Yes, under city ordinance Sec. 4-10-21. It is issued automatically for new buildings, and an existing property may need one if none was issued or the use changes.

What does a typical Amarillo owner-occupied home cost?

The Census Bureau's 2020-2024 median value for owner-occupied homes in Amarillo is $196,900.

What should you know before selling a house in Brownsville, TX?

Brownsville is the county seat of Cameron County, at the southernmost tip of Texas across the Rio Grande from Matamoros. Sellers deal with the Cameron Appraisal District, the county clerk and a border economy built on trade and a deepwater port.

The Census Bureau puts the mid-2025 population at 192,957, which is 3.6% above the 2020 estimates base. Residents often handle paperwork in two languages, since 83.6% of people age five and older speak another language at home.

How did the border, the river and the port shape Brownsville neighborhoods?

Per the Handbook of Texas, the town started beside Fort Brown, named for an officer killed during the 1846 siege. Charles Stillman and partners platted a 4,676 acre townsite in 1848, lots sold for as much as $1,500, and the new Cameron County seat was Brownsville by January 13, 1849.

Ownership of the original land grant stayed contested until a U.S. Supreme Court decision in 1879. The first train arrived in 1904, a rail bridge to Matamoros opened in 1910, and northern farmers introduced irrigated citrus and vegetables. A 1920s land boom lifted the population to 22,021 by 1930. Voters approved a navigation district in December 1928, and the port opened May 15, 1936, using a 17-mile channel to the Gulf.

After the war, shrimpers from Texas and Louisiana made the town a leading shrimp shipper, and cotton briefly turned the port into the world's top cotton exporter in the early 1950s. A Union Carbide plant started construction in 1959. Each of those booms added housing and jobs to the city.

  • Southern end of U.S. highways 77 and 83
  • Postwar shrimp, citrus and cotton shipping, then petrochemicals
  • The fort was deactivated in 1945 and its grounds were eventually given to the city
  • Palmito Ranch, the last Civil War battle, was fought just outside town in 1865

What do Census figures say about Brownsville homes?

The 2020-2024 midpoint for an owner-occupied Brownsville home is $139,900, and 61.7% of units are lived in by owners. Renters pay a midpoint of $923 a month.

Who sets the value of a Brownsville house for tax purposes?

The Cameron Appraisal District sets value, and each taxing unit chooses its own rate. By its own FAQ, the district reappraises every property at least once in three years and can do so yearly where the market moves fast.

A notice of appraised value is not required if value rises by $1,000 or less, so some owners never get a mailing. A homestead's assessed value is capped at 10% growth under Section 23.23 of the Tax Code, in force since January 1, 2008. Added rooms, pools and similar improvements are not covered.

How do homestead exemptions work with the Cameron Appraisal District?

Every owner must show Texas residency, such as a driver's license, and both spouses must apply and supply identification. The primary residence exemptions are homestead, over-65, disabled person and 100% disabled veteran, while a disabled veteran exemption may be placed on any one property the veteran owns.

  • You may claim over-65 or disabled in a year, not both
  • When only some co-owners live in the house, the account splits and the exemption is multiplied by the qualifying owner's percentage of ownership
  • The school tax ceiling rises if you add a pool, garage or room, and transfers to a new Texas homestead on a Tax Ceiling Transfer form

A few exemption types need a fresh application by April 30 every year, so ask the district which applies.

How do you contest a Brownsville appraisal?

The protest has to be written, and the deadline is the later of May 15 or 30 days after the notice was delivered. Mail, hand delivery and email all work, with mailed filings needing a postmark by the cutoff.

The district states that after the deadline neither an appraiser nor the board may change the value. Hospitalization can be good cause, but forgetting the date is not. A timely protest earns at least 15 days' notice of a hearing that usually runs about 15 minutes. Disputing the result opens three options: district court, binding arbitration, or, in Cameron County, the State Office of Administrative Hearings.

  • Identify the owner and the property by address or account number
  • Say what you contest, such as market value
  • Attach comparable sales, photos or repair estimates

How does the Texas tax calendar affect a Brownsville seller?

Value and lien both date to January 1. The Cameron County Tax Office sits at the same East Levee Street address as the clerk, and bills arrive around October 1. Ask that office which units bill your address.

Unpaid balances go delinquent February 1 and pick up a six percent penalty plus one percent interest. The penalty becomes 12 percent after July 1, and a taxing unit's attorney may add as much as 20 percent. Clear title is impossible with delinquent tax outstanding, so pay any balance before closing.

What if a Brownsville property is headed for a tax sale?

Constables or hired agents run tax sales as auctions, and no statewide list exists. County tax office and clerk sites carry the notices.

A homestead, farm or mineral owner can redeem within two years of the purchaser's deed being filed, paying a 25% premium in year one or 50% in year two plus costs. Other property has 180 days and a premium up to 25%. A former owner has two years from the sale to claim surplus proceeds.

How do heirs handle an inherited Brownsville house?

Family land in the Valley sometimes stays in the name of a person who died long ago. An affidavit of heirship is sworn and filed with the county clerk, but no court reviews it and nothing requires a title insurer to accept it.

Sturdier paths include probate inside four years, a muniment of title where the only debts are liens on the real estate, or a transfer on death deed filed before the owner's death. For exemption purposes, heirs missing from a recorded deed give the appraisal district an affidavit of ownership interest, the death certificate and a recent utility bill.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Where does a Brownsville deed get recorded?

The Cameron County Clerk, at 835 E. Levee Street in Brownsville, keeps deeds, liens, plats and maps. Cameron CAD updates ownership after it receives a recorded instrument or its volume and page numbers.

The state clerk manual lists a $5.00 first page and $4.00 for each added page, with further fees. Ask the clerk for the total on your deed.

More questions about Brownsville, TX

What does a typical Brownsville home cost?

The Census Bureau's 2020-2024 midpoint for owner-occupied homes is $139,900. Your own price depends on condition, lot and street.

Will Cameron CAD always mail a value notice?

No. It sends notices to those entitled by law, and none is required when value rises by $1,000 or less.

When is a Brownsville appraisal protest due?

The later of May 15 or 30 days after the notice was delivered. File it in writing by mail, by hand or by email.

Where can I get a copy of my Brownsville deed?

At the Cameron County Clerk's office on East Levee Street. The appraisal district does not supply deeds, surveys or plats.

Does a Brownsville homeowner over 65 get a tax ceiling?

Yes. School taxes on the residence generally stop rising while you own and live there, and the ceiling can move to a new Texas homestead.

Who sells a house fast in Denton, and what are the real choices?

Three routes exist for a Denton house: put it on the market through an agent, find a buyer yourself, or sign with a cash buyer. Your calendar and the shape of the roof, kitchen and systems usually decide among them.

A Denton house is taxed and recorded through Denton County. Investors who want rentals compete here with families who want a home to live in, and that mix can help a seller with a dated or damaged house, because an investor prices the repairs into the offer and does not ask you to fix them first.

  • Agent listing: the largest audience of buyers, paid for with showing disruption, post-inspection repair requests and a wait on mortgage approval.
  • Owner sale: the commission stays with you; so do the contract, the disclosure form and every negotiation.
  • Cash purchase: a faster calendar and fewer contingencies, with the discount that comes from buying a house unrepaired.

What makes Denton homes different when it is time to sell?

Denton has an old core, and that matters when you sell. The city's historic designations page says Denton has 69 local historic landmarks spread across more than seven architectural styles, with a heavy concentration along West Oak Street, plus three local historic districts covering over 80 acres on the west and north sides.

If your house is a landmark, the page says exterior changes go through a design review process and demolition needs approval from the Historic Landmark Commission. Designation does not change the zoned use of the property. A renovator will raise this early. Check whether your address carries a local designation before any contract is signed. The city's development staff take those questions at development@cityofdenton.com.

Newer subdivisions have no such overlay, and buyers there focus on the roof, the foundation and the age of the mechanical systems. Whatever the neighborhood, a written offer that states who pays for repairs is worth more than a verbal range.

Can a buyer in Denton run my house as a vacation rental?

Only with a city registration. Denton defines a short-term rental as renting a whole dwelling unit or a bedroom for at least 24 hours and no more than 29 consecutive days, and every operator must register with the city.

The city's page says the City Council approved amendments to the Denton Development Code on October 22, 2024, that changed these rules. It lists a registration cost of $150, valid for one calendar year, with applications and renewals filed through the city's STR permit system. For the packet and the full requirements, the city points to Development Services at (940) 349-8600 or building@cityofdenton.com.

A city notice for a June 2024 hearing on the revision said violations could carry a maximum penalty of $2,000. The Denton Development Code holds the text that governs, so read it or ask Development Services. This matters to you as a seller for two reasons. If you rent your house on short stays now, a buyer will ask whether the registration is current. And if a buyer wants to use the house that way, the offer depends on rules you cannot promise on their behalf. Send buyers to the city with that question.

What do I need to know about permits before selling in Denton?

Unpermitted work is the most common surprise, so go through your records before a sale goes under contract. Denton runs permitting through its Development Service Center, and the revision to the short-term rental rules sits in the same Development Code that governs residential building, and its permits page notes that as of January 2, 2026 the center closes at noon on Fridays, with Friday afternoon occupied inspections taken by phone at (940) 349-8195.

Request the permit history for your address if you added a room, a deck, a garage conversion or new electrical service. An inspector or lender may ask to see closed permits. If something was built without one, you can still sell, but you will either need to resolve it or accept a lower price from a buyer who takes that risk.

  • Gather receipts and permit numbers for any major work.

How does a Texas sale close once I accept an offer in Denton?

Expect a title company or lawyer to draft the deed, a notary to witness your signature, and a filing with Denton County's clerk, since Texas records deeds in the county of the land.

The Texas Courts clerk manual says an unacknowledged deed cannot be filed, and the closing agent can quote the clerk's charges. The title company can give you the final recording total.

A tax lien for the year attaches on January 1, so whoever owns the house then is liable. Late-payment charges start in February, and the title company normally settles the year's tax at closing. Get your balance from the Denton County tax office early, so the closing date does not catch you out.

What if I inherited the house, am behind on payments or owe back taxes?

Each situation has its own clock, and the state's self-help pages lay them out. If the house came through a death, Texas gives four years to probate a will, and an affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement lodged with the county clerk, which no law obliges a buyer to honor. Title companies set their own proof standards, so raise it early.

If a mortgage is behind, the State Law Library says the lender first sends a default notice, and you can reinstate by paying the arrears within 20 days. An auction notice follows, and the sale takes place on a first Tuesday. A cash buyer can sometimes close before that date.

For back property taxes, ask the Denton County tax office whether the account has gone to a suit. Penalty waivers exist in some cases if you pay promptly and ask in writing, so raise it with the tax office.

More questions about Denton, TX

Is there a fee to register a short-term rental in Denton?

Yes. The city's page lists a registration cost of $150, valid for one calendar year. Renewals go through the same STR permit system.

Not for the sale itself. Permits apply to construction work, so check whether past work on your house was permitted. Call Development Services at (940) 349-8600 if you are unsure.

Who bills property tax on a Denton house?

The tax office of the county and each taxing unit set the bill, and the appraisal district sets the value. Texas has no state property tax. Ask the Denton County tax office for your current balance.

Can I sell a Denton house that has a historic landmark designation?

Yes. The city says designation does not affect the use of a property, which zoning controls. It does add design review for exterior changes and requires Historic Landmark Commission approval before demolition.

How soon can a cash sale close in Denton?

The timeline is set in the contract you sign, so ask for the closing date in writing. Title work, a probate or lien problem, or an unpaid tax bill can add time.

What shapes the Killeen housing market?

Killeen sits right outside the East Gate of Fort Hood, and the post's soldiers and families drive much of the demand for houses and rentals. The city's own newcomer page for the installation links to local resources, transit and parks.

That connection means military moves, deployments and orders affect timing. Anyone with a permanent change of station order cares most about a firm closing date, and an as-is sale can deliver one.

What is downtown Killeen, and do special rules apply there?

Who runs Killeen, and where do I go for a permit?

The 1949 city charter set up a council-manager system. A mayor and seven council members set policy, with four members elected by district and the rest at large, and elections held each May.

Permits and code questions go through city Development Services, while the appraisal side sits with the county. The city's home page also notes its adopted rate for the fiscal year that runs October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027: 73.01 cents, with the notice saying the rate raises maintenance and operations taxes compared with the prior year's rate. Who sets Killeen property tax values and bills?

Bell Central Appraisal District sets values for Killeen in Bell County, and the city and other units set rates. Bell CAD accepts payment at its offices with no fee for check, cash or money order, while its online and phone options go through a vendor that charges fees.

It also lists a quarterly installment agreement, a homestead delinquent-tax installment agreement and a tax deferral option. Its home page notes that homestead assessed value increases of up to 10 percent a year are mandatory under the Property Tax Code until assessed value matches market value.

What exemptions does Bell CAD list?

Bell CAD lists several exemptions, and military households should look at the veteran items in particular.

  • Residence homestead
  • Disabled person and age 65 or older, including surviving spouses
  • 100 percent disabled veteran or surviving spouse
  • Surviving spouse of a service member killed in action or of a first responder killed on duty
  • Donated residence of a partially disabled veteran

It asks for a current driver license or Texas ID, a Social Security letter for disability, and a recent VA award letter for veterans. No annual renewal is needed, though the chief appraiser may request updated applications. When you sell, the buyer applies for their own exemption.

How do Texas tax dates apply to a Killeen sale?

The January 1 value and lien date, the October bills and the February 1 delinquency date set the rhythm of a Killeen closing.

What options do I have if I must sell fast in Killeen?

  • Skipping the agent keeps the commission and leaves buyer management to you.
  • A cash offer takes the house unrepaired and sets the closing date with you, which suits a PCS move, a rental with problem tenants or an inherited house.

If you rent the house out from another duty station, remember the tenant side has its own court process.

What if squatters or an unwanted occupant are in my Killeen house?

Texas Property Code chapter 24B lets an owner ask the sheriff or constable for removal without a court case. The occupant must have stayed after being told to go, the property must not have been open to the public when they entered, no suit may be pending between you, and the occupant cannot be family or a current or former tenant. A removal later found wrongful can bring a lawsuit against the person who asked for it.

A real tenant is different and needs an eviction suit. Adverse possession is another idea: it means an open, hostile claim to land, with a ten-year period in the usual case. A vacant Killeen rental invites trouble, so check on it often.

You can sell with the lease intact or end the tenancy as the lease allows. For unpaid rent Texas requires a written notice to vacate, and the suit is filed in justice court. The tenant is served several days before trial, and either side has only five days to appeal to county court.

Once judgment is final, the writ of possession waits a few days and is then followed by a 24-hour warning. Federal notice rules may add time on some covered properties. A cash buyer may take the house with renters still inside, so you skip the court calendar.

For a seller in a military household, Bell CAD's veteran exemptions are worth knowing about, since the donated residence of a partially disabled veteran and the surviving-spouse items are named on its page.

Texas also lets disabled veterans apply late in some cases, and Bell CAD says that if you file after April 30 you should still submit an application so the office can apply any remedy the law provides once it approves it. Gather a recent VA award letter before you call.

How are deeds recorded, and what about probate or foreclosure?

The Bell County clerk records deeds for land in the county once a notary has acknowledged the signature, and the title company files at closing.

If the loan is behind, Texas runs the foreclosure outside court: a default letter, a short cure window, a courthouse notice and a first-Tuesday auction. If the owner has died, a will normally goes to probate within a few years of the death, and a small estate affidavit is only for modest estates without much real property. It runs between Rancier Avenue (FM 439) and Veterans Memorial Boulevard (Business 190), just outside Fort Hood's East Gate.

Yes, for vacant structures inside the Historic Overlay District. A 2020 ordinance requires registration with Planning and Development Services and an annual fee.

The city's home page announces a 73.01 cent rate for the fiscal year October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027, shown as adopted. Check the full notice and your tax statement for your own figure.

Does Bell CAD offer payment plans?

Yes. Cash buyers can set the closing date around orders. A traditional listing takes longer but can bring a higher price with a house in good condition.

Is a quick sale realistic for a Mesquite home?

Often it is. A Mesquite house can go to a cash buyer, onto the market with an agent, or to a landlord, and the best fit turns on repairs needed and your deadline.

The city's fact sheet places Mesquite 15 minutes east of downtown Dallas. Commuters, investors and landlords all shop here, which helps when a house needs work you would rather skip.

What should a seller know about Mesquite itself?

Mesquite is a large Dallas suburb of more than 155,000 residents, covering almost 50 square miles. The city describes itself as the official Rodeo Capital of Texas and lists 70-plus parks, about 250 dining options and 52 public school campuses.

The town began as a depot on the Texas and Pacific Railway in May 1873 and became a city on December 3, 1887. The 1890 census counted 135 people. Of Mesquite's residents, the city says one in five is foreign-born, so a listing there reaches a varied buyer pool.

Roads are a selling point for buyers. The city places itself at the crossroads of Interstates 20, 30 and 635, State Highway 352 and U.S. Highway 80. The city lists 35 minutes to either DFW International or Dallas Love Field.

  • Major employers named by the city: Ashley Furniture, PepsiCo, FedEx Ground, Walmart, UPS, Orora Visual, Canadian Solar, Mesquite ISD and Town East Mall.
  • Three higher-education institutions are listed.

  • Cash buyer. Quickest path, often with no repairs, at a price that accounts for the buyer's work.
  • Landlord or investor. Natural for houses with tenants; that buyer then deals with Mesquite's license rules.

What does Mesquite require if the house has been a rental?

Every rental in Mesquite must be registered, and a Single-Family Rental Property License is issued only after the home passes an inspection. If your buyer plans to rent the house, they will need to run this process themselves.

The city's review checks that property taxes are current, that no liens are outstanding, and that a local property manager or owner lives within 40 miles of Mesquite. Passing homes receive a green tag valid for 90 days, and the new tenant must start water service within that window. The license ends when the tenant changes or after three years with the same tenant, whichever comes first.

Do I need permits for repairs before selling in Mesquite?

Open permits can stall a sale, so ask the city about any past work on the property. Mesquite's rental pages say all permits must be finalized before an inspection, and the city publishes a document on permit requirements for unpermitted work.

If you finished a garage, enclosed a patio or replaced mechanical systems years ago, confirm the permit was closed. What if a tenant occupies the Mesquite house?

A sale is still possible, though the occupant keeps rights until a lawful process ends. The notice to vacate must be written and give at least three days, unless the lease sets a different period. Delivery options include hand delivery, posting inside the home, mail, or email when the lease allows it.

If the tenant remains, a justice court case follows. Trial comes at least four days after service, with a hearing 10 to 21 days after filing. Appeal to county court is due within five days of judgment, and a writ of possession can issue six days after final judgment. Covered properties may need a 30-day federal notice.

Most sales follow the same sequence regardless of buyer type. Knowing it lets you judge whether a promised closing date is realistic.

  • Offer and contract: you accept written terms and open title with a title company.
  • Title search: the company looks for liens, back taxes and recording problems on the property.
  • Rental or permit review: if the house was a rental or had work done, close out licenses and permits.
  • Closing: both sides sign, the deed is filed with the county clerk, and you receive net proceeds.

A lender-financed buyer adds an appraisal and underwriting step. A cash buyer skips both, which is the main reason cash closings are quicker. Ask your title contact for an estimated closing statement a few days before you sign.

How do Texas taxes get settled when a Mesquite house sells?

The tax lien attaches on January 1, and whoever owns the home that day owes that year's bill. Bills mail around October 1.

  • A penalty and interest begin after January 31.
  • Splitting is allowed: half by November 30, half by June 30.
  • Owners 65 or older can use four installments.
  • A buyer closing after January 1 may claim a homestead for the remainder of that year if you had not.

Expect the title company to prorate and pay the bill out of your funds. Request a payoff and proration sheet before signing. The Comptroller's payment page has the rules.

Where does the Mesquite deed get filed?

The deed goes to the clerk of the county where the parcel lies. Mesquite's own history says the first plat of the townsite was filed with Dallas County in 1873.

Recording needs a signature acknowledged before a notary or similar officer. The 2023 clerk manual shows $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for every added page, plus capped records fees. Ask the clerk for the schedule now in force.

What if I am behind on payments or inherited the house?

Both situations carry deadlines. A lender who forecloses uses a public auction held on the first Tuesday of a month, after 21 days' posted notice. Paying the overdue sum within 20 days of the default notice can stop the process. A sale ahead of the auction date can protect equity.

For an inherited house, probate a will within four years of death. Heirs may need a muniment of title, a small estate affidavit, or full administration to prove who signs. The State Law Library probate guide covers each. A title company may refuse a bare affidavit of heirship.

Pull together your deed, latest tax bill, payoff letter and any rental license or permit papers. Then collect cash offers and compare them to a listing estimate. Ask each buyer about closing costs and timing, and keep the answers in writing.

Should I fix up the house first?

Not for a cash sale. Buyers commonly accept the house as is. Repairs pay off more when you list and expect financed buyers whose appraisers may require fixes.

Does the city regulate houses sold to landlords?

Every rental needs registration, an inspection and a local contact within 40 miles. The license lapses with a tenant change or after three years with the same tenant.

The title company prorates the year's bill and pays your portion from proceeds. Because the lien attaches January 1, review the split on the closing statement.

What happens to liens on the house?

They are satisfied from the proceeds at closing, listed on a payoff statement from the title company. Mesquite's rental review also wants taxes current and no open liens.

The Census Bureau estimated 150,640 residents on July 1, 2025, up 5.9 percent from 142,188 in the 2020 base. Growth is steady rather than explosive, and 28.2 percent of residents are under 18.

McAllen is one of the lower-priced large cities in Texas. For 2020-2024 the median owner-occupied value was $190,400, median household income was $61,579 and the poverty rate was 20.0 percent.

Where is McAllen, and how did it begin?

McAllen is on U.S. Highway 83 in southern Hidalgo County, so Hidalgo County offices handle its deeds and tax accounts. The Handbook of Texas traces the site to Spanish land grants of 1767 and the later McAllen Ranch.

The railroad reached the ranch on August 20, 1904, and a townsite company formed that December and named the town for John McAllen. A rival settlement called East McAllen grew two miles away. The town incorporated in 1911 and adopted a home rule charter in 1927.

A toll bridge to Reynosa opened in 1941, which made McAllen a port of entry and a winter tourist stop. The city took the nickname City of Palms and later hosted a foreign trade zone. The Handbook also notes that colonias of varying size ring the city, so a buyer may ask about utilities and lot status.

  • Ask the Hidalgo County tax office what the account owes, including older years.
  • Confirm homestead, over-65, disability or veteran exemptions with the Hidalgo appraisal district.

Census figures show 87.0 percent of McAllen residents identify as Hispanic or Latino, and 73.7 percent of people five and older use another language at home. Many transactions run in English and Spanish, so a bilingual title officer and translated documents can help a sale move along.

Can I rent out a McAllen house by the night?

Yes, but McAllen requires an annual registration for each rental unit. The city defines a short-term rental as use of a residential dwelling or accessory building for less than 30 consecutive days, and the environmental health and code compliance department handles the paperwork at the McAllen Development Center on North 15th Street.

If you are selling a house that guests have used, a buyer will want to know the registration is in good standing. The ordinance sets the rules a registrant must meet:

  • The operator names a local contact who can be reached around the clock and who must respond in person within one hour to complaints.
  • Every sleeping space needs a working smoke detector, and a map of exits must be posted.
  • Operators file a monthly hotel occupancy tax report even in months with no bookings.

Breaking the article is a Class C misdemeanor, fined up to $500 for each offense, with every day treated as its own offense. The director may revoke a permit, after which the property cannot reapply for twelve months. The article also says registration does not override private deed restrictions, so check any HOA rules too.

How does eviction work if a McAllen house has a tenant?

Eviction starts with written notice to vacate, usually three days unless the lease says otherwise, and moves to justice court.

  • The court sets the hearing within a window of 10 to 21 days from filing.
  • Losing parties have 5 days from judgment to appeal to county court.
  • A writ of possession becomes available on day six after final judgment.

How do Hidalgo County appraisal notices and protests work for McAllen owners?

Each spring the Hidalgo County Appraisal District sends a Notice of Appraised Value to owners whose market value climbed by $1,000 or more. The notice lists three figures: market value as of January 1, the assessed or net appraised value after limits such as a homestead cap, and the taxable value after exemptions.

If the market value looks too high, the owner can protest it. The district's deadline is May 15 or 30 days after the notice is mailed, whichever is later, and a protest can be mailed or handed in at its office on South Professional Drive in Edinburg. After filing, the owner can see the district's evidence through an online account and meet an appraiser in an informal meeting. Anyone who declines the settlement offer goes before the Appraisal Review Board, and a family member or friend can represent you if you file an Appointment of Agent form.

For a seller, a lower value helps only the tax bill, not the sale price. A buyer still pays what the market bears, but a protest filed before closing can lower the tax prorated between you.

What if a McAllen owner is behind or has died?

A sale that closes before a foreclosure auction can keep the equity with the owner and head off a deficiency suit. Inherited houses follow different tracks: a transfer on death deed recorded in the owner's lifetime avoids probate, while heirs without one may file a muniment of title or an affidavit of heirship, which a buyer can decline.

What do McAllen's Census numbers say about growth and health coverage?

McAllen's land area grew from 48.34 square miles in 2010 to 62.31 in 2020, while its population density slipped from 2,686.5 to 2,282.4 people per square mile, which fits a city that has annexed land. The 2025 estimate of 150,640 compares with 129,877 in 2010.

Households average 2.95 people, and 89.0 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier. The Census Bureau reports 26.9 percent of residents under 65 without health insurance and 8.5 percent with a disability, figures that help explain why some owners face medical bills alongside housing costs. About 95.9 percent of households have a computer and 92.2 percent have broadband.

Hidalgo County. The Handbook of Texas places McAllen in the southern part of the county, so Hidalgo County offices handle your deed and tax account.

The 2020-2024 estimate is $190,400 for an owned home. Repairs, size and age move any single house away from that figure.

Sometimes, if the owner recorded a transfer on death deed beforehand. Without one, heirs choose among probate, a muniment of title and an affidavit of heirship.

Expect a hearing 10 to 21 days after filing, then a writ of possession from day six after judgment. Appeals have a 5 day limit.

Will a fast sale work for a Pasadena home?

Yes. Pasadena sits in southeastern Harris County, and houses there sell by cash offer, investor purchase or agent listing. The fastest closings happen when the seller has the deed, a mortgage payoff figure and a tax certificate ready before the contract is signed.

What slows a Pasadena sale is usually not the buyer. It is a title problem, an unpaid tax year, a tenant, or heirs who have not agreed. This page covers the local picture, the Harris County tax steps a seller meets, and the situations that call for extra paperwork.

Because Harris County is large, give the title company your full legal description and the account number from your tax statement at the start. That avoids mix-ups with similar addresses elsewhere in the county.

How did Pasadena grow into an industrial suburb?

Pasadena is an industrial suburb with a farming past. The Handbook of Texas entry, linked from the city's own site, says John H. Burnett of Galveston founded it in 1893 and named it after Pasadena, California. A rail line came through in 1894, and after the 1900 Galveston hurricane the area became a strawberry center for Gulf Coast farmers.

The economy changed in the late 1930s as ship channel industries grew. Pasadena had 3,436 residents in 1940 and 22,483 in 1950, and the city annexed Deepwater, Middle Bayou and Red Bluff. By 1980 it covered 58.6 square miles. Refineries, the Bayport industrial district and the Johnson Space Center in nearby Clear Lake are tied to local jobs.

Pasadena voted to incorporate in 1923, disincorporated in 1924, and voted again in 1928. The residents formed an independent school system in 1899, the first in Harris County, and the Pasadena district absorbed the Genoa and South Houston districts in 1935.

Who bills property tax on a Pasadena house?

The Harris County Tax Office collects on Pasadena homes alongside the other units on the bill, and the Harris Central Appraisal District sets the values. The Comptroller's basics page describes an appraiser of record each January 1 that leaves rate setting to the taxing units.

The county's FAQ says statements are due on receipt and should be paid by January 31 of the next year. Pay by then and no penalty or interest is added. Request a statement from the tax office before you take an offer, so the figure in your contract matches the county's record.

What do Harris County's penalty and payment rules look like?

A seller whose taxes are behind can pay them from closing proceeds, so a delinquency does not by itself block a sale. It does raise the payoff, so ask for a figure dated for your closing day.

What payment plans does Harris County describe for late taxes?

Harris County's FAQ lays out several ways to catch up. A homestead owner can enter an installment agreement at any time once taxes are delinquent, and current-year agreements open on the first business day of February. The county says requests are accepted after January 31 and before March 1, with the 6 percent penalty and 1 percent interest assessed for February.

  • Payment plans run from 12 months up to 36 months for homestead property.
  • A deferral can protect the amount owed, but interest of 5 percent per year is added for each year taxes stay delinquent.
  • Online and phone payments count if completed by 11:59 p.m. on or before the due date.
  • Mail must be postmarked on or before the due date.

A seller planning to move can use a plan to buy time, then pay the balance from closing proceeds.

How do taxes get handled at a Pasadena closing?

The title company asks for a tax certificate showing what is paid, and any unpaid amount comes out of your proceeds. The county FAQ warns about one timing trap: a closing between November 15 and January 31 on a mortgage that escrows taxes. If that is you, call the lender once the date is set so the bill is paid and the certificate is clean.

  • Tell the title company if the lender paid this year's bill from escrow.
  • Ask for any escrow balance back after the payoff.
  • If you claimed a homestead exemption and then sold, the county asks you to correct the account.

Taxes that stay unpaid keep a lien on the property, so the buyer's title will not be clear until they are paid.

What exemptions and caps should a Pasadena owner check before selling?

Exemptions shape the bill the next owner will see. The Comptroller says school districts must grant a $140,000 homestead exemption, with a further $60,000 for seniors and disabled owners.

  • Homestead value growth is capped at 10 percent a year.
  • Disabled veterans may get $5,000 to $12,000 by rating, and a 100 percent rating can mean a full exemption.
  • A late-year buyer may claim the exemption for the rest of that year if you never did.

Several taxing units can sit on one Pasadena bill, so look at every line.

What if the Pasadena house has a tenant or a tax judgment?

A sale is still possible, and each case has its own Texas procedure.

  • Tenant. An eviction begins with written notice to vacate and a justice court case, and a writ of possession is available six days after a final judgment. A buyer will ask for the lease and deposit details.
  • Tax judgment. Harris County says the eight constables hold the tax sales for property taken to judgment, buyers take the property as is, and sales are final.
  • Collection firm. Accounts sent to a law firm face a further 15 to 20 percent penalty.

Clearing the tax before it reaches judgment keeps more of your proceeds. Call the county at the number on its site for a payoff.

Which Pasadena facts help describe the house to buyers?

Buyers care about commute, schools and employers. The state history handbook says employment is tied to ship channel industries, the Bayport Industrial District and the Johnson Space Center in nearby Clear Lake. San Jacinto College and Texas Chiropractic College are in Pasadena.

  • Pasadena runs its own school district, begun in 1899.
  • The city grew from 1.7 square miles in 1893 to 58.6 square miles in 1980.
  • The Pasadena Rodeo and San Jacinto Strawberry Festival are listed as major draws.

Which county bills Pasadena property tax?

Harris County. Its tax office collects, and the Harris Central Appraisal District sets values. Ask for a payoff and a certificate before closing.

Must I clear delinquent taxes before selling?

No. They can be paid from proceeds at closing, though penalty and interest grow, so request a figure dated for the closing day.

When is the county's tax deadline?

January 31 of the year after the tax year, per the Harris County FAQ. Payment by then carries no penalty or interest.

What happens to my escrow if I sell in winter?

Your lender may have paid the bill already. Give it the closing date promptly and ask for any balance after payoff.

Can I sell with a tenant in place?

Yes. The buyer takes it subject to the lease, unless you follow the Texas notice and court steps to clear the house first.

What is the quickest way to sell a house in Waco, TX?

The quickest Waco sales are direct purchases where the buyer pays cash, buys the house in its present shape and closes once the title work is complete. A retail listing can reach more buyers, yet showings, inspections and lender approval stretch the calendar.

Nearly half of Waco's housing is renter-occupied, so many houses here are held as rentals. If yours has a tenant, share the lease terms early, since they decide when a buyer can take possession.

  • Fast route: cash buyer, short inspection period and a closing date you pick.
  • Open-market route: staging, showings and a buyer whose loan must be approved.
  • Slow route: unresolved liens, an open estate or a tenant who will not leave.

Where is Waco and what shaped it?

Waco lies in central McLennan County, about seventy miles south of Dallas, near the point where the Brazos and Bosque rivers join. The Handbook of Texas names Interstate 35, U.S. highways 84 and 77 and State Highway 6 as the main roads.

The first block of the new town was laid out on March 1, 1849, on the old Waco village ground. Cotton carried the early economy, a suspension bridge over the Brazos opened in 1870, and rail lines arrived in 1871 and the early 1880s. Baylor University moved to Waco in 1887, and Paul Quinn College opened in 1872.

The tornado of May 11, 1953 killed 114 people and destroyed 196 business buildings. Connally Air Force Base closed in 1966, and an urban renewal program begun in 1958 had channeled more than $125 million into the urban core by 1978. Today the city mixes older central blocks with newer outer neighborhoods.

Ask your title company how long a typical Waco closing takes so you can plan a move around it.

Which chapters of Waco's past still show up in its neighborhoods?

The Handbook of Texas describes a city that reinvented itself several times. After 1868 Waco sat on a spur of the Chisholm Trail, and by 1871 between 600,000 and 700,000 cattle had come through. By 1900 the city had 163 factories and six banks and had grown to 20,686 people, the sixth largest population center in the state.

The 1909 Cotton Palace fair drew about 500,000 visitors in 1913, and a twenty-two-story insurance building finished in 1911 was meant to be the tallest in Texas. During World War I, Camp MacArthur covered more than 10,000 acres of what is now the northwestern part of Waco and brought roughly 35,000 troops.

Later landmarks include the Texas Ranger Hall of Fame and Museum, dedicated in 1976, and a zoo built at Cameron Park. If you are describing a house to a buyer, tying it to the older core, the Baylor area or a newer outer street helps them place it.

A typical owned Waco home is valued at $221,700 in the 2020-2024 estimates, and only 49.4 percent of units are owner-occupied. That split explains why investors are a visible part of the market.

How big is Waco and what drives its economy?

Waco covers 88.73 square miles of land at about 1,561 residents per square mile, a spread-out layout with an average trip to work of 18.7 minutes. A short commute is worth naming in a listing.

Census data show 2022 retail sales near $3.44 billion, medical and social-service receipts around $2.04 billion and accommodation and food services at about $676 million. With rents near $1,165 a month, a rental-minded buyer will test an offer against that figure, so have the lease, deposit records and repair invoices ready.

How are tax sales handled in McLennan County?

Unpaid property tax is secured by a lien, and the City of Waco says paying back taxes on a property does not make someone its owner. Tax sales are the final remedy, and the city's page says they may occur on the first Tuesday of any month.

  • The McLennan County Tax Office says its tax sales are conducted online through GovEase, so confirm the current format with the office.
  • A property drawing no bid within city limits is struck off to the City of Waco, which resells it after a six-month or two-year redemption period.
  • Property without a homestead exemption can be bought back within six months by paying 25 percent of the auction price plus taxes, costs and fees.
  • Homestead or special-use property has two years, at 25 percent in the first year and 50 percent in the second.

The tax office also says taxes are due on receipt of the bill and are delinquent if not paid before February 1, and that online payments carry a 2.19 percent card fee or a $1.50 flat electronic check fee.
