What else should a Waco seller prepare?

Deeds for Waco property are filed with the McLennan County Clerk after a notary acknowledgment. Ask that office for the full recording charge on your document.

For an inherited house, an affidavit of heirship has no court review behind it, and no law forces a title company to accept it. If a tenant will not leave, a justice court case follows written notice, and a writ of possession cannot issue until six days after judgment.

For homestead owners, school districts must give a $140,000 exemption, and a veteran rated 100 percent disabled can receive a total exemption on the homestead.

Which City of Waco offices answer zoning and building questions?

The city's property page directs zoning and setback questions to the Planning Services Division at (254) 750-5650, and questions about what may be built on a lot to Inspection Services and Plan Review at (254) 750-5674. Water and sewer access questions go to the Engineering Department at (254) 750-5440.

The City of Waco Housing and Community Development Services Department, at (254) 750-5656, runs programs that assist with affordable housing. A buyer using such help may have its own timeline, so ask early.

The same page notes that the city sells tax-foreclosed properties by sealed bid and that most of them are sold at the courthouse auctions through a law firm. A seller whose house might otherwise end up there has far more control by selling before a tax sale takes place.

More questions about Waco, TX

When are Waco tax sales held?

The City of Waco says tax sales may occur on the first Tuesday of any month, while the McLennan County Tax Office says its sales are conducted online through GovEase. Confirm the format with the tax office.

Can a former owner reclaim a Waco house after a tax sale?

Sometimes. Property without a homestead exemption can be bought back within six months at 25 percent of the auction price plus costs, and homestead or special-use property has two years at 25 or 50 percent.

Does a tenant slow a Waco sale?

It can. A buyer needs the lease term and any deposit records. If the tenant must leave, the case runs through justice court after written notice.

Who do I ask about the tax balance on my Waco house?

The McLennan County Tax Office, which also publishes the due-date rules and payment options. The appraisal district sets value but does not collect.

How is ownership of an inherited Waco house documented?

Through probate or a court-backed route, or by a transfer on death deed filed before the owner died. A sworn heirship statement may not satisfy a buyer.

How quickly can a Midland house change hands?

Quickly, when the price reflects condition. Midland has an energy-driven economy, and investors, landlords and cash buyers all buy there. The usual trade applies: speed and certainty against top price.

Ask every buyer how long a written offer stays open, and compare the offers side by side.

What does the Midland economy mean for sellers?

Midland calls itself the heart of the Permian Basin, and its fact sheet lists Chevron, Diamondback Energy, Midland ISD, Midland Health, the city itself and H-E-B among major employers. ConocoPhillips, ExxonMobil, EOG Resources, Oxy and AST SpaceMobile also have headquarters or regional campuses there.

The city reports a metro population of 193,139 for 2026, growth of 8.1 percent from 2020 to 2026, a median age of 31.5 and an unemployment rate of 3.1 percent. It also states that per capita income ranks second highest in the United States. Its own FAQ notes that apartment rents are rising while occupancy has improved, which is relevant if your buyer is an investor.

  • Midland International Air and Space Port serves American, Delta, Southwest and United.
  • The city runs a Midland Development Corporation that offers business incentives.
  • Midland College and Midland ISD are the main education institutions named by the city.

Most owners pick between a listing, a direct cash sale and a local investor. Choose by the house, not by the headline number.

Which Midland permits could trip up a sale?

Midland wants a residential permit for new construction, additions, remodels, repairs and detached accessory buildings, pulled by the owner or a licensed, bonded contractor registered with the city.

Work must begin within 180 days of issue, and a permit lapses if building halts for more than 180 days. Requests go by email to the permit clerk, with 25 percent of the fee due at submission and 75 percent at approval; review usually takes 5 to 7 business days. If earlier work went unpermitted, ask the city how to document it before an inspector raises it. The city building permits page has the process.

Short-term rentals also owe the city a seven percent hotel occupancy tax on the price paid.

What property tax relief applies to Midland homes?

What if a tenant or an unwelcome occupant is in the house?

A tenant goes through eviction; someone who entered without permission may qualify for a quicker route. A tenant gets a written notice of at least three days unless the lease differs, then a justice court case with a hearing 10 to 21 days after filing.

For a person who is not family and was never a tenant, Property Code chapter 24B lets an owner ask the sheriff or constable to remove them with no court case. Conditions include that the person stayed after being told to leave and no suit is pending. A wrongful removal invites a lawsuit, so confirm each condition with the sheriff's office.

Midland takes permit requests by email, so keep scans of old permits handy. If one is missing, the permit clerk can be reached at 432-685-7390.

What does Midland's own growth plan say about the city?

The city's strategic plan lists six goals: more quality jobs, a safe and secure city, quality of life and place, clear communication, sound fiscal management, and stronger infrastructure. It also points to a Vision Midland story map covering capital projects, parks, downtown redevelopment and economic zones.

For a seller, those projects matter only as context. Street, drainage or downtown work near your address can change how buyers see the block, so ask the city's planning office what is scheduled near you. The city's fact sheet says sales tax collections grew 54.63 percent from fiscal 2015 to 2025, and that high-income households earning $200,000 or more grew 20.4 percent between 2023 and 2024. Those figures describe the local economy, not any one home's value, so rely on written offers and an agent's comparable sales for pricing.

When do Texas tax bills come due?

Bills mail around October 1 and turn delinquent after January 31. On February 1 a six percent penalty and one percent interest apply, and charges keep climbing monthly.

The January 1 owner carries that year's lien. A title company usually prorates the bill and pays it from your proceeds. A value protest is due by mid-May or 30 days after your notice, whichever is later. The Comptroller's calendar lists every step.

How is an inherited Midland house conveyed?

Whoever signs the deed must prove authority. Depending on the facts, that proof is an administrator's deed, a muniment of title order, a recorded affidavit of death with a transfer on death deed, or finally an affidavit of heirship.

An estate can use a small-estate affidavit if everything beyond the homestead totals $75,000 or less and all heirs agree. See the State Law Library guide.

Find out who the buyer is, whether the price covers the whole house as is, and who holds earnest money. Ask how many days to close and what happens if a lien surfaces. Read the contract before committing, and let the title company prepare the closing statement.

Cash buyers regularly purchase houses with foundation, roof or plumbing problems. The offer will reflect the repair cost.

Repairs, remodels, additions and detached accessory buildings. An owner or registered bonded contractor applies, and a permit lapses if work does not begin within 180 days.

Midland ISD gives $140,000 plus a 10 percent local option, per the appraisal district's table. A purchaser may claim it right away if you never did.

Who settles the tax bill when the sale closes?

The title company, normally, with your share taken from proceeds. The lien attaches January 1, so read the split on the closing statement.

Court or recorded documents showing authority: a muniment of title, administration, a transfer on death deed, or an affidavit of heirship.

Why does Round Rock's location draw buyers?

Round Rock sits on Interstate 35 in south central Williamson County, roughly sixteen miles north of downtown Austin, and its housing demand is tied closely to Austin's growth and to Dell Technologies, which has its headquarters here.

The town began in 1848 on Brushy Creek, when a blacksmith set up shop. The name came from a round, anvil-shaped limestone rock in the creek, and the Chisholm Trail crossed the creek near it. When the railroad came through in 1876 the settlement moved toward the tracks, and the original site became Old Round Rock. According to the Texas State Historical Association, the 1970s brought dramatic growth as Austin expanded, and the population went from 2,811 in 1970 to 11,812 in 1980.

A seller should expect buyers who commute toward Austin, work at the computer and technology employers that grew up here, or want a house close to Old Settlers Park, the 570-acre park the city built with its sales tax revenue.

Does Old Round Rock's history affect a house sale?

Old Town is a small cluster of restored limestone buildings now surrounded by the rest of the city, and it matters if your house sits in a historic overlay area. The Texas State Historical Association describes the original site on the north bank of Brushy Creek as largely abandoned after the railroad was laid south and east in 1876.

The same history lists a Greenwood Masonic Institute opened in 1867, a broom factory, a lime plant, the Round Rock Cheese Factory that ran from 1928 into the early 1970s, and the capture of outlaw Sam Bass in 1878, which the town commemorates each year during Frontier Days. These details give the older blocks their character, and a house near them may draw buyers who value that setting.

The city's building page says alterations to a structure or site with Historic Overlay Zoning need a Certificate of Appropriateness before a building permit, and that applies to fences and accessory structures too. Preservation staff can be reached through the Planning and Development Services desk at 512-218-5428. If you are selling an older home, ask whether the overlay applies before you promise a buyer an addition or a new fence.

How does Dell shape the Round Rock housing market?

Dell is the city's largest employer and a main reason Round Rock can keep property tax rates lower than many neighbors. The city says Dell moved its headquarters here in 1994 under the state's first Chapter 380 economic development agreement, signed August 26, 1993.

In April 2024 the city council extended that agreement's end date from 2053 to December 31, 2099. The city reports it has kept more than $429 million in sales tax revenue from Dell sales for services and projects, and it says the sales tax revenue has helped reduce property taxes for decades.

A large employer base supports steady buyer interest, but your price still depends on your street, school zone and condition, so compare recent nearby sales rather than city-wide claims.

Which Round Rock building rules can surface during a sale?

Selling needs no permit, yet loose ends from past work can slow a contract. The city's building inspection page says a permit is needed for construction, alteration, repair, demolition and changes to electrical, gas, mechanical or plumbing systems.

  • The city runs a one-permit system, so related electrical, plumbing and mechanical work goes on one permit, and all contractors must be named on it.
  • A permit becomes invalid if authorized work does not start within six months.
  • Contractors and subcontractors must register, with no registration or annual fee.
  • Sheds under 200 square feet and 15 feet tall still need a permit as accessory structures.

Carports, pergolas, pools and similar structures are allowed only in side or rear yards, cannot sit over easements or setbacks, and are capped at 15 feet tall. Properties with historic overlay zoning need a Certificate of Appropriateness before a building permit. Call the Building Inspection Division at 512-218-5550 with questions about older projects on your house.

What does a certificate of occupancy mean for a Round Rock seller?

For a house sale it usually means nothing, because the city issues a certificate of occupancy only when a space is newly built, remodeled or renovated. The city's page says a new occupant who only makes cosmetic changes will not receive one.

  • The Fire Marshal's Office conducts annual fire safety inspections for new and existing occupants of commercial space, so this applies to a business, not a home sale.
  • If you converted a garage or finished an addition, ask the building office whether a permit was closed out.
  • Utility contacts the city lists for a move are Atmos for gas, Oncor for electricity and the city's utility billing office for water, so plan service transfers around your closing date.

The city also notes that the Williamson County and Cities Health District reviews food service plans, which would matter if you ran a home-based food business that you want to hand off with the house.

Can you rent your Round Rock house instead of selling it?

You may be able to, but check the city's current short-term rental and hotel occupancy tax rules first. Round Rock publishes business guidance on its website, and ordinances change, so ask the city before you list a short-term rental.

A tenant in place also complicates showings, and many buyers want the house empty at closing.

How do Williamson County exemptions and tax caps work for a buyer or seller?

Williamson Central Appraisal District values homes, and a homeowner's exemption removes part of the value from taxation. The regular filing period runs January 1 through April 30, and a late application can be filed up to two years after the tax becomes delinquent, per Tax Code Section 11.431(a), according to WCAD.

Source: Williamson CAD exemptions page.

WCAD also explains that the age 65 exemption starts the year you turn 65, that a disability exemption generally tracks Social Security disability benefits, and that a veteran needs a disability rating of at least 10 percent from the Veterans Administration. A mobile home owner must furnish the title or a verified purchase contract. A surviving spouse who is 55 or older can inherit a school tax ceiling, but only when the late spouse received the over-65 exemption.

What property tax deadlines apply to a Round Rock sale?

Round Rock bills follow the statewide calendar, so the unpaid balance for the year and any penalty are the title company's problem to settle at closing. Ask the Williamson County tax office for a current statement beforehand.

What if the house is inherited, in foreclosure or tied up with a tenant?

Inheritance, foreclosure and tenancy each carry their own paperwork.

  • Inherited house: the deed route depends on whether a will exists, whether the owner recorded a beneficiary deed, or whether a court must appoint someone.
  • Foreclosure: a lender's sale is preceded by default and sale notices, so the calendar is fixed and a closing before the auction date matters.
  • Tenant: a written notice to vacate comes first, then a justice court case.

A title company can tell you what must be recorded before a buyer's lender will fund.

Cash buyers are active here, but the price offered depends on repairs and location. Compare a cash offer against a listing estimate minus commissions and carrying costs before deciding.

Does a Round Rock fence repair require approval?

Call Code Enforcement at 512-341-3329, which is the number the city lists for fence permit questions. Building permits and inspections questions go to 512-218-5550.

Can I claim a homestead exemption after buying mid-year?

Possibly. WCAD says that if you buy and move in after January 1, you may qualify for the rest of that tax year when the previous owner had no homestead exemption on the property.

When do Round Rock area property taxes become late?

After January 31. The state comptroller says tax unpaid on February 1 is delinquent and begins to collect penalty and interest.

What does Lewisville say about its own taxes?

The city's budget page says Lewisville adopted a fiscal 2026 rate of $0.419009 per $100, its lowest since 1987, and that the rate has risen three times and fallen nine times in 28 years. Because the page also prints a comparison rate of .422435 for another year, ask the Denton County tax office for the rate on your own bill.

Do Lewisville rental rules affect a sale?

Yes. Lewisville runs an inspection program for single-family rentals, with no fee or registration, that began July 1, 2008. An inspection is triggered when the owner or future tenant notifies the city, when a tenant requests a water transfer, or on a complaint.

Minor violations do not block move-in, but life-safety issues do. The inspection covers items like a posted address, maintained roofing, gutters and siding, working windows, fences, an accessible water meter, trimmed vegetation near the right-of-way, and no inoperable vehicles or stagnant water. The program does not cover apartments, mobile homes or houses outside city limits. Fixing these items before listing can remove a common buyer objection.

  • House number visible from the street.

In most cases by January 31, with penalty and interest from February 1. Some owners can use a split or installment plan.

What is Carrollton like for a seller?

Carrollton is described by its own city site as a centrally located city in the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex. It has three DART light rail stations, including Downtown Carrollton Station on the Silver Line, and is served by IH-35E, SH 121 and the President George Bush Turnpike. The city's historical designations page names two dozen sites that give different parts of town their character. Downtown Carrollton centers on the Town Square, where a spring once ran through the middle of the early business district, and the A.W. Perry Homestead Museum on North Perry Road preserves a house finished in 1909.

  • Josey Ranch, at Keller Springs Road and Josey Lane, now holds a city sports complex on a lake that began as a clay quarry for a brick factory.

  • Trinity Mill, near IH-35E and the President George Bush Turnpike, began about 1851 as a steam mill serving settlers.

That legacy means older core neighborhoods hold houses from several eras, and a house near the Elm Fork or old creek beds may carry flood history. What if a Carrollton house is inherited or in foreclosure?

For inherited property, check whether the estate used a muniment of title, a small estate affidavit or an administration, since each leaves different paperwork for the county clerk. An affidavit of heirship is only a sworn statement, never checked by a court, and buyers can refuse it.

With a loan in default, expect 20 days to reinstate, then a notice of sale 21 or more days before a first Tuesday auction. Lenders have two years after the sale to sue for a deficiency. Selling before the auction date can keep equity that would otherwise be eaten by costs.

What if Carrollton property taxes go unpaid before a sale?

Unpaid tax becomes a larger problem every month. Penalty and interest start accruing after January 31 and grow with each month. Interest has no ceiling, and a lawyer retained by the taxing unit can add up to 20 percent.

  • Collectors may offer installment plans on delinquent tax, up to 36 months in some cases, and a plan is required for a residence homestead.
  • A tax lien lets the unit sue to foreclose even if the owner changes, so unpaid tax must be paid off at or before closing.

No. Ordinances passed December 2, 2025 say no new short-term rental or bed and breakfast will be allowed, with only certain existing properties able to qualify for a lodging license. Call the city before assuming any rental use can continue.

How is Abilene laid out?

Abilene fills the northeast corner of Taylor County on level ground at an elevation of 1,708 feet, with railroad tracks dividing the city. Interstate 20 is the main east-west road, and U.S. 83, 84 and 277 handle north-south traffic. The city covers 106.67 square miles, which works out to 1,173.6 residents per square mile in 2020.

Workers spend 15.6 minutes getting to their jobs on average. The Texas State Historical Association reports a southward shift toward Buffalo Gap during the 1970s and 1980s, around Cooper High School, the Mall of Abilene and Fairway Oaks, as most stores left downtown.

How did Abilene's history shape the city?

A group of ranchers and land speculators steered the railroad across their own acreage, and the townsite was platted there in 1881. Lots went to auction on March 15, 1881. Voters approved incorporation on January 2, 1883, and in October that year Abilene took the county seat.

Scarce water held growth back, since normal rainfall is just 23.78 inches a year. The city responded with Lytle Lake in 1897, Lake Abilene in 1919, Lake Kirby in 1927 and Lake Fort Phantom Hill in 1937. Camp Barkeley and the air base at Tye came with the war, and Dyess Air Force Base was approved by Congress in 1952. The Census counts 7,422 veterans in the city.

The state handbook lists Hardin-Simmons, Abilene Christian and McMurry universities and a Texas Tech health sciences center among local campuses. It also names Abilene ISD and Wylie ISD, so confirm which district serves a particular address.

According to the state handbook, Abilene moved from near-total reliance on agriculture to a blend of oil, farming, commerce, light manufacturing and services. World War II was the watershed, and Dyess has kept federal money flowing since 1952.

Census business figures for 2022 list $3,054,251 thousand in retail sales, $1,889,429 thousand in health care and social assistance receipts, and $520,527 thousand in transportation and warehousing. Retail sales per person were $23,965. Of residents 16 and older, 57.3% are in the labor force, and 27.3% of adults have a bachelor's degree or more.

Nearby sights, including the ruins of Fort Phantom Hill, Buffalo Gap Historic Village and downtown museums such as The Grace Museum, give the area some visitor traffic, though most owners sell to local buyers.

Expect a posted stop work order and an investigation fee equal to the permit fee, with a release fee for an owner. Work that was covered up before inspection may have to be opened at the owner's expense. A contractor's second violation within 12 months costs ten times the fee.

Before listing, ask Building Inspections whether earlier remodel permits were finaled.

Which tax and recording steps come with an Abilene sale?

Each January 1 a tax lien forms and travels with the house. The owner that day stays personally responsible, and no buyer gets clean title while delinquent tax is open. Closing staff obtain a payoff number and pay it out of your sale funds.

Deeds are recorded by the county clerk where the land lies. Fees in the state manual start at $5.00 for page one, $4.00 for each extra page, plus add-on fees of up to $10 each for records management and archive and $2.00 for technology. A deed needs a signature and a notary's or other authorized officer's acknowledgment before recording. The Taylor County appraisal district can confirm your exemption status.

Can I sell an Abilene house in foreclosure, probate or with a tenant?

Yes, though the timing rules differ. Foreclosure auctions take place on a first Tuesday after at least 21 days' notice. Probate of a will is generally sought within four years of death, and the small estate affidavit is limited to estates of $75,000 or less outside the homestead.

Where a tenant lives in the house, the landlord begins with a written notice to vacate and then files in justice court. Ask a Texas attorney or the county clerk which route applies before you list.

Most likely Brazoria County, but not always. The city's finance page says Pearland is primarily in Brazoria County, with portions extending into Fort Bend and Harris counties, about 20 miles south of downtown Houston.

The same page lists the city's land area as 47.5 square miles and its population as approximately 132,900 as of January 1, 2024. Look at your tax bill or the appraisal district record to see the county. That answers which clerk gets the deed and which office bills the tax.

How did Pearland grow from a rail-line farm town?

Pearland is a planned community that grew into a Houston suburb. The city's own history page says William Zychlinski bought 2,560 acres in 1892 around the Gulf, Colorado and Santa Fe rail line and platted the town in 1894, naming east-west streets Walnut, Pear, Broadway, Jasmine, Plum and Orange.

Hurricanes shaped it. The 1900 storm destroyed nearly all of the early town and cut the population by almost three-quarters. A second hurricane in 1915 did similar damage, and the fig industry was the only one to grow afterward. The city incorporated in 1959, adopted a Home Rule Charter in February 1971, and uses a council-manager form of government.

For a seller the lesson is practical. Storm damage, drainage and flood insurance history are the questions buyers raise in a coastal area, so keep claims records and repair receipts together.

It lists police, fire, ambulance, parks, water, sewer, streets, planning and zoning among its services.

  • Elections are held annually on the second Saturday in May.

  • The City Secretary handles public document requests.

Pearland's city hall moved from the Old Townsite to Liberty Drive in 1987. Buyers who like an older neighborhood may ask about the Old Townsite, the original plat.

A deferral does not cancel the tax. It stays due, with interest, until the owner no longer owns and lives in the home, so a sale ends the deferral and the balance comes out of proceeds.

The title company prorates the current year and pays off anything delinquent. The Comptroller's state calendar puts the penalty start at February 1, at 6 percent with 1 percent interest.

What if the Pearland house is facing foreclosure?

You can sell right up to the sale date, and the loan is paid from the proceeds. The State Law Library says most home loans cannot start foreclosure until the loan is over 120 days delinquent.

  • A notice of default gives the borrower 20 days to bring the loan current.
  • The notice of sale goes out at least 21 days before the auction and is posted at the courthouse and filed with the county clerk.
  • Auctions run on the first Tuesday of a month, in the window the attorney general's guidance describes.
  • After a sale, a deficiency suit must be filed within two years.

Get a payoff figure and sale date from the servicer and pass both to the title company. The State Law Library page gives the steps.

What does Pearland's flood and drainage setting mean for sellers?

Clear Creek runs through the Pearland area and drains parts of Brazoria, Fort Bend, Galveston and Harris counties, according to a city news release on federal funding for flood control. Buyers in the Houston region ask where a house sits relative to the creek and whether it has flooded.

A seller should have the facts straight before listing or taking an investor's offer. Gather insurance claims, repair invoices and any elevation certificate you have, and note which FEMA flood map covers the lot. The city's floodplain document says the current FEMA map for Brazoria County was issued December 30, 2020, for Fort Bend County January 6, 2017, and for Harris County January 29, 2021, so the map date depends on which county the parcel is in.

  • Disclose past water entry plainly in the contract.
  • Ask your title company whether any drainage easements cross the lot.
  • Keep records of repairs after any storm.

How does Pearland governance affect permits and annexation?

Pearland is a home rule city with a council and city manager. The finance page says the council meets the second and fourth Monday of each month at 6:30 p.m., and that the city can extend its limits by voluntary annexation when a landowner and the council agree.

That matters if your lot sits near the edge. A parcel that was annexed may have changed tax units, and the bill on your account tells you which ones apply. The city also provides planning and zoning, community development, water and sewer, so ask city staff about any open permit before a buyer's title search finds it.

For anything the city site does not spell out, such as a fee or inspection rule, ask the city office directly and get the answer in writing before closing.

Partly. The city is mainly in Brazoria County, with parts in Fort Bend and Harris counties. Your tax bill shows which county covers your lot.

No. A cash buyer accepts the property in present condition and prices the work. Keep repair receipts and insurance claim records so you can describe the history accurately.

The clerk of the lot's county. A title company normally files it and shows the fee on the settlement statement.

When does the tax penalty begin?

On February 1, according to the Comptroller, which prints a 6 percent penalty and 1 percent interest at that point. Ask the tax office about local dates.

It describes a student-heavy city. The 2025 estimate is 127,472 people, 5.8% above the April 2020 base, and the owner-occupancy rate for 2020-2024 is just 35.4%.

Workers average 17.4 minutes getting to work, which is short for Texas. Land area is 51.16 square miles, and the 2020 count works out to 2,355.6 people on each one. Only 66.1% of residents kept their address from the year before, a sign of churn in student housing.

How did College Station start as a college town?

The city website says Texas A&M, the first state institution of higher education in Texas, was inaugurated in 1876. The Postal Service designated the area College Station in 1877, taking the name from a train station west of campus.

A petition from 23 men started the move to incorporate, and voters approved it 217 to 39 on October 19, 1938. College Station became the first general law city in Texas to employ a city manager, and in 1952 voters adopted a home rule charter once the population passed 5,000.

The university enrolls nearly 80,000 students, and the George H.W. Bush Presidential Library and Museum draws more than 125,000 visitors a year, both according to the city. Those facts keep demand for housing tied to the academic calendar.

Must a College Station rental be registered?

Yes, with limits. The city's rental housing page requires registration of every single-family, townhome, duplex, tri-plex, four-plex, five-plex or six-plex dwelling that the owner does not occupy, whether or not rent is charged. Condos and buildings with more than six units are not covered.

Selling a rented house? Ask the city if any penalties are open, because the page says they must be paid before registration can be finished.

It reports an area unemployment rate of 3.7 percent as of June 2024 and says the property tax rate is among the lowest in Texas.

The page also says the city is working with Texas A&M and the City of Bryan on a high-tech research hub. Parks, a university and a short commute are the features most likely to matter to a buyer, so mention them with the house details.

How do Brazos County property tax dates work?

The Brazos appraisal district lists January 1 as the valuation date, with notices of appraised value sent in several runs from April 15 to June 1. The protest deadline is May 15, or the 30th day after notice. Rates are set from July to September, and the tax assessor-collector mails bills in October and November.

Statewide, the Comptroller sets the due date at January 31 and the first delinquent day at February 1, when penalty and interest begin to run at six and one percent. The district is at 4051 Pendleton Drive in Bryan, takes exemption applications by email at an address on its contact page and is open on weekdays.

What does a College Station buyer inherit from the tax year?

A tax lien attaches each January 1, and the Comptroller says whoever owned on that date stays liable after a sale. Buyers who take title after January 1 may claim a homestead exemption right away if the seller had none. Ask for a tax certificate before you sign so the year is split correctly.

A delinquent owner can ask the collector to waive penalty and interest, provided the tax is paid within 21 days of learning of the delinquency and the request is made in writing within 181 days of the delinquency date.

What if the house came through an estate or a lender is calling?

A will can go to probate up to four years after death, and a muniment of title fits when no administration is needed. Use a muniment of title when no administration is needed. A foreclosure sale happens on a first Tuesday after a notice of sale, and the State Law Library notes a 20-day window to reinstate after the default notice.

A deed is recorded by the county clerk, which per the Texas Courts manual requires acknowledgment before a notary or two witnesses, with fees listed in the manual.

Do tenants have to register a College Station rental?

No. The city page puts the duty on the owner and says tenants are not required to register. An owner who lives elsewhere must name a local contact who is not on the lease and lives close enough to reach the house quickly.

$90 per building, one time, as of October 24, 2022 according to the city. Late registration adds daily penalties, so do not wait past the first notice deadline.

Contact the Brazos appraisal district, which lists a phone number and email address on its contact page. General exemption applications are due before May 1, and some special applications are due April 30.

May 15 or the 30th day after notice, whichever comes later. The district's process page states this, and the notice itself prints the exact date.

Can I sell with a lien for back taxes?

Yes. The title company orders payoff figures and pays the balance from your sale funds.

Odessa is Ector County's largest city and its seat, in the Permian Basin of West Texas. The Texas State Historical Association says boom and bust swings have driven the local economy since the 1920s. Owners facing a job move, an inheritance or a missed loan payment usually weigh three paths: an agent listing, a deal with an investor, and an offer from a company that pays cash for houses.

What should a seller know about Odessa?

Odessa is a mid-sized West Texas city whose workforce leans on energy. The Census Bureau estimates 122,707 residents for mid-2025, against 114,428 counted in 2020.

The town began when the Texas and Pacific Railway crossed the South Plains in 1881. Its townsite was platted in 1886, Ector County organized in January 1891 with Odessa as seat, and city status followed in 1927. The county's first producing oil well came in on December 28, 1926, and growth accelerated after that. Commuters rely on U.S. 80, U.S. 385 and Interstate 20.

Education can help a listing. Odessa High and Permian High are part of the Ector County school system, and Odessa College and the University of Texas of the Permian Basin are in town.

Day to day, the handbook describes a warm, dry climate with about 300 days of sunshine a year, a water supply drawn from lakes on the Colorado River plus wells in Ward and Ector counties, and a council-manager government with a mayor and five council members. Local attractions it names include the Globe of the Great Southwest on the Odessa College campus, the Meteor Crater and the White-Pool House, built in 1887.

Ask each buyer for proof of funds, the title company's name, the split of closing costs and the length of any inspection window. Then rank the offers by the amount that reaches your account.

Since appraisals use a January 1 date, the district can tell you what is on file for your parcel. The Comptroller's property tax basics explains how the appraisal district, review board and collecting offices split the work. The State Law Library has plain-language pages on both, and an attorney can say which suits your family.

How should I prepare an Odessa house for a quick sale?

Missing documents slow more closings than repairs do. Put the deed, the newest tax statement, the lender's payoff contact, any HOA papers and recent utility bills in one folder.

  • Photograph roof, foundation and mechanical problems so the buyer's number rests on real conditions.

How does the Odessa oil cycle affect a sale?

Demand for Odessa houses follows the oil patch. The state history handbook says the swings have run in roughly ten-year intervals since the 1920s, and that local leaders have tried to diversify, including through a University of Texas of the Permian Basin center started in 1990.

Timing therefore matters. In a slow stretch, a buyer with cash and no loan condition removes one risk. In a strong one, a listing may draw more bids. Judge written offers by your net after payoffs, and ask how long each inspection period lasts.

German immigrants founded the town on March 21, 1845. Its economy grew from mills, manufacturing and a commercial center, and later tourism: Landa Park, the rivers, Canyon Lake after 1964, Natural Bridge Caverns and Wurstfest. Those draws keep short stays and second homes in the market.

Can I use a short-term rental or a rented house as a seller?

The city has repeatedly absorbed new land. Land area was 45.18 square miles in 2020, up from 43.87 in 2010, and density rose from 1,316 to 2,001 people per square mile.

Workers average 27.1 minutes on the road, which is longer than in smaller Texas towns, and 98.0 percent of households have a computer. Those commuters often want a move-in-ready house near I-35 or Farm Road 725, so a home that needs updates may do better with an investor than with a typical family buyer.

Older neighborhoods near Landa Park and the river carry the city's German-era history, while newer subdivisions on the edge follow the growth. Tell any buyer which category your street falls in and whether your lot has flood or drainage history, since the rivers shape much of the town.

How does closing and recording work?

The title company prepares the deed and settlement statement, and the county clerk where the property sits files the deed. A deed needs a notarized or otherwise officially acknowledged signature before it can be recorded.

The County Clerk Manual sets the base recording fee at five dollars for page one. Ask the Comal County Clerk, or the Guadalupe County Clerk if your parcel is there, for the current schedule.

Often in a few weeks if the title is clear. A shared inheritance, a lien or a tenant adds time. Request the closing date in writing with the offer.

Is New Braunfels in Comal or Guadalupe County?

Both. The city is the Comal County seat and extends into Guadalupe County, per the Handbook of Texas. Your tax bill shows which county's appraisal district applies.

QuickFacts reports $339,400 as the median for owner-held homes from 2020 to 2024. Your own house's price depends on condition, location and size, so treat the figure as context only.

Yes. Cash buyers take on the repairs themselves, and the offer accounts for them. Compare it with a repaired listing estimate to see which nets more.

Flood history, an HOA, a municipal utility district charge or a Public Improvement District assessment can all change what a buyer will accept, and each is worth checking before you list.

What does a League City seller get from the Clear Lake location?

The Handbook of Texas calls League City the biggest city in Galveston County, crossed by State Highway 3 and Interstate 45. It lies in the Greater Houston area along Clear Creek and Clear Lake.

The same source describes a town that began as a brickyard and railroad stop in the 1850s, took the League name in the early 1890s, and grew after NASA began building the Manned Spacecraft Center on the north shore of Clear Lake in 1961. Population went from 45,444 in 2000 to 83,560 in 2010 and 112,129 in 2022. The Clear Lake area is also described as one of the nation's biggest boating destinations. Waterfront and boating access are real selling points here, while the Galveston hurricane of 1900, which wrecked the Clear Creek bridge, is a reminder of the coast's storm history. Buyers will ask about insurance and drainage.

How did League City become a Clear Lake suburb?

The Handbook of Texas traces the area to the Akokisa people, then to Anglo settlers in the 1830s and 1840s. A brickyard opened in 1858 as the first business, and the Galveston, Houston and Henderson Railroad passed through in 1859. A post office called Clear Creek opened in 1874. J. C. League, a Galveston businessman, bought land in the early 1890s and renamed the town League City.

Farming defined the early twentieth century. Japanese farmers began growing rice in 1903 and later switched to truck crops, and thirty Italian families arrived in 1923 to grow vegetables. By 1914 four railroads served a town of about 500 people, and State Highway 3 replaced the old Houston to Galveston road in 1939. The population was 1,341 in 1950, and NASA's arrival in 1961 changed the economy. For a seller, this history means a range of housing, from historic homes near the old townsite to large newer subdivisions with MUD and PID charges.

Butler's Courtyard is the restored 1909 Butler Building, the town's first brick commercial structure, which once held the first bank, a drugstore, a doctor's office and a hardware store. South Shore Harbor Resort and Conference Center is one of several waterside resorts.

Why does this matter to a seller? Buyers who work at the Johnson Space Center or nearby Clear Lake employers choose League City for the commute and the water. A home within reach of the Clear Creek and Clear Lake shoreline tends to be marketed on boating, while a home farther inland leans on schools and new subdivisions. The Kilgore Lumber Company, which opened in 1915, is still described as operating in the 2020s, a small sign of how long some businesses have stayed.

Every short-term rental in League City needs a permit and must show the permit number in online listings. The city issues it through the Building Department and requires annual renewal with a safety inspection.

Texas sets the lien date at January 1, so the owner on that date is liable for the year's tax. Galveston County follows the state calendar of October statements and a split option of November 30 and June 30.

Late payment brings a six percent penalty and one percent monthly interest. Seniors, disabled owners and disabled veterans may qualify for four installments. Ask the Galveston County Tax Office to confirm which plans apply to your account.

What if a League City home is behind on its mortgage?

Texas lenders usually foreclose under a power of sale rather than in court. A borrower who has fallen behind can cure the default with a payment within 20 days of the notice. The lender then sends a notice of sale at least 21 days ahead.

The auction takes place on a first Tuesday. Selling beforehand can pay off the loan and keep any equity, while a surplus after an auction goes to junior lienholders and then the former owner.

Beyond the permit itself, the city's short-term rental page sets a sequence owners must follow, and it applies whether the house is owner-occupied or an investment. Understanding it helps a seller explain the property's income history to a buyer.

Call the Building Department at 281-554-1429 with questions. Your permit does not pass to a buyer, so take any active listings down by closing.

Timing depends on the buyer and the title work. Cash buyers can often close faster than buyers who need a mortgage, but a clear title and payoff letter are what set the date.

Taxing units, including the city, Clear Creek ISD and Galveston County, set rates, and Galveston County's tax office handles bills. Confirm your balance with that office before closing.

You can still sell it as-is. Cash buyers account for the damage in the price, and you should disclose what you know and keep any insurance claim paperwork.

Very. QuickFacts estimates 119,564 residents on July 1, 2025, up 33.0% from an April 2020 base of 89,899. The city's land area went from 52.71 square miles in 2010 to 72.00 in 2020.

How did Conroe become the Montgomery County seat?

Houston lumberman Isaac Conroe set up a sawmill in 1881, according to the Texas State Historical Association, and the place was first called Conroe's Switch after its railroad junction. In 1889 Conroe won the county seat from Montgomery and incorporated in 1904 with 1,009 residents.

Oil discovered on December 13, 1931, about seven miles southeast of town, revived a Depression economy and pushed the population to an estimated 5,000 by 1933. Chemical and manufacturing firms later joined the old lumber trade.

Interstate 45 brought Houstonians to the margins of town, and Lake Conroe, impounded in the late 1960s and early 1970s seven miles northwest, added more housing demand. Conroe Independent School District reached its present size of 330 square miles in 1925, so the district extends well past the city line.

What older landmarks and growth stages shaped Conroe?

The same Handbook entry lists details that explain the older core near the courthouse square. Fires in 1901 and 1911 destroyed much of the business district. The State Hotel opened in 1933, the Crighton Theater went up on the square in 1935, and a new courthouse followed in 1936 with a county hospital two years later.

Delta Land and Timber opened one of the South's largest milling operations southwest of town in 1913 and eventually employed 700 people. Conroe's schools were desegregated in 1968, the Montgomery County Library opened in 1946, and a local airfield, built during the war on Farm Road 1484, has served civilian flying since 1945.

Population counts in the entry trace the growth: 27,610 in 1990, 43,617 in 2000 and 63,322 by 2015. The 2025 estimate of 119,564 is almost double that last figure. Houses on the older grid, lake-area homes and new subdivisions all price very differently, so expect a buyer to ask which era yours belongs to.

When do Montgomery County tax bills come due?

Bills are usually mailed in October and are payable on receipt, says the Montgomery County Tax Office. Interest and penalty begin on February 1, and payments count by postmark.

The office prints a penalty of 6 percent at the start, adding a point each month and a last 2 points on July 1, for 12 percent in all, plus 1 percent interest monthly. Partial payments are accepted, though a balance left after January 31 keeps accruing. Call the tax office at (936) 539-7897 or visit 400 N. San Jacinto Street.

Questions about value, exemptions or protests go to Montgomery Central Appraisal District instead. The state deadline to protest is May 15 or 30 days after the notice arrives, whichever falls later.

How does location inside Conroe affect a sale?

Conroe is large, so distance matters. The Handbook places Lake Conroe seven miles northwest of the city and the old oil field seven miles southeast, which gives a sense of the spread. A house near the courthouse square, one near the interstate and one toward the lake attract different buyers, and the 28.6 minute average commute reported by the Census Bureau weighs on all three.

Conroe Independent School District covers 330 square miles, so the campus assigned to a house depends on its address, not only on a Conroe mailing label. Give buyers the exact street address when you ask the district about zoning.

What should a Conroe seller know about exemptions?

Homestead status changes what a buyer will owe, so confirm yours is on file. The Comptroller describes a $140,000 school exemption, an extra $60,000 for owners 65 and up or disabled, and a school tax ceiling. Questions about qualifying belong with the appraisal district, as the county tax office itself points out.

What if the Conroe mortgage is behind?

Texas foreclosure follows a calendar kept by the State Law Library. Servicers generally wait past 120 days of delinquency, then mail a default notice that leaves 20 days to cure. Auctions are held on a first Tuesday after a posted notice. Closing a sale before that Tuesday keeps the price in your hands, and a lender may still pursue a shortfall for two years after an auction.

What about a tenant or an heir in a Conroe house?

Tenants must get written notice, usually three days unless the lease says otherwise, and a contested case goes to justice court. A squatter who was never a tenant is handled under property code chapter 24B through the sheriff or constable. Heirs should have probate, a muniment of title, a small estate affidavit or a recorded transfer on death deed in place before a buyer will close.

Montgomery County. Its tax office sits at 400 N. San Jacinto Street in Conroe and answers bill and payment questions.

February 1. The January 31 postmark deadline passes first, and a first-month penalty of 6 percent plus 1 percent interest follows.

It is. The closing agent pays the balance out of your proceeds, so request a tax certificate early to see the exact amount.

What is Richardson's Home Improvement Incentive Program?

It is a city program that pays homeowners who spend heavily on a single-family remodel. The payment equals ten times the increase in city taxes that results from the higher appraised value.

  • You apply to Community Services before any construction starts and agree to inspections.

The city pays on April 1 of the first full calendar year after the work is done, under an economic development agreement. Which schools, colleges and transit routes serve Richardson?

Richardson ISD covers 46 square miles in Dallas County, parts of Richardson, Dallas and Garland, with more than 36,000 students and 50 campuses: 37 elementary schools, eight junior highs, four high schools and one alternative school. Plano ISD takes in northern parts of Richardson on the Collin County side across about 100 square miles.

Colleges nearby include the University of Texas at Dallas, which opened in 1969, Dallas College Richland Campus and Collin College. The city also lists West Coast University and Galen College of Nursing campuses.

For getting around, the city's page describes DART rail and bus, Trinity Railway Express and NTTA tollways. It also lists hike and bike trails and a transportation and mobility department. The city also publishes Richardson Today, a week-in-review email and a MyRichardson app for reporting issues. How are property taxes and exemptions handled at a Richardson closing?

The year's tax lien attached on January 1, so the title company splits the bill between seller and buyer at closing. Bills go out around October 1, and January 31 is the usual cutoff.

From February 1, penalty and interest build, and by July the penalty reaches 12 percent. Installment plans exist for homeowners who are over 65 or disabled. Every school district must give a $140,000 homestead exemption. Disabled veterans get an exemption tied to their rating, and a 100 percent rating exempts the whole homestead. Appraised value on a homestead is capped at a 10 percent yearly increase.

Ask the appraisal district which exemptions sit on your account, since a buyer may need to apply for their own.

What if a Richardson owner has a foreclosure or an inherited house?

A lender that holds a defaulted Texas loan can sell without going to court. The borrower has 20 days after the default letter to catch up, and the sale notice must go out three weeks or more before a first-Tuesday auction.

For an inherited house, the right path depends on the estate. A will can be offered for probate during the four years after death. Estates worth $75,000 or less, not counting the homestead, can use a small estate affidavit that a judge approves. An affidavit of heirship is only a sworn statement, and buyers need not accept it. If the owner signed a beneficiary deed of that kind, the heir records proof of death before selling.

Recording is done by the clerk of whichever county covers the parcel, and the state clerk manual sets the per-page recording charge and the other records fees.

Is Richardson in Dallas County or Collin County?

How can a Tyler, TX owner close a sale quickly?

A fast Tyler sale needs three things lined up: a buyer who can close without waiting on a lender, a clear title, and a payoff figure you can trust. A cash purchase tends to hit all three more often than a retail listing does.

Gather the mortgage payoff, your latest Smith County tax statement and any letter about a lien, a code complaint or a missed payment. Those papers show what the closing must pay off and whether a clock is already running.

  • Retail listing: more buyers see it, and you absorb showings, repair requests and a lender's schedule.
  • Private sale: price and terms are yours, along with every form.
  • Cash buyer: fewer contingencies, with an offer that already accounts for repairs.

Where is Tyler and how did it take shape?

Tyler is the Smith County seat, ninety-nine miles southeast of Dallas, and the Handbook of Texas lists U.S. highways 69 and 271 plus State highways 14, 31, 64, 110 and 155 among its routes. The legislature authorized the townsite in April 1846, and the city was named in honor of President John Tyler.

Commissioners paid $150 in February 1847 for a 100-acre tract and laid out twenty-eight blocks around a central square. Tyler was incorporated on January 29, 1850. Railroad machine shops arrived in the late 1870s and 1880s, and the population nearly tripled between 1880 and 1890.

Census data give the modern footprint of 57.45 square miles of land. Older streets near the square and newer subdivisions farther out mean house ages vary, so an inspector will focus on whichever systems date a particular house.

Which industries have shaped demand for Tyler homes?

Oil, roses, health care and education each left a mark. The 1930 East Texas oilfield discovery drew oil companies and field developers to Tyler, and the population climbed past 25,000 by 1933, according to the Handbook of Texas.

Rose growing was the other signature business. By the 1940s more than half the rose bushes sold in the country grew within ten miles of the city, which is how the Texas Rose Festival came about, held each October. The same entry names the University of Texas Health Center at Tyler, Mother Frances Hospital, Texas College, Tyler Junior College and the University of Texas at Tyler.

Census figures put 2022 retail sales near $4.84 billion and medical and social-service receipts around $3.47 billion, far above lodging and restaurant sales of about $617 million.

How does Tyler compare on Census housing measures?

The 2020-2024 estimates value a typical owned Tyler house at $235,300, with 55.4 percent of units occupied by their owners. Any one house can sit well above or below that point.

Which Smith County offices value a Tyler house and collect its tax?

The Smith County Appraisal District values property and handles exemptions, while the Smith County Tax Office sends the bills and takes payment. The tax office says plainly that it has no role in valuations and that the district is not part of county government, so value questions go to the district at 903-510-8600.

Payments can be made in person, online, by mail to P.O. Box 2011, Tyler, Texas 75710, or in a drop box, and the tax office line is 903-590-2920. Card payments add a 2.30 percent fee with a $1.50 minimum, while electronic checks carry no fee. Substations at Noonday and Lindale also take property tax payments.

The tax office prints this schedule of penalty and interest on current-year tax left unpaid after January:

  • 7 percent in February, 9 in March, 11 in April, 13 in May and 15 in June.
  • 18 percent in July with a 15 percent collection fee added, then 19 in August and 20 in September.
  • Interest keeps adding one percent a month, and tax unpaid on June 30 goes to the delinquent tax attorney.

Where can a Tyler owner see proposed tax rates?

Smith County runs a Truth in Taxes site for property owners. According to the county's property tax page, it shows property values, proposed tax rates, an estimate of the taxes those rates would produce, and the dates and places of public hearings on rates. It also carries information on taxing unit budgets, revenue and rate calculations.

That calendar matters because several units tax a Tyler address. The county's page notes that the county and the local school district tax every property, and that owners may also pay a city and special districts such as a hospital, junior college, water or fire district. Elected officials of each unit adopt rates in August or September. Between January 1 and April 30 the appraisal district is processing exemption applications and agricultural appraisals, and around May 15 the review board starts hearing protests.

If you are selling, the rates adopted in late summer decide the bill that arrives in October, so ask your title company how the year will be prorated.

How does a protest work at the Smith County Appraisal District?

Notice to the district has to be in writing and reach it within 30 days of the date on the notice of appraised value. If no notice was generated, a protest can still be filed by May 20. A letter that names you, identifies the property and shows dissatisfaction is enough, and an online system is available using the ID on your notice.

The district's taxpayer liaison officer can explain the process at the same number, 903-510-8600. A review board of citizens hears the protest, and you and the district exchange evidence at or before the hearing. Photographs and other records help.

If you lose and appeal, the options include state district court, binding arbitration or the State Office of Administrative Hearings. Weekend or holiday deadlines roll to the next working day, and a late filing is excused only for good cause, such as a medical emergency.

What exemptions and caps apply to a Tyler homestead?

The district's FAQ says a qualifying homestead's taxable value cannot climb past 110 percent of the prior year's value. The cap does not exist in the first year an owner qualifies, so a buyer starts uncapped.

Owners 65 or older receive a ceiling on school taxes, set at the amount paid in the year they first qualified. That ceiling can rise when they add improvements such as a room, a pool or a garage, and it changes if they move. State law also gives school districts a $140,000 homestead exemption.

Applications are available at the district office, 245 SSE Loop 323 in Tyler, between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. on weekdays, or by calling 903-510-8600.

More questions about Tyler, TX

Which office handles a Tyler valuation complaint?

Call the Smith County Appraisal District at 903-510-8600. The Smith County Tax Office states that it does not handle valuations.

Where can I pay Tyler property tax?

At the Smith County Tax Office in person, online, by mail or in the drop box, and at the Noonday and Lindale substations. Card payments carry a convenience fee, while electronic checks do not.

What happens if Tyler taxes go unpaid after January 31?

The county's schedule adds penalty and interest starting at 7 percent in February and rising monthly. After June 30, unpaid tax goes to the delinquent tax attorney and a collection fee applies.

What is the deadline to protest a Tyler value?

Thirty days from the date on the notice of appraised value, with a May 20 fallback if no notice was generated. Your own deadline is printed on the notice.

Can I sell my Tyler house while a parent's estate is still open?

Only with proper authority. A personal representative can sign after appointment, or a muniment of title or recorded transfer on death deed may apply. A title company will tell you what it needs.

Which sale route suits an Allen homeowner?

An Allen owner has three routes: a brokered listing, a private sale, or a cash purchase. Which one fits depends on how much time and repair work the house can take. Allen lies in southwestern Collin County along U.S. Highway 75, and Census figures put it at 113,447 people in mid-2025.

  • Private sale: you set the price and run the showings, and you also draft the paperwork.
  • Cash purchase: one buyer, a sale in present condition, and a closing date that you choose.

How expensive and how crowded is housing in Allen?

How did Allen grow into the city it is today?

Allen began as a railroad stop. According to the Texas State Historical Association, an agent for the Houston and Texas Central Railway established the town in 1870, and it was named in 1872 for a former Texas attorney general who promoted the line. A post office opened in 1876, and by 1884 the settlement had a school, three churches, a chair factory and a flour mill.

Growth came late. The town had 1,940 residents in 1970 and 8,314 in 1980, a jump the Handbook of Texas ties to the economic growth of Dallas and Plano and the construction of Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport. By 2000 the population had reached 43,554.

That history explains the housing stock. Allen is a commuter city built mostly in the decades after 1970, so most sellers are dealing with homes that are decades old rather than a century old, and the questions that come up at sale are usually roofs, foundations and updates, not historic districts.

Which Allen city rules should a seller or landlord know about?

Allen has recently added a rental program that matters to anyone selling a house that was leased. At its October 13 meeting, the Allen City Council approved an ordinance creating a registration and inspection program for single-family rental properties, covering houses, townhomes and duplexes.

The city is matching ownership and utility billing records to find rentals. If you receive a notice for a house that is not a rental, the notice explains how to contact the city. If the home has been a short-term rental, ask Allen's permitting staff whether a rental permit is on file before you list.

For remodeling and repair permits, Allen's Building and Permitting Division is the first call. Open permits left behind by a prior owner can slow a closing, so ask for the permit history on the address.

Who bills the tax on an Allen house, and what changes at sale?

Collin County's tax assessor-collector sends the bill, and the Collin Central Appraisal District sets the value. Statements are mailed in October, and the county's page advises payment by January 31 to avoid penalties. The Property Tax Office is at 2300 Bloomdale Road, Suite 2324, McKinney, and the county says tax certificates and similar special requests are handled only at the McKinney location.

Exemption paperwork goes to the appraisal district. Its FAQ says the standard homestead form is accepted January 1 through April 30, never before, never by email, and never for a fee. Missing the window is not fatal: the district allows a late filing up to two years after the bill went delinquent.

The district's 2023 table of rates and exemptions listed these entries for Allen city, and the current year's table may differ:

  • Homestead: 5.00% of value, with a $5,000 floor.

  • Disabled person: $25,000.

Older sellers (65 and up) holding a school tax ceiling can carry the ceiling to a replacement Texas home as a percentage, according to Collin CAD. A buyer who moves in files a fresh homestead application of their own.

How is the deed recorded in Collin County?

The Collin County Clerk files Allen deeds. The clerk's land recordings page says to bring an original or a clerk-certified copy that is signed and notarized. It adds that House Bill 4350 led to redactions in parts of the online database, which is not the official repository of real property records.

Under Texas law, a deed has to be acknowledged before a notary or similar officer, or witnessed, before the clerk will record it. Fees vary by document and change over time, so request the current schedule from the clerk.

In most sales the title company orders the tax certificate, pays off mortgages and files the deed. Because a tax lien attaches each January 1, any earlier unpaid year must be cleared for the transfer to be clean.

What if the Allen house is inherited, in foreclosure or rented?

Three situations come up often, and each has a short set of Texas rules.

  • After a death: the court window for offering a will is four years. If nothing needs administering, a muniment of title lets heirs convey after the order and will are recorded with the clerk in the land's home county.
  • Behind on the mortgage: default notices give 20 days to reinstate, and a posted sale notice precedes the auction by 21 days or more.
  • Renters in the house: three days' written notice to vacate is the baseline unless the lease differs, followed by a justice court filing.

Closing before the auction date or before an eviction is finished leaves you more choices than waiting does.

The Collin County Tax Assessor-Collector collects it. The Property Tax Office is in McKinney, and Collin Central Appraisal District sets the value and handles exemptions.

When can I apply for a homestead exemption on an Allen house?

File between January 1 and April 30 with Collin CAD. The district does not accept early or emailed applications and charges no fee, and a late application is allowed up to two years after the taxes become delinquent.

Can I sell an Allen house if property taxes are unpaid?

Yes, but the taxes have to be paid at or before closing. A tax lien attaches on January 1 each year, so the buyer cannot take clear title until the balance is cleared.

What makes a fast house sale in Beaumont, TX different from other Texas cities?

Beaumont is a refinery and port city on the Neches River, and its housing market follows an industrial economy that has swung up and down for more than a century. Owners here often deal with older houses, mixed neighborhoods and a county tax system that runs through a separate appraisal district.

Census estimates put Beaumont at 112,967 people in mid-2025, down 1.8% from the April 2020 estimates base. Buyers have room to shop around, so a seller who arrives with a clear tax statement and a clean deed usually moves faster.

How did oil, rice and shipping shape Beaumont's neighborhoods?

The Handbook of Texas traces the city to a farm settled on the Neches in 1824 and describes a rice and lumber river port by the late 1800s. The Beaumont Rice Mill, founded in 1892, was the first commercial rice mill in Texas.

Then came Spindletop. After the 1901 gusher, the population rose from 9,427 in 1900 to 20,640 in 1910, and refineries and pipelines followed. Three oil companies that became Texaco, Gulf and Exxon formed in the first year of the boom, and a second Spindletop discovery in 1925 brought another burst of building. Houses from those waves still stand, so a Beaumont owner may be selling a property that predates modern code.

  • Seat of Jefferson County, 85 miles east of Houston along Interstate 10
  • One corner of the Golden Triangle with Port Arthur and Orange
  • Lamar University's main campus sits inside city limits
  • The city's two school districts merged in 1983

Which Beaumont landmarks and events appeal to buyers?

The same source lists more than thirty community and neighborhood parks, the Babe Didrikson Zaharias Museum, the McFaddin-Ward House, the Gladys City Boom Town Museum and the Texas Energy Museum. Yearly events include the South Texas State Fair and the Neches River Festival.

The Neches was channelized to Port Arthur in 1908 and deepened by 1916, and shipping and refining stayed central to the local payroll for decades. A seller can point to that employment base when describing the area, and buyers who work at the plants or the port often look at houses close to those jobs.

What do Census figures show about Beaumont housing?

Who collects the tax on a Beaumont house, and when does it go late?

Three offices matter: the Jefferson Central Appraisal District values your house, each taxing unit picks its rate, and the Jefferson County Tax Assessor-Collector takes payment. The district itself says it levies, sets and collects nothing.

Texas values property as of January 1, and the lien for that year attaches the same day. Statements are mailed in October, and the Comptroller says you generally have until January 31 before February 1 delinquency begins. At that point the collector adds a six percent penalty and one percent interest.

  • Request a payoff statement from the tax office before signing a contract
  • Ask whether a prior-year balance sits on the account
  • Keep the receipt for the title company

Which homestead breaks matter to a Beaumont seller or buyer?

A buyer who moves in gets a school district exemption of $140,000, and a buyer who is 65 or disabled gets another $60,000 for school taxes, per the Comptroller. Cities and counties may adopt their own homestead exemptions too.

The Jefferson district's FAQ lists school districts, Jefferson County and the City of Port Arthur as the units that freeze tax for older and disabled owners. Anyone who missed the April 30 filing date can still apply for up to two years after the bill went delinquent, and the district charges nothing to file.

A separate cap holds a homestead's taxable value to a 10% yearly climb. For other real property worth $5,000,000 or less, the district says a 20% circuit breaker covers the 2024 through 2026 tax years and ends before 2027. New rooms or pools sit outside both caps.

What if a Beaumont appraisal looks too high?

Put the dispute in writing by whichever comes later: May 15, or the thirtieth day after the district mailed your notice. Jefferson notices for homes typically go out in mid-April, and an appraiser calls for an informal review ahead of any board hearing.

Losing at the Appraisal Review Board leaves two routes: a lawsuit in district court filed no later than 60 days after you receive the written decision, or binding arbitration, which the district says is open to every residential homestead no matter the value.

  • Bring sales of similar Beaumont houses from near January 1
  • Bring photos of foundation, plumbing or roof problems
  • Bring a survey if the district's measurements look off

How does foreclosure timing work for a Beaumont home?

Most Texas home loans carry a power of sale, so a lender can auction the house without a judge. Auctions happen on a first Tuesday, with bidding open from 10 a.m. until 4 p.m. at the place the commissioners court designates.

After a default notice the owner has 20 days to catch up and halt the process. The notice of sale must then land at least 21 days ahead of the auction, and the State Law Library notes a lender can still sue for a shortfall for two years. Ask the servicer for a payoff letter right away if you hope to sell first.

How do heirs sell an inherited Beaumont house?

When a will exists, it must go to probate within four years of the death, and a muniment of title can work if the only debts are liens on the property. With no will, a small estate affidavit covers estates worth $75,000 or less outside the homestead, but it does not fit other land.

An affidavit of heirship is sworn but not verified by a court, and no law forces a title insurer to accept it. A transfer on death deed skips probate if it was recorded before the owner died. Heirs who stay in the house can ask the appraisal district to extend the homestead exemption across the property by supplying the death certificate and an ownership affidavit.

Can a buyer run a Beaumont house as a short-term rental?

Only with a city permit. Beaumont requires one for any stay shorter than 30 consecutive days, and the permit comes from Planning and Community Development and must be renewed yearly.

The permit number belongs on every online listing, and a hotel occupancy tax certificate is part of the package. Owners who advertise first may be fined, so a buyer with that plan should confirm the process before closing.

Where is the Beaumont deed filed after closing?

The Jefferson County Clerk keeps deed records for land inside the county, and a deed needs a signature plus an acknowledgment to be accepted.

The 2023 clerk manual lists a $5.00 fee for page one and $4.00 for every added page, plus records fees of up to $10 each for management and archives. The appraisal district changes ownership by looking at recorded deeds, which is why a mismatch on the tax roll usually points to a missing recording.

More questions about Beaumont, TX

Does a Beaumont seller pay a state transfer tax?

The Comptroller and county clerk material describes recording fees on a deed and no deed transfer tax. Ask the Jefferson County Clerk for the exact fee schedule before you file.

What date do Beaumont taxes become late?

February 1 is the delinquency date for most bills. Statements arrive in October, and the Comptroller says payment is generally due by January 31.

Is a Beaumont homestead exemption still available if I forgot to file?

Probably. The Jefferson Central Appraisal District accepts a homestead application up to two years after the tax for that year turned delinquent.

Do Beaumont short-term rentals need permits?

Yes. The city requires a permit for stays under 30 consecutive days, a hotel occupancy tax certificate, and the permit number on each listing.

Who hears a protest of a Beaumont appraisal?

The Appraisal Review Board hears it after you file with the Jefferson Central Appraisal District. Your filing limit is the later of May 15 or 30 days after your notice was mailed.

Sugar Land began as plantation land and later became a company town built around sugar. The Handbook of Texas says the area was granted in 1828, a raw-sugar mill started in 1843, and the last sugarcane crop in Fort Bend County was harvested in 1928.

The Imperial Sugar Company and affiliated firms ran daily life until the family that owned the town began selling its businesses, homes and land for development in 1958, with incorporation following in 1959. How did Wichita Falls grow, and how does it affect houses today?

Wichita Falls was platted in July 1876. The arrival of the first train on September 27, 1882 triggered a lot boom, the town became county seat in November 1883 and was incorporated on July 29, 1889. The city adopted the city manager form of government in 1928.

Population swung with the economy: 1,987 residents in 1890, 43,607 in 1930, 55,200 in 1940 and a peak near 110,100 in 1955, then 101,724 in 1960 and 104,197 in 2000. Industry diversification brought Gates Rubber in 1964 and several other plants through the 1970s, though some later left. A large mall in the southwest corner of the city pulled retail away from downtown.

The lakes tell a similar story. Lake Wichita opened around 1901 and became a recreation center with a streetcar line, a pavilion and a boardwalk, and a municipal auditorium followed in 1927. By 1940 the city counted ninety-two miles of paved streets, seventy-seven manufacturing plants and 741 retail stores. Those figures help explain why so many Wichita Falls neighborhoods date from the 1920s through the 1950s.

That history leaves a mix of housing ages, from 1920s oil boom homes to postwar and later houses. Older homes often need updates to wiring, plumbing and foundations, which is where a repair estimate matters most to a buyer.

The April 10, 1979 tornado swept through the southern part of Wichita Falls, destroyed twenty percent of the dwellings in town and injured more than 3,200 people, according to the Texas State Historical Association. Within three years most damage had been repaired.

That event is one reason local building officials care about permits. Water supply is a topic buyers raise in this part of Texas. The primary supply now comes from Lake Arrowhead, built in 1966, after earlier reservoirs including Lake Wichita, Lake Kemp, Lake Diversion and Lake Kickapoo. If a buyer asks about utilities, the city's utility office can answer for a specific address.

The permit notice gives four reasons for a licensed, permitted job: bonded contractors, code compliance, safety inspections and insurance coverage. A homeowner whose roof went in without a permit might find that insurance does not cover damage tied to that work. Seller paperwork that shows a closed permit answers that worry before a buyer raises it, and an invoice from the roofer adds detail.

Any additions, a pool or a roof replacement that happened during your ownership should be matched against permit records. Where a permit was never closed, contact Building Inspections about the steps to resolve it before you list.

The $140,000 school homestead exemption, plus $60,000 more for owners over 65 or disabled, belongs to the owner who qualifies, so they end when you sell. Disabled veterans may qualify for amounts that rise with their disability rating.

The Wichita County Clerk records deeds for property in Wichita Falls. A deed needs a signature and an acknowledgment, and the clerk manual puts the first page at $5.00 with $4.00 for each added page.

Why does San Angelo's history matter to a home seller?

San Angelo serves as the Tom Green County seat, at the meeting of three Concho rivers, and its housing market draws on military, university, medical and ranching employers.

The Handbook of Texas places the town's start in the late 1860s, on the far bank of the North Concho from Fort Concho, a post founded in 1867. The Santa Fe Railroad arrived in 1888, and cattle, sheep, wool and mohair made it a major regional market. Oil from the Permian Basin boom of the 1920s and the 1940 selection of the town for Goodfellow Air Field pushed the population from 10,050 in 1920 to 52,093 by 1950. It stood at 88,439 in 2000.

Water shaped the place too. A flood in 1882 destroyed the courthouse at Ben Ficklin, then the county seat, and voters chose San Angelo as the replacement. The architect who designed the new courthouse stayed and drew about forty downtown buildings, some of which still stand. The Handbook calls Fort Concho one of the best preserved frontier forts in the United States and a National Historic Landmark, which gives the older streets near downtown a tangible anchor in the town's frontier past.

  • Goodfellow began as an air field in 1940 and later became an Air Force intelligence training base.
  • A college opened in 1928 and later became an accredited senior college and then Angelo State University.

What is the quickest way out of a San Angelo house?

A San Angelo owner weighs a brokered listing, a sale by owner and an as-is investor purchase against how fast the money is needed.

A listing with an agent exposes your house to the full market, which helps if the roof, systems and cosmetics are sound. It also brings buyer financing, an appraisal and repair negotiation. For 2026 the district named midnight on May 15 as the protest cutoff for many residential parcels and told owners to confirm the date on their own notice. A protest could be emailed, postmarked, left in the drop box or filed online. Owners of business personal property use a separate email for rendition forms.
