What are the ways to sell a house quickly in Corsicana?

Three paths exist for a Navarro County homeowner: an agent listing, a private sale, or a direct purchase by a cash buyer. Speed, price and effort trade against each other, so decide which of the three you value most before you call anyone.

Pull together the deed, the newest tax statement, the lender payoff and a plain list of defects. With those four items, any buyer can quote you quickly and you can compare quotes on what you would net.

  • Ask which repairs a buyer expects before closing.
  • Ask who pays for the title policy.
  • Ask how many days the quote stays valid.
  • Keep every quote in writing.

How did oil and railroads shape Corsicana's neighborhoods?

Rail came first and oil second. The Handbook of Texas says Corsicana was laid out in 1848 on 100 acres donated by an early settler, and the Houston and Texas Central Railroad arrived in November 1871, with merchants setting up near the depot on East Collin Street.

In 1894 a company drilling for water struck oil and gas instead. The same entry calls it the first significant oil find west of the Mississippi, and reports wells inside city limits by 1896, five that year and fifty-seven the next. A bigger deposit, the Powell field, came in during 1923, and some estimates put the town at 28,000 residents at the height of that rush. The city's own history page adds that 500 wells inside the limits produced 800,000 barrels a year within six years of the first strike.

A 1956 discovery in East Corsicana put roughly 500 wells in the ground within months, nearly one for every backyard in the entry's phrasing. Layered boom periods mean the housing stock mixes pre-1900 lots near downtown with mid-century streets, and buyers will ask about each house's age, wiring and foundation.

Where is Corsicana, and what jobs and roads matter to buyers?

Corsicana is the county seat and largest city of Navarro County, about 58 miles southeast of Dallas where Interstate 45 meets U.S. highways 75 and 287 and State highways 22 and 31. A commute to Dallas along I-45 is a normal selling point.

The Handbook's 1950s list of leading employers includes a hat maker, an iron works, a chili and tamale company, textile plants and the fruitcake bakery founded at the end of the 1800s, which shipped to all fifty states. In 1991 the entry lists oil and gas extraction, meat packing, canning, business forms, furniture and oilfield machinery among leading industries. During World War II a flight training center opened in 1942, and thousands of pilots trained there. Mention proximity to major roads and long-standing local employers when you describe the property, and name the highway access a buyer would use for the daily drive. A buyer comparing small Texas towns will want that detail early, and it costs you nothing to include.

Which Corsicana projects need a city permit?

Structural work does. The city requires a permit to build, alter, enlarge or repair any home or commercial building within the limits, and the building inspector and Planning and Zoning Department review applications.

Registered contractors pull permits. A homeowner may pull a homestead permit for personal work. Fees track job value and appear in Chapter 13 of the city code. Contractor registration costs $110 the first year and $55 after that. The permit holder schedules inspections on the permit page line, weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and calls before 3 p.m. can often be inspected the same day.

What will Corsicana code enforcement look at?

The Community Support Department covers property maintenance, zoning, addressing, fencing and screening, and trash containment. Per its page, staff answer complaints, inspect and write citations. Staff also run the city cemeteries, which hold Woodland, Oakwood and Modrell.

  • Cut tall grass and haul away debris.
  • Repair broken fence sections and screening.
  • Make the house number visible from the street.
  • Store trash carts properly.

Got a notice already? Ask the department what must be corrected and by what date, and hand a copy to the title company.

How do Navarro County taxes figure into a Corsicana sale?

The Navarro Central Appraisal District values all taxable property in the county, and its website shows weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and says the tax assessor sets neither values nor rates.

Per the Comptroller, appraisals are as of January 1, which is also when the year's lien attaches. Delinquency starts after January 31. School districts exempt $140,000 of a homestead, with $60,000 extra for owners 65 or older or disabled. Ask the title company how that year's bill will be split between you and the buyer.

What landmarks and milestones will Corsicana buyers recognize?

The courthouse square anchors the older core. The Handbook of Texas says the first courthouse was a two-room log structure built in 1849, a brick courthouse followed in 1858, and the building in use at the time of the entry opened in 1905. A public school system was organized in 1880, and the city added a fire department, waterworks and a first telephone system during the 1880s.

Population gives a sense of scale. About 5,000 people lived in town in 1885, 9,313 in 1900, 15,202 in 1930 and 24,485 in 2000, per the same entry. The city history page adds that Corsicana adopted its home rule charter in 1917, last amended in May 2007, and that a refinery built in 1898 by a local company became Mobil while another local startup became Texaco.

A seller can use this history in a listing, but a cash buyer will care more about condition and title. Keep a folder with permits, receipts and any old survey.

How do heirs and borrowers in default handle a Corsicana sale?

Heirs may probate a will within four years of death. If there is no will and few assets, a small estate affidavit may work, and a recorded transfer on death deed avoids probate. Ask the Navarro County Clerk what documents it needs.

A borrower in default can still sell. Lenders usually wait until a loan is over 120 days late, give 20 days to cure, then post a sale notice at least 21 days ahead of a first-Tuesday auction. Contact your servicer for a payoff.

More questions about Corsicana, TX

How soon can a Corsicana house close?

Anywhere from a couple of weeks for a cash purchase to a month or more for a financed sale. Payoff letters, title work and any probate step set the floor, so request those documents on day one, before you accept any offer. An open permit or a code notice on the lot can also add days.

Is a permit needed for a fence in Corsicana?

Yes, the city lists fences among permit items, along with accessory buildings, demolition, drive approaches, irrigation systems, signs and moving a structure. Check the permit page or call the inspection line.

Who files the deed after closing in Corsicana?

Your title company normally records it with the Navarro County Clerk. The deed must be signed and acknowledged before a notary or witnesses.

Will a Corsicana buyer inherit last year's tax bill?

The lien attaches January 1 and follows the property, so the title company settles the bill at closing. Delinquent amounts must be cleared for clear title.

Can heirs sell an unprobated Corsicana house?

Often not without a court step. A muniment of title, a small estate affidavit or a recorded transfer on death deed may work. A bare affidavit of heirship may not satisfy a title insurer.

How does a quick sale work for a University Park house?

A quick sale in University Park usually means a buyer with cash, a clear title and a closing date that suits you. With a median home value above $1.8 million, most sales also involve a sizable payoff or an estate or trust as owner, and those details drive the timeline more than the choice of agent.

  • Open-market listing: staging, showings and a buyer's lender to schedule.
  • Private sale: you manage the contract, disclosures and title yourself.
  • Cash sale: no loan approval, with the offer reflecting the work the buyer must do.

Whichever path you pick, order a payoff letter and read the vesting on your deed before you talk price.

Where is University Park and why does it carry that name?

University Park sits five miles north of downtown Dallas in central Dallas County, with Dallas on its north and east and Highland Park to the south. The Handbook of Texas says the two towns are the Park Cities and share the Highland Park Independent School District, headquartered in University Park.

Southern Methodist University opened in 1915 on land donated by Alice Armstrong and W. W. Caruth, Sr., and houses rose around it for faculty and staff. When the university could no longer supply water and sewer lines, Dallas and Highland Park declined to annex the area, so the city incorporated in 1924 with about 1,200 people and moved to a commission form of government in 1926.

Snider Plaza opened in 1927, and Leonard Volk began developing a tract along Turtle Creek that became Volk Estates. A building boom followed World War II.

What do the Park Cities share, and what does University Park run itself?

The Handbook of Texas explains that each of the two Park Cities has its own police and fire departments, while they share the Highland Park Independent School District. University Park, as the more populous of the two, hosts the district headquarters.

The city adopted a master plan process in 1987, and one major recommendation was a public library, which opened in 2001 in rented space in a bank building in Snider Plaza for one dollar a year. A 2011 agreement with The Plaza at Preston Center secured more than 19,000 square feet for a new library, which opened in January 2013. Details like these show a small city that tends its services closely, which is part of why buyers pay attention to the address.

Why can't University Park grow outward?

After the Park Cities turned down a merger with Dallas in 1945, Dallas annexed land around University Park and sealed off expansion, leaving the city at 3.69 square miles. Few vacant lots remained, and Census figures show about 6,858 residents per square mile in 2020.

Almost every sale is therefore an existing house on an established lot, and the land can weigh as heavily in a buyer's mind as the structure. The Park Cities formed their own Water Control and Improvement District in 1947, and a water purification plant, reservoir and pressure tank were completed in 1950.

How has the University Park population changed over time?

The Handbook of Texas lists the city's population at 4,200 in 1930, 14,458 in 1940 and 23,823 in 1950, with an estimated peak of 28,500 in 1956. It stood at 22,259 in 1990 and 24,401 in 2020, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 25,323, only 0.2 percent above the 2020 estimates base.

That near-flat line fits a city with no room to expand. The Handbook adds that as of 2019, with median household income above $200,000 and an average home price of $1.3 million, University Park ranked among the most affluent cities in the nation. It also notes about 640 acres of open space in 2021, covering parks, schools, parkways and lawns, and the city library opened in its current space on January 26, 2013.

What do the Census numbers show about University Park homes?

The 2020-2024 estimates put a typical owned home at $1,861,800, and 83.2 percent of housing units are owner-occupied. Pricing here is mostly a conversation about lot and location.

What do education, income and retail data add?

Census QuickFacts shows 99.0 percent of adults 25 and older with at least a high school diploma and 90.8 percent with a bachelor's degree or higher. Poverty is 4.7 percent, per capita income is $113,291 in 2024 dollars, and 3.5 percent of residents under 65 lack health insurance. About 360 residents are veterans.

Retail sales in 2022 were about $331.8 million, and accommodation and food services sales were about $148.2 million. Median age was 29 in 2010 according to the Handbook, and 65 and older make up 8.6 percent of residents today and 28.9 percent are under 18.

What permit and zoning rules affect a University Park seller?

The city's Community Development Department enforces its building codes, and its guidance says most new construction, remodeling and additions require permits. Since January 1, 2025 every application goes through a mandatory completeness meeting before it enters plan review.

  • By department policy, demolishing more than 50 percent of a structure triggers a full rebuild to current codes, counted as 50 percent exterior walls, 25 percent foundation and 25 percent roof.
  • Nothing may be built over utility easements.
  • Replacing a water heater or adding a hardwired light needs a permit, while painting and wallpapering do not.
  • A permit expires after 60 days if no inspection occurs, and unpermitted work can bring fines or an order to restore the site.

Contractor registrations expire on the same annual date as the state license, and contractor signs are not allowed in residential districts. Construction hours are 7 a.m. to 6 p.m., Monday through Saturday, with no work on Sundays or listed holidays. Permits are issued at the Peek Service Center, 4420 Worcola in Dallas, from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. Call 214-987-5411 to check what a given project needs.

What tax and probate points matter in a University Park sale?

Values and exemption eligibility are set as of January 1, and bills arrive around October 1. On a high-value house the cost of delay is steep, because unpaid tax picks up a six percent penalty and one percent interest on February 1 and the penalty rises to 12 percent by July 1.

If the owner has died, a will can generally be offered for probate within four years. A muniment of title suits an estate with only real-estate liens, and a transfer on death deed must have been recorded before death. An affidavit of heirship carries no court review.

Why is University Park so densely built?

The city covers only 3.69 square miles, and Dallas annexed the land around it after 1945, so it could never expand. Existing houses on established lots make up nearly all sales.

Is a permit needed to swap a water heater in University Park?

Yes. The city says replacing a water heater or adding a permanently wired light fixture requires a permit, while painting and wallpapering do not.

What happens if I demolish part of my University Park house?

City policy says demolishing more than 50 percent of a structure requires a complete rebuild to current codes, measured by walls, foundation and roof.

When can contractors work in University Park?

Construction is permitted from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m., Monday through Saturday, except by special permission, and it is prohibited on Sundays and listed holidays.

Can an inherited University Park house be sold without probate?

Sometimes. A transfer on death deed recorded before the owner's death avoids probate, while other cases use a muniment of title or an executor's deed.

How did Corinth grow from a railroad stop to a commuter suburb?

The Handbook of Texas says the Dallas and Wichita Railway named the community when it built tracks through the townsite in 1880, and Corinth marked its 100th anniversary in 1980. Growth followed development along Interstate 35 between Dallas and Denton in the 1970s.

  • 461 residents in 1970
  • 1,264 in 1980
  • 3,944 in 1990
  • 11,325 in 2000

In the 1980s a few independent farmers remained, though most residents commuted to Lewisville, Denton or Dallas for work. That commuter pattern still defines the market: the city points to the I-35E corridor and rail stations, and its own new resident guide says the population is just over 20,000 with more than 150,000 people within five miles. A house priced for a household that works in Dallas or Denton should highlight drive and train times. Source: Handbook of Texas, Corinth.

Which county handles Corinth property taxes and recording?

Denton County. The deed is recorded with the Denton County clerk, and the appraisal district for Denton County values the house each January 1.

Local taxing units, not the state, issue the bills. The lien for each year's tax is tied to the property from January 1, so title work on a Corinth sale will check for unpaid balances. The clerk's office also keeps liens and foreclosure sale notices for parcels in the county.

Read the Comptroller's property tax basics.

What homestead freeze helps older Corinth owners?

Under the ceiling rule, a school district cannot increase the yearly tax on a qualifying older or disabled owner's homestead beyond what applied when the owner first qualified, except for new improvements. A surviving spouse aged 55 or more can keep it.

The ceiling can follow the owner, in proportion, to a new Texas homestead. Older Corinth owners thinking about downsizing should ask the appraisal district how that transfer works before committing to a purchase elsewhere. The added $60,000 school exemption is a separate benefit.

Details: the Comptroller's tax limitations page and exemptions page.

What are the foreclosure steps if a Corinth owner falls behind?

Most Texas home loans let the lender sell through a power of sale written into the deed of trust. A default notice starts a 20 day window to bring the loan current, and the sale notice follows at least 21 days before the auction.

  • The courthouse door and the clerk's files carry the sale notice.
  • Auctions take place on a set monthly day, with a daytime window.
  • Federal rules generally hold off a foreclosure start until the loan is well past 120 days late.
  • A lender seeking a shortfall has two years after the sale to sue.

A sale ahead of the auction can protect equity and credit. Get a written payoff figure from your servicer and talk to a Texas attorney or HUD-approved counselor about options. Sources: State Law Library before the sale and after the sale.

Which Corinth sellers should consider a cash purchase?

A direct cash purchase tends to suit owners who face a deadline or hold a house a lender would not finance. Examples include an owner behind on the mortgage, an heir living out of state, or a landlord with a vacant rental that needs work.

Judge each offer by what lands in your account, not by the headline figure. Subtract agent fees, repair costs, the months of taxes, insurance and utilities you would carry while waiting, and the closing costs you would absorb. Then compare how many weeks each route is likely to take. Read the written offer for who covers title and recording charges.

  • Is the price firm after the buyer walks through the house?
  • How long is the inspection period, and can the buyer cancel in it?
  • Does the buyer pay for the title policy?
  • What is the target closing date, and can you stay past it if you need time to move?

Written answers to these four questions let you compare a Corinth cash purchase with a listing on equal terms.

How do heirs handle a Corinth house?

Heirs begin by learning how title reads and whether a will exists. Corinth parcels are recorded in Denton County, and a title company decides which order or affidavit it will insure.

If the owner recorded a beneficiary deed before dying, the property can pass without probate. An heir who is not on the recorded deed and wants the homestead exemption gives the appraisal district an ownership affidavit and supporting papers. Collect the original will and a list of every heir first.

Source: State Law Library guide to deeds after death.

What paperwork should a Corinth seller gather first?

Begin with documents a buyer and title agent will ask for: the recorded deed, a recent mortgage statement, the latest property tax statement, any homeowners association papers and receipts for major repairs. Having them ready shortens the gap between acceptance and closing.

  • Photo ID for every owner who will sign.
  • Payoff letter from each lender with a lien.
  • Utility account details for the final meter reading.
  • Keys, garage remotes and gate codes.

Corinth is a compact city of about 8 square miles, and neighbors a few streets apart share the same market, so recent sales on nearby streets are the best guide to pricing. A figure grounded in nearby sales also gives you a way to judge a cash offer.

Yes. The city says it sits in Denton County north of Lake Lewisville. Your deed and tax records are with Denton County offices.

How far is Corinth from Dallas and the airport?

The city lists it about 20 miles north of downtown Dallas. DFW International Airport is 15 miles southwest, roughly a 20 minute drive.

Does Corinth have commuter rail?

Yes. The city says the Denton County Transportation Authority commuter rail passes through with two access points, linking to Denton and downtown Dallas.

Can I sell if I owe more than the house is worth?

Only if the lender agrees in writing to take less than the payoff. Call your servicer before listing.

How do I sell fast in Paris, Texas?

The fastest path is a cash sale to a buyer who takes the house in its present state, with a title company handling the deed and payoffs. A normal listing reaches more people but adds showings, inspections and a lender's schedule.

Paris is the Lamar County seat in Northeast Texas, so the courthouse, the clerk and the appraisal district are all in town. Most paperwork, from the deed to a tax certificate, can be handled close together. Below is what applies here, from the town's past to its tax calendar.

What should a Paris seller know about the town?

Paris is an old town by Texas standards. According to the Texas State Historical Association, George W. Wright donated fifty acres in February 1844, voters made the place the county seat that year, and the Congress of the Republic of Texas incorporated it on February 3, 1845. An employee named Thomas Poteet suggested the name, after Paris, France.

The city sits on U.S. highways 271 and 82 in the middle of Lamar County, between the Red and Sulphur river drainages. Railroads shaped it early: the Texas and Pacific arrived in 1876, with more lines following through 1910. Paris Junior College opened in 1924, and the town has long served as a regional medical and shopping center for Northeast Texas and southeast Oklahoma.

Fires forced rebuilding in 1877 and 1916, and a tornado on April 2, 1982 destroyed more than 1,500 homes. Owners of older houses get asked about roof, wiring and foundation age, and should keep any repair receipts handy.

What drives the Paris economy and housing demand?

Paris has long combined farming, rail, education and manufacturing. The state history handbook describes a cattle and farming center before the Civil War, and later agribusiness with beef and dairy cattle, hay, wheat and soybeans. It also lists factories that included Campbell Soup, Flex-O-Lite and Kimberly-Clark in the early 1990s, so check current employers before assuming those are still open.

Paris Junior College opened in 1924, and the handbook describes a regional medical center that served Northeast Texas and southeast Oklahoma. Two military sites sat in or near the city: the Gaines Boyle Memorial Reserve Center and Camp Maxey National Guard Training Site.

  • Rail lines reached the town between 1876 and 1910.
  • Population reached 25,898 by 2000, per the handbook.
  • Cox Field provided air service to Dallas-Fort Worth in the early 1990s.

A buyer may ask how close a house is to the college, a medical office or a rail line, so note those distances when you describe the property.

Who sets and collects property tax on a Paris house?

The Lamar Central Appraisal District values every parcel in the county, and the taxing units set the rates. Its office is at 521 Bonham Street, and the posted phone line is (903) 785-7822.

The district's protest guide says a written protest is due by May 31 or 30 days from mailing of the appraisal notice, whichever is later. The Comptroller's deadline calendar prints May 15 for most protests, so read the date at the bottom of your own notice. Hearings begin around June 1, and a letter arrives about 15 days before yours.

How does a protest hearing work at Lamar CAD?

Delinquent tax can be handled before or at a sale. Under the Comptroller's rules, a penalty waiver is possible in most cases if the tax is paid within 21 days after the owner learns of the delinquency and a written request is filed before day 181 after the delinquency date.

Some collectors offer delinquent-tax payment plans of up to 36 months, and a residence homestead qualifies for one. Homestead values also face a 10 percent yearly cap that begins the year after the exemption is first granted.

  • A taxing unit's private attorney may add up to 20 percent.

What payment options and caps apply to Paris homeowners behind on taxes?

An heir needs proof of ownership before a buyer will close, and the paperwork depends on the estate. Wills generally must be probated within four years of death, with the filing made in the court of the county where the decedent lived.

  • Muniment of title. A court order plus the will, filed with the clerk where the property sits.
  • Small estate affidavit. For estates under the $75,000 cap, homestead excluded, with no will and all heirs agreeing.
  • Affidavit of heirship. A sworn statement that third parties are not required to accept.

The State Law Library probate guide covers each route. Ownership papers go to the Lamar County clerk.

How does probate work for an inherited Paris house?

An heir needs proof of ownership before a buyer will close, and the right paperwork depends on the estate. A will is generally probated within four years of death, and the case is filed with the probate court, usually where the decedent lived.

  • Small estate affidavit. For estates under the $75,000 cap, homestead excluded, with no will, and all heirs agreeing.
  • Affidavit of heirship. A sworn statement that no law makes third parties accept.

The State Law Library probate guide sets out each route. Ownership papers go to the Lamar County clerk.

What did the 1982 tornado and earlier fires change?

They changed the housing stock and the way buyers think. The state history handbook says fires hit Paris in 1877 and 1916, and the April 2, 1982 tornado destroyed more than 1,500 homes and left 3,000 people homeless. Downtown businesses then put nearly $7 million into renovation through the early 1990s.

A seller of an older house can answer buyer questions faster with records in hand. Keep roofing invoices, electrical permits and insurance claims where you can find them, and disclose any known damage plainly in the contract.

Begin with the deed and the newest tax statement, then add the lender's payoff contact and any lease. A title company will ask for the same items.

Typically. No lender appraisal is needed and few repair requests follow, so the title search and your calendar set the pace. Listing can bring more money if you can wait.

It becomes easy once ownership is documented, which may mean a probated will, a small estate affidavit or an affidavit of heirship at the Lamar County clerk.

Which selling paths suit a Horizon City owner?

Use a broker, sell privately, or take cash. Census data shows owners in 85.2% of Horizon City homes, so most sellers are families giving up a house they have lived in.

Lean toward cash when you need a firm closing day or hate the idea of paying for repairs. Pick a listing if the house is in good order and a buyer's loan timeline does not bother you. Whichever you pick, do the same prep first.

  • Gather your deed, the newest tax statement and any utility district bills.

Where is Horizon City and how was it built?

The town's comprehensive plan places Horizon City on the Hueco Bolson about 15 miles east of El Paso, with the Franklin Mountains to the west and Mexico roughly 20 miles south. The plan gives 4,022 feet of elevation, about 7.77 inches of annual rain, and a July average high of 94 degrees Fahrenheit.

According to that plan, a Chicago-based developer announced the project in December 1959, and a planning outfit from Tucson laid the town out beside the proposed Interstate 10 route. The first house sold on October 31, 1962, and by 1971 only about 94 homes were occupied. Horizon City incorporated on August 13, 1988, and voters adopted a charter in November 1997. It is a home rule city with a mayor and seven council members.

Desert sun and dry air are tough on roofs, stucco and paint, and inspectors check cooling equipment closely. Handle cheap repairs before showing the house, or price in the ones you leave.

What do the numbers say about Horizon City homes?

QuickFacts puts the midpoint home value at $170,200 for 2020 to 2024, and the 2025 head count of 25,118 sits 11.8% over the 2020 base of 22,461. Steady growth keeps new subdivisions coming, so your house competes with new construction.

Who is buying in Horizon City, and what do they want?

Horizon City skews young. Children make up 33.7% of residents and seniors just 5.5%, per QuickFacts, and 92.5% of people kept the same address for a year, which points to settled families. Larger households tend to look for extra bedrooms, a yard and an easy run to Interstate 10.

Language plays a part as well. 73.5% of residents speak something other than English at home, and 23.2% were born abroad. If a family member who reads Spanish will help you with the sale, ask the buyer to give you the contract and disclosures in a form you can read before you sign.

Median household income is $65,737, and the poverty rate is 22.0%. A clean, working house with a documented repair history will draw more interest than one with open questions.

Does the town have rules for building and land use?

Yes. Per the comprehensive plan, a Planning and Zoning Commission and a Board of Adjustment advise the council on zoning and other development matters. If you added a room, fence, carport or pool, ask town hall whether it was permitted, because lenders and title companies sometimes ask.

The plan also notes that the town has about 5.7 square miles within its limits as of 2011, while QuickFacts counts 8.71 square miles of land in 2020, so ask the town for the current boundary. If your lot is near the edge, confirm whether it sits inside the town or in the county, since that decides who issues permits and provides services.

The same plan suggests studying bike routes, sidewalks and street lighting on principal streets such as Darrington Road and Eastlake Boulevard. Buyers who care about traffic and walkability may ask about plans for the street your house faces.

Which schools and offices matter to a Horizon City seller?

The plan names the Socorro and Clint school districts and the Horizon Regional Municipal Utility District among local agencies. Buyers ask which district serves a home, so confirm it on your tax bill.

El Paso County's Central Appraisal District appraises every parcel of real property and business personal property inside the county. Its home page links to protests and appeals, exemption forms, a deadline calendar and a taxpayer liaison who helps with complaints about the review board. Check that calendar for the protest date that applies to you.

How are deeds recorded in El Paso County and what does it cost?

The El Paso County Clerk records deeds. A land deed is accepted for filing only after the signer acknowledges it before a notary or comparable officer, or two witnesses swear to it.

In the 2023 clerk manual from Texas Courts, page one costs $5.00, every added page $4.00, and each indexed name past five adds $0.25. It also lists records fees, such as $2.00 for technology and up to $10 each for management and archive. A missing grantee address can add $25. Fees change, so check the clerk's current schedule.

A title company normally files the deed for you. Filing happens in the county containing the land, which for a Horizon City house is El Paso County. The manual mentions no transfer tax. A settlement statement from your title company will itemize every charge on your side.

What does an unpaid tax bill mean for a sale?

Each year's tax lien fastens to the land on January 1 and stays with the land through a sale. The Comptroller adds that a court can order the property sold even after a transfer, which is why clear title waits on delinquent taxes.

A bill left open past January 31 is late, and charges start accruing February 1. Should the house be auctioned for taxes, an opinion of the Texas Supreme Court explains the buy-back right. Homestead, farm and mineral land gets two years from the filing of the purchaser's deed, at a 25 percent markup in the first year and 50 percent in the second. Other land gets 180 days. Any surplus from a tax sale can be claimed by the former owner for two years, according to the State Law Library.

If you are behind, selling before a suit saves court costs. Get a payoff figure from the tax office, and ask about an installment plan, which some collectors grant on a residence homestead.

About 25,118, per the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate, an 11.8% gain on the 2020 base.

The county clerk manual lists recording fees and says nothing of a transfer tax. Ask your title company for the full settlement statement.

Can I sell with back taxes owed?

Yes, provided the balance is cleared by closing, because the lien stays with the house. The county tax office can issue a payoff statement.

The El Paso Central Appraisal District. Use its calendar for protest dates and its taxpayer liaison if you have a complaint.
